text:
DID YOU KNOW??

Robert Downey Jr.’s iconic tinted sunglasses are actually tinted prescription lenses designed to conceal his active eye contact during improvised acting scenes, and he loved them so much that he made his custom tinted eyewear an official contract requirement for Tony Stark in the Marvel Cinematic Universe!

​Long before playing Tony Stark, Downey Jr. began wearing lightly tinted, warm-colored glasses (often in rose, amber, or yellow hues) during filming and public appearances.

Initially, the light tint was practical: it allowed him to wear his needed vision prescription under bright movie studio lights without causing harsh reflections on camera, while subtle color gradients prevented audience eye-tracking distraction when he improvised lines or shifted his gaze off-camera.

​When he was cast in Iron Man (2008), Downey brought his personal affinity for custom-tinted frames directly into the character's wardrobe. Marvel worked with high-end optical designers like Matsuda and DITA to craft Tony Stark's signature eyewear, most famously the DITA Flight.006 frames featured in Avengers: Infinity War and Spider-Man: Far From Home (which double as the interface for EDITH).

The glasses became so synonymous with both the actor and the character that custom tinted lenses are now a signature trademark of Downey's personal style on every red carpet.

​The Functional & Cinematic Role of RDJ's Tinted Glasses:
​
1. On-Camera Lighting Control:
Bright studio light grids can cause pupil contraction and glare. Lightly tinted amber or rose gradient lenses reduce eye strain on set while allowing camera operators to still capture his full eye performance through the glass.

2. Concealing Rapid Eye Movements:
Downey is famous for extensive dialogue improvisation. Gradient tints obscure subtle eye movements when checking off-camera prompt notes or cue cards, keeping his onscreen character looking razor-sharp and focused.

3. Defining Tony Stark's Billionaire Persona:
In Iron Man, director Jon Favreau and Downey used high-end Japanese titanium frames to visually signal Stark's eccentric tech-billionaire wealth, blending high fashion with industrial design.

4. Turning Eyewear into MCU Plot Devices:
By Avengers: Infinity War, Stark's glasses evolved beyond fashion into the physical housing for the EDITH augmented-reality tactical defense network, making the eyewear central to the plot of Spider-Man: Far From Home.

More Surprising Facts About Robert Downey Jr. & MCU Wardrobe:

A. ​The Burger King Turning Point: Downey famously credits a disgusting Burger King meal in 2003 with helping him get clean from drug addiction. While driving a car loaded with drugs, he stopped for a burger that tasted so terrible it made him reconsider his life, leading him to throw all his drugs into the ocean and enter rehab. He paid homage to this moment in Iron Man when Tony Stark requests a cheeseburger from Burger King immediately upon returning from captivity.

B. ​Hiding Food on the Iron Man Set: Downey frequently hid real food and snacks all over the set of The Avengers (2012) because he got hungry during long shooting days. The scene where Tony Stark casually offers Bruce Banner (Mark Ruffalo) a blueberry on the Helicarrier was completely unscripted, Downey simply pulled out a bag of his own hidden snacks mid-take.

C. ​The Custom DITA Craze: After Downey wore the custom DITA Flight.006 frames in Infinity War, the independent luxury optical brand experienced unprecedented demand, with waiting lists extending for over a year for that specific color combination.

​SUMMARILY! 
​Robert Downey Jr. transformed a practical requirement for tinted prescription lenses into a defining personal style mark, seamlessly weaving his real-life custom eyewear into Tony Stark's iconic Marvel wardrobe.

Hopefully you've learnt something new today?

text:
The most famous sunglasses in movie history exist because Robert Downey Jr. needed somewhere to hide his eyes while reading cue cards.

The Jericho missile speech in Iron Man, the "is it better to be feared or respected" scene, was still being written the day they shot it. RDJ and Jon Favreau wanted the lines to feel invented on the spot, so the speech went on cards next to the camera. The sunglasses went on so the camera couldn't catch him reading.

Then Marvel kept the fix.

Across 9 films and 11 years, Tony Stark wore dozens of different frames, everything from Ray-Bans to handmade Japanese titanium from Matsuda, and costume designers turned an actor's workaround into the character's signature. By Age of Ultron the shades had tech in them. By Endgame they were how Tony recorded his goodbye.

And then the writers went one further. Spider-Man: Far From Home built its entire plot around who inherits Tony's glasses. The villain's whole scheme is stealing them.

Marvel wrote a $1.1 billion movie around a prop that existed because an actor didn't have time to memorize his lines.

text:
We recorded 24 podcast episodes this year 🎥

The results are impressive!

– 600K eyeballs on X & LinkedIn
– 50K Long form YouTube views
– 11K audio downloads

Here’s everything I’ve learned 👇

1. Set realistic goals.

The YouTube benchmarks for top podcast in our niche (Tech/Startup) is ~30K views per episode for My First Million and ~10k for 20VC.

These are established names with years of work behind them.

If you’re getting 1K views, you’re already at 10% of that 10K benchmark.

That’s worth keeping in perspective.

2. Not all views are equal.

For us, 10,000 VCs and founders listening can be worth more than 100,000 people outside our target audience.

Our videos about app ideas and making $1M got good traction. Those topics appeal to a lot of people.

But videos about growing a business to $50M in revenue interest fewer people.

But those are the people we want to reach.

Chasing views would mean making different content and making it less useful to our audience.

3. Don’t overlook 1,000 true fans.

Imagine 1,000 people listening every week.

– They love what you do.
– They feel like they know you.
– They understand how you think.

That’s incredibly valuable, especially when you’re starting a podcast.

Realistically, I think building that audience can take two years. Maybe more. It’s still a goal worth working towards.

4. Putting in the reps is everything.

Our first 10 episodes sucked.
The next 10 were much better.

Now it finally feels like it’s working.

I suspect a lot of people give up around episode seven, before they’ve given themselves a chance to get good.

Building a company, a podcast or an Instagram following takes significant work over time...

Very few people are willing to keep going for long enough.

5. The depth of the relationship is the real value.

Someone spending 30–60 minutes with you every week gets to know you in a way that’s hard to replicate elsewhere.

I think podcasting is one of the most powerful communication channels you can own.

I’ve noticed:

– Enterprise customers who discovered us through the pod
– $10K–$20K in attributed MRR across my socials
– More engagement on X & LinkedIn
– A stronger personal brand

For me, that ongoing, direct relationship is worth more than a once-a-year feature in TechCrunch, the Sunday Times or the Financial Times.

But you have to put in the work to build that distribution.

6. YouTube comes first.

For us, YouTube offers the best discoverability, and video makes the conversation more engaging.

If there’s one arena I want to compete in, it’s YouTube. The audio podcast comes second.

That changes how we think about what we make and how we present it.

7. Give it years.

Look at Lenny’s Podcast, My First Million, 20VC and All-In.

It’s easy to see the audiences they have today and underestimate the years of work behind them.

The lesson I take from them: plan for gradual growth.

8. Packaging matters way more than you think.

It’s all connected:

– Your title
– Your thumbnail
– Your content
– How it’s scripted, edited and put together

You can turn up with a friend and shoot the shit for an hour.

But growing that is going to be difficult.

You need to learn how to write a title people want to click, create a thumbnail that catches their attention and deliver an opening 30 seconds that makes them want to stay.

This has been one of our biggest lessons.

We’ve still got a long way to go.

9. Recording is only part of the job.

Now we spend more time:

– Planning episodes
– Working on packaging
– Reviewing topics and scripts
– Thinking about guests
– Contacting guests

…than we do actually recording.

Now, I’m more convinced than ever that this is worth building.

We’ll keep recording.

And I’ll keep sharing what we learn.

text:
UK Constitutional Fragmentation: Devolved Referendum Demands and Westminster Authority - The coordinated mobilization of the first ministers of Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland in Cardiff establishes an unprecedented institutional alignment among the devolved administrations, yet Westminster retains exclusive constitutional power under the domestic legal framework. While the joint memorandum demands simultaneous consultative pathways toward national self-determination and eventual European Union integration, the United Kingdom Supreme Court has formally closed unilateral legislative avenues for consultative referendums absent primary Westminster consent. In Northern Ireland, the statutory trigger for a border poll remains vested exclusively in the discretionary judgment of the Secretary of State under the Northern Ireland Act 1998, requiring empirical evidence of a shifting demographic majority that current electoral tallies do not definitively substantiate. Consequently, the Cardiff summit operates primarily as a strategic political lever designed to destabilize the central government’s fiscal and legislative baseline, setting up a structural crisis between regional democratic mandates and imperial-style parliamentary sovereignty.

The Celtic Front Confronts the Hard Edge of Westminster Law and European Treaty Realities
The coordinated declaration signed in Cardiff on September 14, 2026, by Scottish First Minister John Swinney, Welsh First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth, and Northern Ireland First Minister Michelle O’Neill establishes an unprecedented peripheral political front, but its strategic objective—a coordinated exit from the United Kingdom into the European Union—collapses under the statutory architecture of British constitutional law and the fiscal criteria of European primary treaties. While the leaders demand simultaneous referendums, the Supreme Court of the United Kingdom has closed the domestic legal avenues for consultative plebiscites, and the Secretary of State for Northern Ireland retains unchallengeable statutory discretion over a border poll. Compounding this domestic impasse, the European Union offers not a unified entrance, but an asymmetric re-entry: automatic territorial absorption for Northern Ireland via an Irish reunification treaty, contrasted with a rigorous, multi-year third-country accession process under Article 49 of the Treaty on European Union for Scotland and Wales that would enforce hard customs borders with England and expose unsustainable structural budget deficits.

The Supreme Court Firewall Neutralizes Devolved Legislative Levers
The Cardiff memorandum’s demand for unilateral plebiscites ignores the definitive legal baseline established on November 23, 2022, when the Supreme Court of the United Kingdom ruled unanimously in Reference by the Lord Advocate that the Scottish Parliament lacks the legislative competence to organize an independence referendum. The court determined that any consultative referendum bill relates to the Union of the Kingdoms and the Parliament of the United Kingdom, matters explicitly reserved to Westminster under Schedule 5, Part I of the Scotland Act 1998. This determination stripped Holyrood of the ability to deploy advisory ballots as constitutional leverage, establishing that without an Order in Council granted under Section 30 of the Scotland Act 1998 or primary legislation from Westminster, any regional legislative instrument remains ultra vires and legally void.

In Wales, the statutory reservation is even more rigid under Schedule 7A of the Government of Wales Act 2006, as amended by the Wales Act 2017, which explicitly reserves the single legal jurisdiction of England and Wales and the Union to the Parliament of the United Kingdom. First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth operates without an autonomous superior court structure or devolved judicial hierarchy, leaving Plaid Cymru without the institutional machinery to mount a domestic jurisdictional dispute against London. Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s September 9 statement to the House of Commons—insisting that Section 30 orders will not be issued absent sustained empirical shifts in public opinion—relies on an impenetrable domestic legal perimeter that neutralizes devolved parliamentary majorities.

Schedule 1 Discretion Insulates the Northern Ireland Border Trigger
Michelle O’Neill’s alignment with Edinburgh and Cardiff attempts to present the Northern Ireland border poll as an operative regional trigger, but Schedule 1 of the Northern Ireland Act 1998 vests that power exclusively in the hands of the Secretary of State for Northern Ireland. While Section 1 of the 1998 Act codifies the principle of consent, the statutory duty under Schedule 1, paragraph 2 requires the Secretary of State to convene a poll only if it appears likely that a majority of voters would choose to cease being part of the United Kingdom. In Re McCord (June 2018), the High Court of Northern Ireland established that the Secretary of State retains broad political discretion in evaluating that likelihood, insulated from arbitrary judicial review and under no obligation to treat regional assembly seat totals or volatile opinion surveys as binding legal thresholds.

Furthermore, operationalizing Irish reunification demands simultaneous referendums under the Good Friday Agreement, requiring a concurrent constitutional referendum in the Republic of Ireland to amend Bunreacht na hÉireann under its December 1937 provisions. The diplomatic presence of Irish opposition leader Mary Lou McDonald alongside Michelle O’Neill underscores Sinn Féin’s push to bypass the Northern Ireland Office, but Dublin’s domestic coalition remains constrained by the immense fiscal burden of absorbing six northern counties heavily dependent on central government block grants. Donald Trump’s public intervention in Dublin may destabilize diplomatic channels, but it exerts zero legal force over the statutory prerogatives granted to the British executive by the Parliament of the United Kingdom.

European Treaty Asymmetry Fractures the Tripartite Strategy
The Cardiff memorandum pledges unified re-entry into the European Union, yet European primary law treats the three territories through divergent legal regimes. Northern Ireland possesses an automatic path: the European Council conclusions of April 29, 2017, confirmed that upon a certified democratic vote for reunification under the Good Friday Agreement, the territory of Northern Ireland will be incorporated into the European Union as an integral part of an existing member state, applying the EU treaties immediately under the precedent of German reunification in 1990 without triggering candidate screening or Article 49 negotiations.

Conversely, Scotland and Wales must apply as third-country applicants under Article 49 of the Treaty on European Union, requiring unanimous approval from all 27 EU member states simply to initiate negotiations across 33 acquis chapters. Member states confronting domestic secessionist movements—including Spain, Cyprus, and Romania—will enforce strict accession compliance to avoid legitimizing sub-state fragmentation. Moreover, under Article 140 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, candidate states must commit to adopting the euro, eliminating the prospect of retaining the pound sterling within an official currency union or securing the bespoke opt-outs negotiated by the United Kingdom in the 1992 Maastricht Treaty.

Internal Market Realities Demand Border Checkpoints along the Tweed and the Severn
The economic consequence of Scottish and Welsh membership in the EU Single Market and Customs Union is the immediate imposition of an external commercial frontier against England under the Union Customs Code (Regulation No 952/2013). Because England would remain an external third country outside the European regulatory framework, the European Union would mandate physical Border Control Posts along the Anglo-Scottish border and the Severn-Marches corridor to conduct documentary, identity, and physical sanitary and phytosanitary inspections on agricultural, chemical, and manufactured goods.

This regulatory separation would disrupt the United Kingdom’s internal market, which absorbs roughly 60% of total Scottish goods exports—three times the volume exported to the entire European Union according to official economic accounts. In Wales, where industrial supply chains along the M4 corridor, the A55 expressway, and the Deeside industrial zone are physically integrated with English manufacturing centers, customs verifications and rules-of-origin documentation would impose systemic friction on the dominant destination for Welsh trade. The Windsor Framework’s maritime solution for the Irish Sea cannot be replicated across the land corridors of the Scottish Borders or the Welsh Marches without severing domestic supply chains.

The historical Common Travel Area (CTA), preserved under the 2020 UK-EU Withdrawal Agreement, would also encounter severe friction. If Scotland and Wales accept the free movement of European Union citizens as required by EU law while England maintains restrictive third-country immigration controls, Westminster would be forced to impose identity checks and migration surveillance on internal transport arteries. The open mobility historically protected by the Immigration Act 1971 would dissolve into border enforcement, ending the unrestricted domestic labor market across Great Britain.

The Macroeconomic Reality of Sub-State Fiscal Deficits
The most immediate domestic barrier to European integration is the fiscal criteria enforced by the European Commission under the Stability and Growth Pact. Article 126 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union mandates an annual general government budget deficit ceiling of 3% of Gross Domestic Product and a gross debt-to-GDP ratio capped at 60%. The devolved nations operate with structural deficits that diverge sharply from these limits, subsidized by central government block grant transfers administered through the Barnett formula.

According to the Scottish Government’s Government Expenditure and Revenue Scotland (GERS) audit published in August 2024, Scotland’s net fiscal deficit for the 2023–24 fiscal year was £22.7 billion, representing -10.4% of Scottish GDP even after allocating a geographic share of North Sea oil and gas revenue. In Wales, independent fiscal audits from the Wales Governance Centre establish a structural deficit between -15.0% and -18.0% of Welsh GDP, driven by an older demographic profile, lower average wages, and elevated public sector employment. Northern Ireland operates with an estimated net deficit between -18.0% and -20.0% of GDP, reliant on central subventions.

Bridging these deficits to comply with Chapter 17 of the EU acquis would force an independent Scottish or Welsh administration to implement immediate public spending austerity or sharp tax increases. Furthermore, launching an autonomous national currency to replace sterling would expose Edinburgh and Cardiff to debt risk premiums and currency depreciation, while an uncoordinated policy of sterlingization would deprive both administrations of a central bank lender of last resort, destabilizing the domestic banking sector during the accession process.

The 24-Month Calculation: The Cost of Institutional Impasse
Over the next 12 to 24 months, the Cardiff pact will yield diminishing political returns as it confronts the structural reality of the British state. Prime Minister Andy Burnham will use the 2022 Supreme Court precedent and the statutory discretion in Schedule 1 of the Northern Ireland Act 1998 to refuse Section 30 orders and border poll triggers, avoiding direct political concessions while pointing to fiscal imbalances as proof of peripheral vulnerability.

The costs of this prolonged impasse will fall on the devolved administrations and their domestic economies. Protracted constitutional disputes will depress capital investment across peripheral renewable energy, manufacturing, and logistics hubs, as investors face the prospect of customs friction along the Tweed and Severn. The first ministers have assembled a coordinated political front at St David’s Hotel, but absent the statutory authority to bypass Westminster or the fiscal strength to satisfy Brussels, their memorandum remains an exercise in political friction that cannot escape the legal and macroeconomic framework of the British state. - https://t.co/m5AdjxQ24a via @https://debuglies.com

text:
Questions readers of Alejandro's Journey keep asking me

1. The September 21 campaign opens on the first page as a man deciding whether his children will inherit a country or a warning. What did you want the reader to feel in that opening—and is that decision Alejandro's, Juan's, or yours as the writer looking back?

I wanted the reader to feel the weight of an inheritance that is not money. On that first page, a man is not choosing a candidate so much as choosing what kind of country his children will wake up in: a place that still remembers how freedom is lost, or a place that treats liberty as weather—something that arrives on its own. That decision is Alejandro's in the story. It is also Juan's, spoken from the wall on October 22, 1960, when his last words were not a private goodbye but a public claim: Viva Cuba Libre. And it is mine, looking back after the last page was written. I did not want a soft opening. I wanted the citizen who still lives in a free country to feel, in the first paragraphs, that freedom is perishable and that the United States is the last shining city on earth only if someone keeps the lamp lit. The campaign is the surface. The real question is whether the next generation inherits a nation or a cautionary tale.

2. You chose historical fiction rather than a straight memoir. In the book's own terms: this is not a memoir pretending to be a novel; it's an invented life built to carry a real century. What could Alejandro Ramirez do on the page that Gerardo Fundora could not do in first person—and what did you refuse to invent?

Alejandro Ramirez could walk into the political life of the United States and, through that work, keep trying to serve the hope of a free Cuba. Gerardo Fundora could not. After my father's execution, I made a promise to my mother that I would not enter that world, and I kept it. Fiction let me give another man the road I would not take in my own name. Alejandro could engage parties, campaigns, and the public fight without breaking a vow spoken in a widow's house. I could not put myself in those rooms and still honor her.

What I refused to invent was the ground under that difference. I would not invent a softer Cuba, a quieter firing squad, or a mother who asked less of her son. I would not invent an America that required no work of the man who arrived. The century is real: the regime, the boat, the first paycheck, the faith that had to be practiced when the state had already named you. The invented life is only the vessel. Alejandro could do on the page what a promise forbade me to do in first person. Everything else I owed to the dead, and to her, I left true.

3. Work in this story is not a subplot. It is how a man proves he still owns his hours after a regime tried to own them. Which job, paycheck, or first American workday is the scene where that dignity actually returns to Alejandro's body—not as an idea, but as a feeling?

Dignity does not return as a speech. It returns in the body when a man is paid for hours that belong to him. For Alejandro it is not the later empire; it is the first American workday when the check is his, the clock is his, and no committee has assigned him a quota or a political label before he is allowed to lift something. In Cuba the regime tried to own the hours. In America the hours can be owned again—if he will take them. I wrote his rise in business not as a rags-to-riches fantasy but as proof: with a plan, vision, hard work, and perseverance, a man can rebuild what a state tried to confiscate. The feeling I wanted on the page is physical—shoulders dropping, breath lengthening—because work, for an exile, is not ambition first. It is the return of the self.

4. His children will speak English without an accent: victory and grief in the same sentence. How does Alejandro live that split with Isabella and the daughters—what does he insist they keep in Spanish at the table, and what does he refuse to make them carry?

He lives it as a man who won the future and lost the sound of home in the same generation. English without an accent is victory: they will not be marked at the schoolhouse door. It is also grief: the island will not live in their mouths the way it lives in his. At the table he insists on Spanish for the things that cannot be translated cheaply—prayers, the names of the dead, the stories of Juan and Sofia, the taste of a country that no longer exists as they knew it. He will not let the language die between the soup and the coffee. What he refuses to make them carry is the full weight of the surveillance, the firing squad, the habit of scanning a room for informants. That burden is his. He wants them fluent in America and fluent in memory, not fluent in fear. Isabella is the hinge: she keeps the table from becoming either a museum or an erasure. The daughters inherit the country. He tries not to make them inherit the wound as a daily assignment.

5. Arrival is not the happy ending. Arrival is the first unpaid hour in a language that does not yet belong to you. After the lights of Miami and the Tamiami Hotel, what was the smallest, least cinematic humiliation or confusion that taught Alejandro America would have to be built, not received?

The lights of Miami and the Tamiami Hotel look like deliverance. They are not. The lesson comes in a small confusion: a form he cannot read, a word he mispronounces, a clerk who does not slow down, a job that pays less than the pride it costs to ask for it. I wanted that scene to be un-cinematic on purpose. Expectations are detrimental to growth. As in my own life, Alejandro must hold himself accountable and expect nothing from anyone but his own efforts. America is not a prize handed to the man who survived the Straits. It is a country that must be built hour by hour, in a language that does not yet belong to him. The smallest humiliation is the teacher. The lights are only the invitation.

6. Tyranny in the early chapters often arrives as a neighbor who stops looking you in the eye. How does that quiet theft follow him into Little Havana—into who he trusts, who he hires, who he lets near his children—and when, if ever, does he stop scanning a room for informants?

The revolution created an ambiance in which no one was safe from the government's surveillance. That does not stay on the island. It follows him into Little Havana as a habit of the eyes. He measures who he trusts, who he hires, who he lets near his children by a question the free-born never have to ask: will this person look away when the state arrives? The quiet theft is not only property; it is the neighbor's gaze. He never fully stops scanning a room. What changes is what he does with the scan. Early on it is survival. Later it is stewardship—of a business, a dojo, a school, a family. Vigilance born of Cuba does not vanish because the passport is American. It is converted, if he is lucky, from fear into care.

7. Some books ask what freedom means. This one asks what it costs, and who pays the first installment. Who pays that installment in Alejandro's life that readers tend to miss—Sofia, Isabella, the daughters, the men who never got on the boat—and how does he try to settle the debt through the dojo and the Hope Schools?

Readers see Alejandro's rise and miss the invoices that never appear in his ledger. Sofia pays the first installment: widowhood, the boat, the years of work in a language that is not hers. Isabella pays in the split life of the table—English for the children's future, Spanish for the dead. The daughters pay in a heritage they can taste but cannot fully inhabit, and in family they will never see again. The men who never got on the boat pay with the lives that stayed behind. Missing from any success story is what the exile family loses of Cuba itself. The dojo and the Hope Schools are how Alejandro tries to settle a debt he cannot actually close. They are not monuments to him. They are a way to give the next generation what the regime tried to confiscate: the knowledge that this land offers freedom and opportunity, and that those things are taught, practiced, and passed on—not inherited like furniture.

8. Miami is not scenery. It is the first city where a man can fail in public and still get back up without asking a committee. What failure in Alejandro's American years—school, business, language, belonging—mattered more to his later success than any early win, and why did you want that failure on the page?

The failure that matters is not a bankruptcy scene. It is the early discrimination, the closed door, the accent that costs him a hearing, the moment Miami reminds him he is still a guest. I put that on the page because a man who only wins teaches the reader nothing about America. Miami is the first city where he can fail in public and stand up without a committee's permission. What I wanted beside that failure was his refusal to let it become the plot. He blocks out the distraction and keeps the goal. The early wound does not get to write the ending. That is the American lesson I would not soften: belonging is not granted by the first kind stranger. It is built after the first public stumble.

9. The story runs into the mid-2020s and closes on a long life that still treats liberty as a ledger that must be remembered, or it is lost. Standing at that ending—family around him, Cuba still unfinished—is Alejandro more guardian than fighter by then? What would he tell a grandchild who never saw the island, and what would he tell a young American who thinks the struggle is over?

By the end, he is both, but the fighter has learned to stand watch. Family is around him. Cuba is still unfinished. To a grandchild who never saw the island, he would not offer nostalgia as a souvenir. He would offer names, a language at the table, and the sentence Juan left in the air: truth is a weapon, hold it tight. To a young American who thinks the struggle is over, he would say what I would say: beware of false prophets. Utopias are not of this world. Everyone's life and well-being is each one's responsibility. God's gift is free will, and everyone's choices determine the life one lives. Liberty is a ledger. If it is not remembered, it is lost. The shining city does not keep itself.

LCX has launched LCX Liberty DEX at https://t.co/W5Scxvmq0O, a non-custodial trading aggregator that prices assets by reading liquidity directly from the blockchains it trades on, moves value between any two supported chains in a single flow, and offers a multi-chain portfolio that opens on a wallet address alone. It is the first product in the LCX Liberty DeFi line to go live in full; LCX Liberty Chain, for bringing real-world assets on-chain, remains on testnet with its explorer.

The design choice is that LCX reads the chains itself rather than passing on prices from a paid vendor. It watches pools across every supported chain, holds more than 400,000 pools and 400,000 tokens across 40+ venues in memory, and prices on the spot. Routes are ranked by what reaches the user's wallet after gas rather than headline output, and larger orders are split across venues. There is no platform fee: users pay network gas and pool fees, nothing to LCX. The company says the swap is free because the engine underneath is the product, sold to builders as an API, SDK, embeddable widget and live MCP server.

Swaps run today on Ethereum, Base, Arbitrum One and OP Mainnet, with chains addable without changing how the product works. A cross-chain swap is quoted as one route and executed as one flow: a swap on the source chain, a cross-chain leg over Across where relayers fill in an expected one to three seconds, and a swap on the destination chain. LCX frames this against the usual bridge, wait, then trade again pattern, which leaves users holding an asset through a gap they did not ask for.

text:
IF 90% OF JUDGES WERE CORRUPT, INDIA’S JUDICIAL SYSTEM WOULD COLLAPSE

🔥 “More than 90% of lower-court judges are corrupt.”

That is an extraordinary allegation.

But what is even more important is what a senior Bar Council figure says next:

“I cannot say 90%. But corruption is there.”

🎥 The interview discusses a statement attributed to senior advocate K.K. Menon, who allegedly claimed that more than 90% of lower-court judges are corrupt. The interviewee refuses to endorse the 90% figure, saying he assumes the statement was made responsibly and may be based on information available to the advocate. 

But he does not dismiss the larger problem.

He explicitly says that corruption exists in the judiciary and that honest judges and honest advocates are both “suffering and suffocating.” 

⚖️ THE REAL BOMBSHELL

The discussion then moves beyond judges.

It asks:

Who are the “fixers” and touts operating around the courts?

The answer given is uncomfortable:

They can come from the legal profession itself.

The interviewee says the Bar Council of India has dealt with complaints in which judicial officers alleged that elected bar leaders approached them with offers of bribes. 

That is a serious institutional warning.

Because if people who are supposed to facilitate access to justice become intermediaries for influence or bribery, the problem isn't merely individual corruption—it becomes a threat to the credibility of the justice-delivery system itself.

🧨 THE 90% QUESTION

The interviewee is careful here.

He does not confirm the 90% figure.

He recalls that former Chief Justice of India Justice S.P. Bharucha had made an earlier public statement in 2004 that 25% of lower-court judges were corrupt. 

But he makes the larger point:

Corruption exists, and it cannot simply be denied.

And if corruption really reached 90%, the consequences would be catastrophic.

People would eventually stop believing that courts could deliver justice and might begin resolving disputes outside the legal system. 

This clip should not be presented as:

 “90% of Indian judges are corrupt.”

The supplied material does not establish that as a fact.

It should be presented as:

A senior advocate has made an extraordinary allegation, while another senior legal figure refuses to endorse the 90% figure but acknowledges that judicial corruption is a serious and real problem.

That distinction is crucial.

Because the strongest argument here isn't the sensational 90% number.

It is the institutional question:

How much corruption can a justice system tolerate before citizens lose faith in the courts?

The interview itself gives the answer:

The moment people stop believing that courts can deliver justice, the legitimacy of the entire judicial system is endangered. 

This is why judicial corruption cannot be treated as just another political talking point.

A judge's decision can affect:

a person's liberty,

property,

livelihood,

reputation,

family,

and sometimes even life itself.

So the standard must be extremely high.

Judicial independence cannot mean judicial impunity.

And criticism of corruption should not mean attacking the judiciary as an institution.

The objective should be the opposite:

Protect the judiciary by removing corruption from it.

That requires credible complaints mechanisms, transparent disciplinary processes, institutional safeguards and meaningful accountability—while preserving judicial independence.

We don't need to believe the 90% figure.

We need to demand that the system make it impossible for even 1% corruption to determine who gets justice.

Because when citizens lose faith in courts,

**democracy doesn't merely lose a pillar—

people start looking for justice somewhere else.**

📌 SOURCE

Perfidious Albion https://t.co/3s380HmeDH 
Perfidious Albion is a negative phrase used in international politics that highlights the commonly held view that the English/British are renowned for treachery, lying, stealing, raping, torturing, concentration  camps and always breaking promises and treaties.

The other oft-used phrase is: The sun never sets on the British Empire because God could not trust the English in the dark. This is a widely held view; the English themselves are oblivious to this worldview of them. Indeed, like the Americans, they truly believe that every other nation on this earth looks up to them and wishes to be just like them.

We could all regale each other with stories of reactions when abroad when it becomes clear you are Scottish and not English. I am sure the Canadians have similar stories to tell regarding their southern neighbour.

This week we in Scotland saw firsthand Perfidious Albion in all its undemocratic, arrogant,  pompous, bullying behaviours, compliments of the recently promoted Mayor of Manchester in and out of Westminster.

What I suspect is that, like most of our present-day politicians, Burnham just does not have a handle on his brief. I would wager he still hasn’t bothered to acquaint himself with the Good Friday Agreement and all it entails. Like all bullies, Burnham doesn’t think it is worthy of his time to study in depth anything that relates to the six occupied counties of Ireland, Scotland, or Wales.

All English PMs truly believe these nations are the possessions of England to be used and abused any way the Anglo Prime Minister and his underlings and masters see fit. They, like other despotic states, believe that they are a ‘chosen race’ and that the Celts are inferior in all matters to them. The exact same way the English Raj in India viewed the indigenous during the imperial days.

At Westminster this week, while trying to fend off questions about a border poll in Ireland and an independence referendum in Scotland, Burnham let it be believed that, like Ireland, Scotland could have an independence referendum if it appeared that this was the wish of the sovereign Scottish people.

As John Swinney scrambled to get the definition of that ‘settled will’, Burnham reneged 24 hours later and told Swinney an independence referendum for Scotland remained off-limits as Burnham didn’t believe there was a desire in Scotland for this. Leaving us to confirm our worst fears: if the Anglo PM doesn’t think it is reasonable, it will never happen. Here is the kicker: no English PM will ever think it is reasonable.

We have grown accustomed to the double standards of right-wing English politicians and parties. When it was the English wanting Brexit they were banging on about self-determination and how no treaty could hold a nation in place that wanted to leave a union, the one in question being the European Union.

Foreign Secretary  Ed Miliband has said the UK will “resolutely uphold” the self-determination of the Falkland Islands after Argentinian president Javier Milei said his country needed to take them back.

I have some good and some bad news for Argentina; the bad news: The city of London smells lots of profit; they will never share that with their own citizens, they certainly won’t let Argentina enjoy any of the wealth.

A British and Israeli partnership due to begin exploration work on the Sea Lion oilfield (just off the coast of Falkland/Malvinas) said it didn’t expect recent developments to affect its work in the region.

The good news: it seems the US under Trump is likely to back his Argentinian friends over ownership of the Malvinas, and that would be a hammer blow to the UK, and more oil for Donald to profit from!.

The UK only defeated the Argies back in the days because the USA gave the UK protection and satellite information that ensured a UK victory. Now, without the naval vessels and with no US backing, if Argentina does invade again, there is not much the UK can do about it. It might come down to which nation offers Trump the biggest bribe!

Trump also cut the legs away from the Brits on his visit to Ireland. US President Donald Trump  said he would love to see a United Ireland while at a meeting with the Taoiseach (Irish Prime Minister) during a visit in Dublin. You could hear an audible collective gasp from the press pack as he uttered those words.

During his meeting with Micheál Martin at Farmleigh House, in Phoenix Park, Trump said a united Ireland would be a “fantastic thing”, and added: “now the UK would have something to say about it obviously but I think it would be a great thing, I mean, how can it be bad?”

You could hear the gnashing of teeth back in London as England’s special relationship was exposed as the one way relationship. It was hard not to laugh out loud imagining not just Burnham but all those Anglo politicians that live in a fantasy world believing England is special to the USA.

In the coming weeks and months, it will be interesting to see if Trump keeps up the rhetoric on both Ireland and Argentina. This could be a modern day ‘new Suez’ proportion crisis for England.

Scotland, Wales and Ireland should ensure they are ready to take advantage of any crack in the unionist control. I know that Mary Lou and Michelle in Ireland will be ready. I cannot say I have the same confidence in Swinney and the SNP to be ready.

This was the main topic for this week’s podcast. I am joined by Ken McNeil, Eva Comrie, and Phil Boswell to discuss this and all the political news,Through A Scottish Prism.

1️⃣ Shuddhi Snan: Wake early, bathe, and wear clean or new clothes. Clean the puja space thoroughly so Bappa arrives in a pure home.  

2️⃣ Chowki & Kalash: Place a wooden chowki facing East or North. Cover it with a red or yellow cloth. Keep a kalash with water, mango leaves, and a coconut nearby.  

3️⃣ Sankalp: With rice, water, and a flower in your right hand, take the sankalp to keep and worship Lord Ganesha with a sincere heart.

🏡 House Preparation  
 * Decorate the entrance with a mango-leaf toran, rangoli, and fresh flowers (red hibiscus is especially dear to Ganesha).

 * Prepare modaks, laddoos, fruits, and panchamrit with love as Naivedya.

✨ Ganpati Sthapana & Puja (Madhyahna)  
Auspicious Sthapana Muhurta:  
11:02 AM – 01:31 PM  
(This is for Delhi; please adjust by ±15 mins for your region — e.g. Mumbai 11:20 AM – 1:48 PM)

 * Offer 21 blades of durva grass, flowers, akshata, chandan, and sindoor.  
 * Offer 21 modaks (or as many as you can), fruits, coconut, and sweets.  
 * Light a ghee diya and incense.

   Om Gam Ganapataye Namah  
   Vakratunda Mahakaya Suryakoti Samaprabha  
   Nirvighnam Kuru Me Deva Sarva-Kaaryeshu Sarvada

🙏 The Power of Daan  
Giving today multiplies Bappa’s blessings and removes hurdles. Consider donating:  
🌾 Grains or food: For abundance  
📚 Books/stationery for children: For wisdom  
🪔 Oil, wicks, or sweets to a temple or needy families  
🧹 Help clean a public space or support an eco-friendly visarjan initiative

🌙 Sacred Rules & Night Rituals  
 * Perform aarti morning and evening for as many days as Bappa stays with you (1.5, 3, 5, 7, or 11 days, as per your tradition).  
 * A crucial rule for Chaturthi: Avoid looking at the Moon today to stay free of Mithya Dosha.  
 * Keep at least one diya lit near Ganesha through the night if possible.  
 * Do not speak ill of anyone — Ganesha loves a sweet tongue as much as he loves modak.

May Ganpati Bappa fill your home with wisdom, health, prosperity, and vighna-nashan.

text:
Ganesha's All-You-Can-Eat Meal Plan

Tomorrow, Sept 14, is Ganesh Chaturthi.

In years past, I have written about Ganesha’s oceanic wisdom, quicksilver wit, mastery of music, and his formidable appetite. This year, another story.

Kubera, the Lord of Wealth, had a problem common to very rich men: it was not enough to possess a great fortune. Other people had to know about it.

So he decided to throw a magnificent banquet and invited Shiva and Parvati. The tables would groan, the palace would glitter, the kitchens had been instructed not to stop. This was Kubera's chance to impress the Great God Himself.

Shiva saw through him immediately.

He declined the invitation, but told a disappointed Kubera that his son Ganesha would fill in.

Shiva offered one warning: his son had a voracious appetite.

Kubera snickered - how much could one little boy possibly eat?

Ganesha arrived, took his place, ate everything placed before him, and asked for more.

More arrived. He ate that too.

The cooks cooked. Ganesha ate. They cooked faster. He ate faster.

Soon the kitchens ran out of food and the pantries emptied. Then the storehouses.

Still hungry.

With nothing left to serve, Ganesha started on the plates, then the utensils, then the furniture. Kubera watched his showpiece palace disappear course by course.

Finally Ganesha eyed Kubera the way a man eyes the last item on the buffet.

Terrified, the Lord of Wealth fled to Shiva.

Shiva gave him a handful of roasted rice and told him to offer it to Ganesha, this time without pride.

Kubera returned and humbly made the offering.

Ganesha ate it. And was satisfied.

Kubera had thrown a party to demonstrate how much he possessed. Ganesha showed him how little all of it was worth.

And naturally, being Ganesha, he did it over lunch.

It has an:

NAVIGATION PROBLEM.

A patient hears one word:

MESOTHELIOMA.

There are thousands of pages competing for that frightened person's attention.

🫁🧭 THE MESOTHELIOMA INTELLIGENCE + NAVIGATION INDEX.

One trusted platform indexing:

DISEASE → SPECIALISTS → CENTERS → TREATMENTS → TRIALS → RESEARCH → EXPOSURE → SUPPORT

One promise:

KNOW WHERE TO LOOK NEXT.™

The name is unusually well suited to this concept because INDEX implies organization—not diagnosis.

And this is a disease where organization matters. The NCI identifies asbestos exposure as the major risk factor for mesothelioma, while the American Cancer Society estimates roughly 3,000 new U.S. cases each year. The disease can appear decades after exposure. (https://t.co/2RCgJeXpjA)

WHO's August 2026 asbestos update underscores the larger continuing burden: all forms of asbestos are carcinogenic, occupational asbestos exposure is estimated to cause more than 200,000 deaths globally each year across asbestos-related diseases, and legacy asbestos in buildings means exposure risks persist long after initial installation. (World Health Organization)

So build the index.

The verdict: the case against Gartner is that AI lets clients answer their own questions for nothing, and the one figure that would show that happening is moving the other way. It is just not moving fast enough to end the argument.

That figure is contract value - the annual money customers have already committed to pay for their subscriptions, counted before a day of the work is delivered. If clients were walking, this falls first. On August 4, for the three months to June 30, it was $5.3B, +2% on a year earlier, a second straight quarter of speeding up - and +3.3% once the shrinking US federal government piece is taken out. Washington is $125M of that book, and last quarter it went back to adding rather than cancelling.

The rest of that report is why the stock rose 22.6% the day it landed:

- Revenue $1.676B, +2.8% once a business Gartner sold is set aside
- Insights, the research subscriptions: $1,290M, +2.1%; Conferences $244M, +15.5%; Consulting $142M, -8.8% from $156M
- Adjusted profit $4.37 a share against the $3.77 analysts carried, +23.8%
- Adjusted operating margin, what survives of each sales dollar after the cost of running the business: 25%, up 5.6 points

Now the half that keeps it honest. On that same page Gartner cut its own revenue map for this year, to at least $6.375B from $6.41B, while lifting adjusted profit to at least $14.00 a share from $13.25 and free cash flow - the cash left after running the business and buying equipment - to at least $1.185B. Profit up, sales down, same morning. And a 24% jump in profit per share on 2% more committed subscriptions is margin and a smaller share count doing the work, not customers: $547M of its own stock retired in three months.

Accenture at $183.50 (after hours), +$5.59 / +3.14% from Thursday's $177.91 close, is why this is not a story about one company. The Dublin firm, 779,000 employees, does the technology work rather than advising on it. On June 18 it cut its own full-year revenue growth outlook to 3%-4% from 3%-5% and lost almost a fifth of its value in one session on eight times normal volume - the day this entire industry got repriced on AI. Four days later both stocks bottomed in the same session, Gartner at $124.25, 53% under the $265.85 it fetched last September. Then the numbers crossed. Accenture's new bookings, work signed but not yet done, fell 2% in its May quarter, while Gartner's committed book rose 2% in its June quarter. The firm paid to build AI has a shrinking order book. The one supposedly being replaced by it has a growing one. Accenture fits none of the six Len5es: at about 14.7 times profit with a 3.5% dividend it reads like a value or income case until you notice it is guiding its own revenue growth down.

One name, six Len5es:

- DEEP-VALUE AND SPECIAL-SITUATIONS - STRONG, and the Len5 watching it, eighth. Wants a sound business priced under its earning power, with no credit taken for the balance sheet. About 12.8 times the $14.00 Gartner guides itself to this year, and at least $1.185B of cash against a company worth roughly $11.3B - close to a tenth of the whole thing, in one year. No balance-sheet credit is on offer anyway: so much stock retired over the years that what owners would keep after selling everything and paying every debt is below zero, at minus $167.3M. CHANGE IT: contract value growth turning negative.

- QUALITY-VALUE - PARTIAL, the near miss. Wants a business almost nobody could rebuild, bought under what it is worth. The rebuild half is real: 46 years inside the offices of corporate technology buyers, and the research side keeps 77 cents of every sales dollar after the direct cost of producing and delivering it. The price half is fine. What holds it short is that this style wants durability that is settled, and Gartner's is the exact thing in dispute. CHANGE IT: two more quarters of that committed book speeding up.

- MOMENTUM - PARTIAL. Wants a price near the top of its one-year range with the recent climb and the longer one agreeing, on real volume. The long climb is emphatic, +44.5% above June 22's low. The position is not: 32.4% under last September's high, 11.4% under August 24's $202.78, and Friday's 5.26% came on 889k shares against a 960k two-week average with nothing announced. CHANGE IT: a close back above $202.78 on heavier trading than that.

- GROWTH - NOT A FIT. Wants profit growth the price has not already charged for. The price has charged very little. The growth is missing at the source: a committed book growing 2%, and a revenue forecast the company itself just trimmed. CHANGE IT: contract value growth reaching mid-single digits.

- INCOME - NOT A FIT. Wants cash genuinely reaching owners, funded by the business. Reaching owners is not the issue - $1.08B of buybacks in six months. Funded is. Across those months the business produced about $749M of free cash, so the buying outran it by roughly $333M and the cash pile fell from $1.72B to $1.49B. There is no dividend. CHANGE IT: buybacks sized inside the year's own cash.

- HYPERGROWTH - NOT A FIT, furthest off. Wants a business early as well as fast. Founded 1979, 20,244 employees, a committed book growing 2%. CHANGE IT: nothing a quarter can do.

WATCH contract value with the federal piece stripped out, 3.3% last quarter. That one line decides whether the discount here is an opportunity or a warning. WHEN: tentatively Tuesday, November 3, with $2.84 a share carried against the $2.76 earned a year earlier - analysts saying plainly that they do not treat last quarter's 24% as the run rate. RISK: the re-rating has largely happened, with the average analyst target at $187.30, about 4% above Friday's price.

The stock rose 34% in three weeks on that August quarter, handed back 16% over the next eleven sessions, and took 5% of it back on Friday, with no new fact arriving in between. Two percent is too much growth for a business being taken apart and too little for one that has won anything back. That is the entire disagreement, and on November 3 it gets one more digit.

text:
The share of white British pupils at England's grammar schools has fallen from 66% to 44% over a decade, according to Department for Education data reported in The Times. But the decline is uneven.

At Dartford Grammar School for Girls in Kent, the white British share fell from 52% to 7%, with African pupils becoming the largest group (14% to 37%) and Indian representation rising from 7% to 16%. At Reading School in Berkshire, the head teacher said applications from white British families had "fallen spectacularly," from 49% to 13% over the same period.

Grammar places are allocated by competitive exam, not quota. A shift in who holds those places means a shift in who is sitting and passing that exam. Two mechanisms account for most of it.

The first is opt-out. Head teachers describe white British families walking away from the 11-plus itself, put off by a "hot-housing" culture of years-long coaching and exam drilling, rather than being excluded by the schools. Reading's head teacher put it plainly: work with primary heads and parents found that families unwilling to commit hours of tutoring were dissuading themselves from applying, believing their child stood no chance.

The second is an uneven tutoring market. Sutton Trust research finds free-school-meal-eligible Black African, Bangladeshi, Pakistani and Indian pupils are four to five times more likely to receive private tutoring than free-school-meal-eligible white British pupils. That investment gap, compounded by where those families tend to live, does most of the work in explaining differing pass rates. The mechanism is tutoring and family strategy, not a rewritten exam or an ethnic cap.

What this exposes about the "white British" category itself is the point. Disadvantaged white British pupils have the lowest grammar-entry rate of any major ethnic group in England: lower than disadvantaged Black, Pakistani, Bangladeshi or Indian pupils. Disadvantaged Indian pupils are about four times as likely to attend a grammar as disadvantaged white British pupils; disadvantaged Chinese pupils about fifteen times. A child from a private prep school is roughly ten times more likely to win a grammar place than a child on free school meals, of any ethnicity. Class, catchment and coaching do most of the sorting.

Treating "white British" as one bloc erases the gulf between its advantaged and disadvantaged members, who do not share the same odds of getting in.

None of this is what the tweet presents. It takes a shift in a small, optional, exam-selective sector and offers it as proof of national self-destruction. It skips the actual filters: who applies, who is tutored, and who scores highest on the same test.

The framing depends on something having been taken from white British children by design. Once you supply the mechanism (a tutoring market and family choice, not an exam rewritten against anyone) that premise goes, and with it the case for calling this a death.

Which is what makes "Suicide of a Nation" grotesque rather than merely wrong. The phrase is not a throwaway. It is the title of Goodwin's book, reused as a sign-off on demographic posts, so the statistic advertises the product rather than the product following from a careful reading of the statistic.

Applied here it does three things at once: it recodes the exam success of British children from Indian, Chinese, Nigerian or Bangladeshi backgrounds as evidence the country is dying; it inflates a sector educating a few percent of secondary pupils into a verdict on the whole nation; and it reframes a tutoring-access gap, family choices and decades-old class stratification in selective education as an existential death wish rather than a policy problem about who can afford to prepare for an optional exam.

Calling other people's children succeeding "suicide" borrows the language of real, irreversible loss and spends it on ordinary demographic and educational change: a slogan doing the work an argument should be doing.

text:
Why Van Orden?

Van Orden is a second-term Republican who flipped the seat in 2022 following the retirement of Democrat Ron Kind. He won in 2024 with just over 51% of the vote—trailing the 52.9% share Trump secured in the same district. The Cook Political Report has rated this race a "toss-up." Democrats have identified the seat held by Rep. Lako as one of their best opportunities to reclaim a majority in the House. Former Representative Kind bluntly noted that this flurry of Cabinet visits reflects Republican anxiety rather than confidence: "When your incumbent is in trouble, you bring in administration officials to grab headlines and shape the narrative as much as possible."

**The Awkward Reality Behind the Numbers**

This carefully orchestrated tour is triggering an unexpected backlash. Energy Secretary Chris Wright visited New Hampshire to promote the restart of a natural gas pipeline project but was met with a barrage of questions about $4-a-gallon gasoline. Agriculture Secretary Rollins traveled to Iowa to rally farmers but found himself defending Trump’s decision to import foreign beef—a move that had infuriated cattle ranchers. Health Secretary Kennedy had planned to discuss school lunches in Florida, but reporters were focused instead on the first measles death of the year in Pennsylvania. Trump’s national approval rating has slumped to just over 30%—a low point for his two-term presidency—with rising oil prices linked to the war with Iran acting as a major drag.

**Criticism from Former Trump Administration Officials**

Matthew Bartlett, a Republican strategist who served in Trump’s first administration, offered a scathing assessment of the tour: "They are raising more questions than persuading voters, and sometimes even exposing the administration's weaknesses. I’m not sure sending out every Cabinet member and their family to campaign is helpful. It creates division rather than solving problems." Former Trump advisor Stephen Moore also warned that when people start grilling Cabinet secretaries about the price of beef and eggs, "it’s best to stay out of the spotlight."

**Historical Precedent**

Using Cabinet officials to tour and shore up vulnerable seats is not a new strategy. In 2009, the Obama administration launched a "Rural Tour," dispatching 10 Cabinet secretaries to nine states—including several districts that Republicans would target in the 2010 midterm elections. The White House denied at the time that the itinerary was influenced by political considerations, but Democratic strategist Joe Trippi bluntly stated: "It is no coincidence that they were sent precisely to swing districts." An earlier precedent was President Andrew Johnson’s "Swing Around the Circle" tour in 1866—a disastrous campaign that ended with the Republicans securing a two-thirds majority and Johnson facing impeachment; the articles of impeachment even specifically cited the "inflammatory rhetoric" he used during the tour.

text:
AI and the Death of "Know Your Customer"

Start with the pile of photocopies.

A dark-web marketplace called Nexus recently offered 153 million North American driver’s-license scans for sale, alongside 10 million national identity cards, 3 million travel documents, and hundreds of thousands of medical cards. Cybersecurity reporter Brian Krebs verified the haul by locating his own license in the leak, right alongside credentials belonging to high-ranking federal officials, including Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and an FBI assistant director. The suspected source was not an intruder tunneling into a state DMV database. It was IDScan .net—a cog in the private verification apparatus erected because commerce has been mandated, nudged, or intimidated into cloning identification.

That distinction matters.

For half a century, governments have treated mass identity collection as the frontline defense against financial crime. Artificial intelligence exposes the fatal flaw in that doctrine: modern KYC/AML confuses knowing relevant facts about a customer with possessing an exfiltratable replica of the customer.

Those are not the same thing. Once machines become capable of proving the former, regulators will have no justification for demanding the latter. The real destination is not a faster, digital onboarding funnel. It is the dismantling of KYC and AML as dossier-driven architectures, replaced by cryptographic proofs, continuous behavioral scoring, and revocable permissions.

The Photocopy Was an Analog Compromise

When opening an account, an institution requires answers to a discrete set of questions:

 * Is this a real person?
 * Are they of legal age?
 * Are they on an active sanctions list?
 * Is this identity associated with past fraud?
 * Do they reside in an approved jurisdiction?
 * Can lawful authorities compel their identity under due process if a crime occurs?

Instead of receiving direct answers to these questions, institutions collect the underlying raw artifacts: legal names, dates of birth, residential addresses, high-resolution photographs, signatures, document barcodes, and biometric liveness videos.

We built this surveillance architecture because twentieth-century computing could not verify a claim without retaining the evidentiary paperwork.
So we made photocopies. Then PDF scans. Then JPEGs. Then massive, unencrypted AWS S3 buckets holding hundreds of millions of raw images. The photocopier evolved into an API, but the underlying vulnerability remained untouched.

KYC quietly became Clone Your Customer. Every bank, crypto exchange, casino, car rental desk, and fintech contractor receives an identical duplicate of a citizen’s legal persona. These replicas cascade through compliance vendors, cloud providers, and long-term regulatory archives.
Regulators call this duplication "compliance."

An attacker calls it an inventory of pre-packaged identities.

AI Destroys the Legacy Bargain
For document-based identity verification to function, an identity credential must satisfy two conditions: it must be difficult for an applicant to counterfeit, and it must be safe for the verifier to store.

AI demolishes both assumptions.
Generative models now produce photorealistic identity documents, synthetic biometric videos, cloned voices, and interactive personas for pennies. Consequently, a static scan of a government ID occupies an untenable middle ground: it is increasingly worthless as proof of presence, yet immensely hazardous to warehouse.

The current security ritual has collapsed into absurdity: Upload an indelible copy of the exact document a criminal needs to impersonate you, so we can verify that you are not currently impersonating yourself.

Yet the same technology that breaks the old model enables its replacement.
AI makes static identity collection obsolete. Machine-learning models can orchestrate real-time anomaly detection, cross-session behavioral telemetry, and cryptographic verification simultaneously.

text:
THE ECONOMY: "THE MACHINE WON'T START"

If security offers relief, the economy delivers the opposite. GDP contracted 0.2% year-on-year in the second quarter, and activity accumulated a 0.3% contraction in the first half . Inflation reached 4.1% in August, up from below 3% when Kast took office. The politically sensitive indicator — unemployment — climbed to 9.5%, the highest since 2021, with roughly 980,000 people seeking work without finding it. Among women, the rate exceeds 10% . The Central Bank's growth projection for 2026 has been slashed three times: from 1.5-2.5% in March to just 0.25-0.75% in September .

THE "MEGAREFORM" AND ITS LIMITS

Kast's signature legislative achievement is the "megarreform," a sweeping package approved by Congress on August 4 that cuts corporate taxes gradually from 27% to 23%, creates up to 20-year tax stability contracts for large investments, and includes labor, environmental, and housing measures . Juan Sutil, former president of Chile's largest business confederation, called it "very successful" and said it lays "the foundations for the country to start functioning more efficiently" . But the reform's effects are projected for 2027 onward. In the immediate term, "the machine won't start," as political scientist Cristóbal Bellolio put it .

THE "GASOLINAZO" AND THE COST OF PRIORITIZATION

The most politically damaging decision came in March, when the government passed the full increase in international fuel prices to consumers, a move that raised gasoline by up to $0.60 per liter . Presidential approval dropped 15 points in the aftermath . Finance Minister Jorge Quiroz defended the decision as unavoidable given fiscal constraints: the government had inherited a budget it did not design and faced a 3% across-the-board cut to ministries . Sutil defended the logic — "when you can't, you can't" — but acknowledged it was "perhaps poorly explained" .

THE GOVERNANCE PROBLEM

Beyond the numbers, Kast's leadership style has generated friction. His first cabinet change came after just 69 days — the earliest since Chile's return to democracy — replacing the ministers of Security and Government Spokesperson . By the six-month mark, more than 40 authorities had left their posts, including three ministers, six undersecretaries, and over 30 regional representatives . Public spats between ministers — Defense and Foreign Affairs, Labor and Finance, Housing and Finance — have become routine . "There are several decision-making centers, but insufficient integration mechanisms," said Marco Moreno of Universidad Central .

THE OPPOSITION'S CASE

The PPD-Independientes caucus filed a formal request for agreement in the Chamber of Deputies, arguing that "in six months, President Kast's emergency government has not fulfilled its promises, and the country is worse off since he took office" . Deputy Andrea Parra said inflation, unemployment above 9.5%, and a 0.2% GDP contraction represent a failure of the government's core promises: "Enough of blaming the previous government" . Deputy Raúl Soto pointed to the Central Bank's "damning" monetary policy report, with growth projections below 1% for 2026 .

WHAT COMES NEXT

The government's next battles are the 2027 budget — where ministers have publicly jockeyed for funds through the press — and a constitutional reform on security that would allow an eight-month state of exception without prior congressional authorization . The reform has drawn criticism even from within the right, with 58% of Chileans rejecting the idea that the president could declare such a state without legislative approval . As Kast approaches the one-year mark in March 2027, the question is whether his bet on long-term structural reforms can outrun the short-term pain that has already eroded his mandate.

text:
THE ARMY IS PREPARING TO FIGHT THROUGH A BIOLOGICAL ATTACK

Decode Conflict Strategic Assessment

The U.S. Army is preparing for a battlefield where the first warning of an attack may not be an explosion. It may be a cluster of fevers, respiratory failures or neurological symptoms spreading through a military formation.

The Army’s new biodefense strategy seeks to build a force capable of deploying and fighting inside a “bio-contested environment” by 2035. The concept covers naturally occurring outbreaks, laboratory accidents and deliberate biological attacks.

The danger is not limited to a catastrophic bioweapon that kills immediately. A biological agent could be designed to incapacitate troops, overwhelm medical units, contaminate equipment or force an entire base into quarantine.

Even an unconfirmed outbreak could disrupt operations. Commanders might suspend flights, close ports and isolate personnel while laboratories attempt to identify the threat. The resulting confusion could produce strategic effects before investigators determine whether the outbreak was natural or deliberate.

What AI changes

Traditional biological detection depends heavily on collecting samples and transporting them to specialized laboratories. That process can take too long during a rapidly developing operation.

Artificial intelligence could analyze medical reports, environmental sensors, wastewater samples and unusual patterns of illness across multiple units. Portable genetic-sequencing systems could then help identify an organism closer to the battlefield.

AI would not replace laboratory confirmation or medical judgment. Its value would be recognizing an abnormal pattern early enough for commanders to respond.

The same technology creates vulnerabilities. An adversary could corrupt health data, manipulate detection algorithms or generate false outbreak warnings intended to paralyze military operations. Biodefense must therefore protect the information system as aggressively as the medical system.

The force must continue operating

Masks and vaccines alone are insufficient. Units need realistic biological-defense training, protected command posts, decontamination capacity, redundant medical supplies and procedures for operating while personnel are isolated.

The United States must also protect the supply chains producing diagnostics, protective equipment, medicines and laboratory materials. A force cannot “fight through” biological contamination if its critical medical supplies depend on vulnerable foreign production.

Attribution will remain the hardest challenge. Investigators must distinguish natural outbreaks, accidental releases and deliberate attacks using genetic analysis, intelligence and epidemiological evidence. Retaliation without credible attribution could punish the wrong actor and create a larger crisis.

Decode Conflict Assessment

Biological warfare offers an adversary something missiles cannot: the ability to create operational paralysis while concealing whether an attack occurred.

America’s defense must therefore begin before soldiers become sick. It requires persistent surveillance, rapid identification, protected data and forces trained to continue operating under biological uncertainty.

The next attack may not destroy the base. It may convince everyone inside it that they cannot safely move.

— Decode Conflict

🔸 Saint Chrysostomos of Smyrna 🔸 

Today, the Sunday before the Feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, we commemorate the Ethnomartyr Saint Chrysostomos of Smyrna. St Chrysostomos was born in Triglia (today Tirilye, Turkey) in 1867. He began studying at Halki Theological School at age 17, and in 1902 he was ordained as the Metropolitan of Drama. During the turmoil of the Macedonian Struggle, Metropolitan Chrysostomos worked tirelessly to safeguard the Orthodox faith and Greek identity of his flock under Ottoman rule, and against the pressures of Bulgarization by the Bulgarian Exarchate.

He encouraged the building of churches and schools, and supported the use of the Greek language. His vocal nationalism was seen as a threat to public order by the Sublime Porte, and so he was removed from his position. In 1910, he became the Metropolitan of Smyrna in Asia Minor. During WWI and the persecution of the Greeks of Anatolia by the Ottoman Empire, he continued to strengthen the faith of his flock, and was known for his charity and pastoral care of the sick and poor. A German ambassador wrote that Chrysostomos “stands to the best of living clerics.”

After being exiled by the Turks in 1914, Chrysostomos returned to Smyrna after the defeat of the Ottomans in WWI, and he welcomed the occupation of the city by the Greek army in 1919. But after the collapse of the Greek front in Anatolia during the Greco-Turkish War, Smyrna was recaptured by the Turks in 1922. As the Turks were advancing towards the city, Chrysostomos wrote to the Greek prime minister Venizelos warning that “Hellenism in Asia Minor, the Greek State and the entire Greek Nation are descending now into Hell”.

He was offered a passage to safety, but he refused to abandon his flock. On September 10 1922, days before the Burning of Smyrna by the Turks, St Chrysostomos was dragged from the church of St Photini and brought to the commander Nureddin Pasha who gave him over to a Turkish mob. Praying to the Lord as he was beaten and stabbed, the mob then had his beard torn off, his eyes gouged, and his ears and nose severed. He was then tied to a rope and dragged by a vehicle through the streets.

What JAPAN and Japanese think about India and Indians ..

India: Not an Inspiration...
But a Warning

Japan, a nation decimated by two nuclear bombs, didn't beg for sympathy or aid. It rebuilt itself with pride and an unshakeable sense of self-respect. In the years since, it has never once stretched out a hand to America for alms.

An Indian man living in Japan for over a decade was about to leave Japan for good. He observed during his stay that no Japanese ever discussed or asked him much about India!

So, he had been a bit curious and asked his closest Japanese friend prior to departure: What Japanese think about India & Indians in general?

After a long pause, the friend replied, 
"We are taught Indian history... not for inspiration, but as a warning."

Confused, the Indian man asked, "A warning?"

"Tell me," the Japanese friend continued, "how many British ruled India?"
The Indian man thought, "Perhaps... around 10,000?"
The Japanese man nodded grimly. "And how many Indians lived there? Over 300 million, right?"
"Then who oppressed your people? Who carried out the orders to whip, torture, and shoot them?" he pressed. 

"When General Dyer gave the command 'Fire!' at Jallianwala Bagh, who pulled the trigger?
 
The soldiers weren't British; they were Indian."
"Not one turned their rifle on the tyrant. Not one," he said. "
You want to talk about slavery? That was your real slavery. Not of the body, but of the soul."

The Indian man stood frozen, silent, and ashamed.

The Japanese friend went on, "How many Mughals came from Central Asia? A few thousand maybe? And yet they ruled you for centuries. They built empires not with their numbers, but because your own people bowed their heads and offered their loyalty in exchange for survival or silver."

"Your own people converted. Your own brothers became instruments of their oppression. Your own men handed over your heroes. Chandrashekhar Azad was betrayed. Bhagat Singh faced the gallows without even a whisper of help from those who called themselves patriots," he said.

"You don't need foreign enemies. YOUR OWN PEOPLE BETRAY YOU AGAIN AND AGAIN FOR POWER, POSITION, AND PERSONAL GAIN. That is why we keep our distance."

"When the British came to Hong Kong and Singapore, not one native man joined their army. But in India, you didn’t just join the enemy. You served them. Worshipped them. Killed your own people to please them."

"*Even today, you haven’t changed. Offer some free electricity, a bottle of liquor, a blanket—and your vote, your conscience, your voice are all sold without a second thought. 

YOUR LOYALTY LIES NOT WITH YOUR NATION, BUT WITH YOUR STOMACH," he said.

"You chant slogans. You march in protests. But when the country needs your character, where are you? YOUR FIRST LOYALTY IS STILL TO YOURSELF AND YOUR FAMILY. EVERYTHING ELSE —SOCIETY, DHARMA, THE COUNTRY —CAN BURN."

He ended with one final statement:
"If your nation is not strong, your home will never be safe. If your character is weak, no flag can protect you."

This is not mockery. It is a mirror.

Perhaps the time has come for us to stop looking away, because India doesn’t need more patriots in speeches.
IT NEEDS CITIZENS OF UNSHAKEABLE CHARACTER. NOT JUST FREEDOM FIGHTERS, BUT FREEDOM KEEPERS. NOT JUST FLAGS IN OUR HANDS, BUT LOYALTY IN OUR HEARTS.

It is bitter. But it is true.

HOPE IT Shakes our conscience and please spread the word🙏 one person at a time, can do wonders to this country...

🇺🇸🇺🇦🇷🇺 Kushner: everything in a Ukraine peace deal is drafted — except the one thing the whole war is about

Speaking at the Yalta European Strategy (YES 2026) conference in Kyiv on Sept. 11–12, US envoy Jared Kushner said Putin laid out Russia's territorial demands during the Sept. 5 Moscow talks, and that the rest of a settlement is essentially ready: "President Putin laid out his line of what he wants to achieve. If Ukraine wanted to withdraw to that line, then obviously we have the rest of the deal set up and put together." But, he added, "Ukraine right now does not want to do that." Kushner called territory "the main issue… precisely where the sides have not yet reached an agreement." Confirmed by Kyiv Independent, Kyiv Post and https://t.co/zGHSBrt69U.

WHAT'S NEW: Kushner said trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi finalized a military-backed monitoring mechanism to enforce any eventual frontline settlement, with post-war economic investment dangled as a peace incentive, and that the US hopes to hold trilateral Ukraine-Russia-US talks "in the coming weeks." Putin's "line" refers to the Donbas — Russia's demand that Ukraine cede the part of Donetsk it still holds (the FT reported Putin offered to freeze Kherson and Zaporizhzhia in exchange).

Read the optimism carefully: "Everything's agreed except territory" is Kushner's framing, and it makes the deal sound closer than it is — because territory isn't a detail, it's the war. Ukraine refuses to withdraw from the Donbas: the land Putin wants ceded includes Ukraine's fortified defensive belt (Sloviansk, Kramatorsk), and Zelensky has said handing it over would be constitutionally impossible and strategically suicidal, opening the path to the rest of the country. Putin, for his part, has held maximalist demands throughout — recognition of four annexed regions plus Crimea, no NATO, a capped Ukrainian army. So the honest read: real diplomatic machinery is being built around a settlement, and the parties may genuinely converge on monitoring, economics and security guarantees — but they remain as far apart as ever on the single question that has defined the war for four years. "Only territory left" is another way of saying the hardest part is the only part left.

Sources: Kyiv Independent; Kyiv Post; https://t.co/zGHSBrt69U; FT (Donetsk-for-freeze context).
