Headline: Democrats Turn Football Into a Campaign Strategy to Win Over Male Voters

 Democrats are increasingly using football and sports culture as part of a broader strategy to appeal to male voters. Recent appearances by Senate candidates in Texas and Michigan have drawn attention to the party’s efforts to build a more relatable image.

Democrats are turning to football and popular sports culture in an effort to connect with male voters ahead of the upcoming elections. Several candidates have highlighted their connection to college football, sporting events and everyday American life as they seek to present themselves as more relatable political figures.

Texas Senate nominee James Talarico celebrated Texas’ victory over Ohio State, claiming that he had broken the “Cruz Curse.”

Meanwhile, Michigan Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed attracted attention with a casual appearance at a University of Michigan tailgate. The event highlighted his connection to college football culture, which remains a major part of American sports and social life.

The strategy reflects a broader effort among top Democrats to build a more relatable image among male voters. Leaders including Kamala Harris and Tim Walz have also been part of efforts to connect with voters through everyday interests, popular culture and a less formal political image.

Democrats face the challenge of strengthening their appeal among key voting groups, including men who may not traditionally identify strongly with the party. By engaging with football culture, candidates are seeking to broaden their reach beyond conventional campaign events and policy-focused messaging.

Political observers say sports can offer candidates a way to appear more accessible and connected to the communities they hope to represent. However, the effectiveness of the strategy will ultimately depend on whether voters see these appearances as authentic rather than simply political performances.

Football-related outreach is unlikely to replace major policy issues such as the economy, jobs, public safety and national security. But it could provide Democrats with another way to communicate with voters and strengthen their public image during a competitive election cycle.

Conclusion: As Democrats look for new ways to win over male voters, football is becoming more than just a game. It is increasingly being used as a cultural connection point in the broader battle for political support.

Sidharth Babu, a 2017-batch Indian Foreign Service officer, has attracted considerable public attention for his role as a diplomatic interpreter during high level engagements involving Prime Minister Narendra Modi and foreign leaders. His calm presence and command of languages have made him a recognisable figure in key diplomatic interactions.

He is currently serving as a Deputy Secretary in the Ministry of External Affairs.

Hailing from Kochi, Kerala, Babu holds a degree in Mechanical Engineering from Mar Athanasius College of Engineering. Before entering the civil services, he worked as a project manager in the e-commerce sector.

His first attempt at the UPSC Civil Services Examination did not yield the desired result. However, he reassessed his preparation strategy and returned with renewed determination. In the 2016 examination, he secured an impressive All India Rank of 15.

Although his rank made him eligible for the Indian Administrative Service, Babu chose the Indian Foreign Service, guided by his interest in international affairs and diplomacy.

Babu’s diplomatic responsibilities have been strengthened by his training in interpretation at the Middlebury Institute of International Studies in Monterey, California.

His professional experience has also included diplomatic assignments in Beijing, China, and San Francisco, the United States, giving him exposure to diverse international settings and complex diplomatic engagements.

Babu’s presence at major international and national events has brought him into the public eye.

During the 𝟕𝟕𝐭𝐡 𝐑𝐞𝐩𝐮𝐛𝐥𝐢𝐜 𝐃𝐚𝐲 𝐜𝐞𝐥𝐞𝐛𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 𝐢𝐧 𝐉𝐚𝐧𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐲 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔,
 he was seen on the VIP podium at Kartavya Path, interpreting during an interaction between Prime Minister Modi and the chief guest, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.

He attracted attention again during the 𝟏𝟖𝐭𝐡 𝐁𝐑𝐈𝐂𝐒 𝐒𝐮𝐦𝐦𝐢𝐭 𝐢𝐧 𝐒𝐞𝐩𝐭𝐞𝐦𝐛𝐞𝐫 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔, where he was seen assisting with communication during high-level interactions involving Prime Minister Modi, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

While interpreters typically work away from the spotlight, Babu’s appearances alongside world leaders have brought unusual public attention to a profession that plays a crucial role in international diplomacy.

His journey from engineering and the corporate sector to the Indian Foreign Service offers an example of how specialised skills, preparation and a clear sense of purpose can open the doors to some of the country’s most demanding public responsibilities.

text:
More prop bets free from Joe Duffy: 

FREE PLAY — COOPER RUSH UNDER 18.5 COMPLETIONS — ATLANTA at PITTSBURGH — 1:00 ET

This is the strongest addition from the new prop information because several independent paths lead to the same result: Atlanta should have less passing volume, Rush historically has not been a high-completion quarterback, and there is even some risk that he does not finish the game.

The most important development is Atlanta's quarterback situation. Tua Tagovailoa is out with an oblique injury and Michael Penix Jr. remains unavailable while recovering from his torn ACL. Rush is expected to start, but he developed back spasms during the week. Atlanta still expects him to play, with undrafted rookie Jack Strand the only other available quarterback.

That creates a very different offensive equation. Atlanta doesn't need to manufacture 20-plus completions from Rush to have offensive success. Bijan Robinson gives the Falcons a legitimate centerpiece for a run-oriented game plan, and the logical adjustment with a backup quarterback is more direct rushing, fewer easy completions manufactured merely to supplement the running game, and selective play-action throws.

The prop handicapper supplying this wager makes an especially good point about game-script asymmetry. If Atlanta stays competitive, a run-heavy approach works directly in favor of the UNDER. If Pittsburgh controls the game, passing volume normally becomes the danger to a completions UNDER—but Atlanta has the unusual option of giving Strand an opportunity if Rush struggles badly. Rush's back spasms introduce another route to reduced playing time. The projection is approximately 17.5 completions with a 58-60% probability of staying below 18.5.

There is also an important distinction between passing yards and completions. Pittsburgh allowed 243.9 passing yards per game last season, but that does not necessarily hurt this wager. Rush can hit occasional intermediate or play-action throws without accumulating 19 completions. His limited 2025 action produced a 65.4% completion percentage, and the current market has his passing-yardage expectation down around 186.5.

We are attacking volume rather than demanding that Pittsburgh completely shut down Atlanta's passing game.

BETTING PARAMETERS: UNDER 18.5 completions is playable through approximately -125. At 19.5, the wager becomes substantially stronger. Do not chase UNDER 17.5 at significant juice.

FREE PLAY — DANIEL JONES OVER 21.5 COMPLETIONS — BALTIMORE at INDIANAPOLIS — 1:00 ET

This is an excellent example of why completions can offer a better proposition than raw passing yards.

Daniel Jones returns from the Achilles injury that ended his 2025 season. The intuitive reaction might be to downgrade him because of the layoff. For this particular market, however, the injury can actually contribute to the handicap. Indianapolis has little incentive to expose Jones unnecessarily as a runner in Week 1. A quicker passing game featuring high-percentage throws gives him a method of protecting himself while still moving the offense.

The matchup supports that approach. Jones attempted deep passes on fewer than 10% of his throws last season. Baltimore's new defensive structure under Jesse Minter is expected to employ three-safety looks, disguised post-snap coverage and special attention to Alec Pierce over the top.

That can funnel attempts exactly where we want them for a completions OVER: underneath and intermediate routes.

Josh Downs, Tyler Warren and Keenan Allen give Jones multiple high-percentage targets. If Baltimore brackets Pierce or keeps a safety over him, Jones doesn't have to challenge that coverage. Taking the available completion underneath moves him toward 22 catches without requiring an explosive passing performance.

There is a useful historical matchup component as well. Jones faced Minter's defense when Minter was with the Chargers last season and completed 23 of 34 passes for 288 yards and two touchdowns. The supplied projection places Jones around 22.5 completions with approximately a 60% probability of clearing 21.5.

Game state gives us another path. Baltimore is currently around a 3.5-point road favorite with a total around 47.5. Indianapolis is therefore more likely than usual to encounter a fourth-quarter situation in which Jones has to continue throwing rather than simply handing the ball to Jonathan Taylor while protecting a lead.

We don't need Jones to be spectacular. In fact, a methodical Indianapolis passing attack consisting of quick throws and underneath completions is preferable to a handful of explosive plays.

BETTING PARAMETERS: OVER 21.5 completions is the play through approximately -125. Over 20.5 is excellent. At 22.5, reduce the wager substantially.

FREE PLAY — JERRY JEUDY UNDER 31.5 RECEIVING YARDS — CLEVELAND at JACKSONVILLE — 1:00 ET

This is primarily a target-distribution wager rather than a bet that Jerry Jeudy suddenly cannot play.

Jeudy's 2025 numbers are instructive. He received 106 targets but converted them into only 50 receptions for 602 yards and two touchdowns. More importantly, Harold Fannin Jr. actually led Cleveland with 107 targets. Fannin enters Year 2 after producing 72 receptions for 731 yards on 103 official targets in his rookie season and now has an even clearer tight-end role following David Njoku's departure.

The wide-receiver room is also considerably more competitive. Cleveland has added rookies KC Concepcion Jr. and Denzel Boston, both of whom are listed as starters entering Week 1. The supplied prop analysis notes that Jeudy commanded a target on only 19% of his routes last season even when his competition for wide-receiver targets was considerably weaker. It projects him around 27 receiving yards, roughly 4.5 yards below the posted number, with approximately a 57% chance of staying UNDER 31.5.

There is independent corroboration of the target-distribution concern. Fannin is being viewed as one of Cleveland's central passing-game weapons, while Concepcion and Boston immediately create alternatives outside.

The beauty of 31.5 is that Jeudy doesn't have to disappear. A stat line such as 3 catches for 27 yards cashes the wager. Even four receptions can stay UNDER if Cleveland uses him primarily on shorter routes.

Jacksonville's mediocre 2025 pass-defense statistics are the biggest reason this remains a free play rather than something stronger. The Jaguars allowed 218.1 passing yards per game. But that weakness can also spread production throughout Cleveland's passing game rather than forcing targets to Jeudy.

FREE PLAY — TYLER SHOUGH OVER 16.5 RUSHING YARDS — NEW ORLEANS at DETROIT — 1:00 ET

This may be the most interesting schematic prop on the board.

Tyler Shough's full-season rushing average last year doesn't jump off the page—16.9 yards per game—but his late-season development does. He became substantially more willing and effective as a runner as the season progressed, posting individual rushing performances of 32, 55 and 34 yards during his final five games.

Looking specifically at Weeks 12-18, Shough averaged approximately 25 rushing yards per game. That is a much more relevant picture of the quarterback New Orleans brings into 2026 than simply averaging every game together.

The personnel change involving Taysom Hill is another important element. Hill was active for all 10 of Shough's starts last season and regularly removed Shough for specialized snaps, including designed quarterback-running concepts. Those plays don't automatically transfer one-for-one to Shough, but removing Hill creates additional opportunities for the starting quarterback to keep the ball.

Detroit's defensive style is equally important. Man coverage naturally creates scrambling opportunities because defensive backs have their eyes on receivers rather than the quarterback. Detroit can also generate pressure, which forces Shough to make decisions outside structure.

Last season Shough was sacked on 25% of his pressures, the second-highest rate among qualifying quarterbacks. A logical developmental emphasis is turning some of those negative plays into escapes. One successful scramble can account for half of this extremely modest requirement.

Game script is favorable as well. New Orleans is approximately a touchdown underdog. More Detroit scoring means more Shough dropbacks; more dropbacks mean more opportunities for pressure to break containment and create scramble yardage. The original handicap projects approximately 18.5 yards with a 59% chance of exceeding 16.5.

There is also independent quantitative corroboration for this exact wager: another current projection source separately identified Shough OVER 16.5 rushing yards as one of its top Week 1 player props.

BETTING PARAMETERS: OVER 16.5 rushing yards is the target. 17.5 remains playable. At 19.5 or higher, the mathematical advantage becomes too thin.

FREE PLAY — ANDREI IOSIVAS UNDER 1.5 RECEPTIONS — TAMPA BAY at CINCINNATI — 1:00 ET

This is a highly specific usage-and-scheme wager, which is exactly the type of prop that can offer value in Week 1 before new personnel tendencies become fully incorporated into the market.

Cincinnati should remain a pass-oriented offense, but overall passing volume isn't the important question. The issue is where those targets go.

Iosivas faces enormous competition in an offense built around Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins, and Cincinnati has indications of using more tight-end-heavy personnel and taking more snaps from under center. Both developments threaten Iosivas' opportunities.

The under-center split is especially notable. Iosivas' target rate fell to only 5% on under-center snaps last season. Tampa Bay provides another schematic negative because Todd Bowles' defense traditionally brings pressure aggressively. Iosivas' target rate against the blitz was only 8%.

Those numbers explain why receptions are preferable to receiving yards. Iosivas can be dangerous vertically and around the end zone. One downfield reception could make an UNDER on a small yardage number uncomfortable. But one reception does absolutely nothing to beat UNDER 1.5 catches.

Fourth-round rookie Colbie Young also adds another player capable of eventually eating into the secondary-receiver snaps. We don't need Young to immediately replace Iosivas. Chase, Higgins, increased tight-end usage and even a modest reduction in Iosivas' route participation can be enough.

The supplied projection is approximately 1.4 receptions with a 59% probability of staying UNDER 1.5.

This is inherently a higher-variance wager because the threshold is so low. Two catches lose it. That's why it belongs behind Rush and Jones despite an attractive modeled probability.

text:
This should set off alarms inside the Hatfield-Dowlin Complex.

Before Oregon becomes last year’s version of Penn State, we need to have an honest conversation about what’s going wrong and, more importantly, what can actually be done about it while there is still time to save the season.

The offensive issues are the most alarming. As reported by @DuckSports, Oklahoma State senior linebacker Tate Romney said after the game that their defense noticed during the week that Oregon’s offensive line had stance tendencies that helped them identify run versus pass before the snap.

That should sound eerily familiar to Oregon fans. After Indiana beat Oregon last season, multiple Indiana players told Yahoo Sports they were able to identify what Oregon was likely running based on formations, alignments and how players were positioned before the snap. Now Oklahoma State players are saying something very similar.

At some point, this stops feeling like coincidence.

And before somebody replies with, “Everybody knows tendencies” or “Defenses always have an idea what’s coming,” that’s not really the point here. These players are talking after the game about Oregon giving them useful information before the ball is even snapped. They aren’t just saying they guessed right a few times. They’re basically bragging about how Oregon helped them diagnose what was coming.

Meanwhile, Oregon fans are sitting there watching a roster with superior talent get dog walked and wondering how the hell this keeps happening. Again, and again, and again.

Teams don’t need Oregon’s entire playbook. If a linebacker can look at an offensive lineman’s stance and increase his confidence that a run or pass is coming, Oregon has already given him an advantage before the play starts. That is a self-scouting and preparation problem.

How does Oklahoma State find that on Oregon’s film during the week and Oregon not correct it before Saturday?

That question deserves a real answer. At the next press conference, Oregon's beat writers and media shouldn't let Lanning off the hook here. Ask the question and press for an actual answer.  @AaronJFentress @johncanzanobft 

Drew Mehringer’s previous Power Five play-calling experience also deserves to be part of the conversation. His only previous season as a Power Five offensive coordinator came at Rutgers in 2016. Rutgers finished 128th out of 128 teams nationally in total offense, 127th in scoring, 122nd in passing and was shut out four times.

He was 28 years old. That matters, and I don’t think it’s fair to pretend a coach can’t improve dramatically over ten years. People get better at their jobs, and the Rutgers roster was obviously nothing like the roster Oregon has today.

But Oregon also isn’t a program that should need two or three seasons to find out whether someone has developed into a championship-level play caller. This roster is ready now.

That doesn’t mean I think Dan Lanning should panic and fire both coordinators three games into the season. There is a massive amount of room between firing everybody and simply hoping the problems fix themselves.

Oregon replaced both lead coordinators this offseason with internal promotions. Drew Mehringer and Chris Hampton were already important members of Lanning’s staff, and Lanning obviously knows both of them far better than any of us do. There were reasons he trusted them with these jobs.

But replacing Will Stein and Tosh Lupoi at the same time was still a major gamble for a team that expects to compete for a national championship immediately. Being a good position coach or co-coordinator is not the same thing as being responsible for the weekly game plan, identifying your own tendencies, anticipating what an opponent is going to attack, making adjustments and calling a game under pressure.

The defensive side is a little different, and I don’t think Hampton and Mehringer should just be thrown into the same bucket. Hampton has legitimate coordinator success on his resume, including what he did at Tulane.

Still, Oklahoma State just put up 554 yards. Oregon has spent years assembling one of the most talented defensive rosters in college football. When a roster like that looks confused, gets hurt repeatedly by the same concepts or struggles to adjust, that deserves serious scrutiny too. And because defense is Dan Lanning’s background, that responsibility doesn’t stop with Hampton.

I’m also not pretending I can diagnose every busted coverage or front adjustment from my couch. That’s actually part of why I think the solution here is pretty straightforward.

Go add experience right now.

Not a new offense. Not a new defense. Not some panic move where half the staff is fired on Monday morning.

Bring in experienced coaches who can immediately help with self-scouting, tendencies, game planning and in-game adjustments. Give Mehringer and Hampton another set of eyes from somebody who has already done these jobs at the highest levels. If those veterans eventually need to take on more responsibility, then Lanning can make that decision after they’re actually inside the building and understand what Oregon is doing.

There’s recent precedent for this. Nebraska brought Dana Holgorsen into the program during the 2024 season. Within days he was deeply involved in the offense, and shortly after that he took over play-calling duties. Nebraska didn’t have to throw away its entire offense or fire everyone involved to make it happen.

Oregon can do something similar.

The NCAA rules aren’t really the obstacle here either. Oregon would need to formally bring the person onto the institutional staff, but once that’s done, that coach can provide technical and tactical instruction. This isn’t a situation where Oregon has to wait until December because some rule says an outside coach can’t join the staff in September.

The more interesting part is how quickly something like this could actually be executed, and this is where the agent side of college football matters a lot.

Dan Lanning is represented by Jimmy Sexton and CAA. Jimbo Fisher is also a Jimmy Sexton client. Gus Malzahn has been represented by Sexton. Hugh Freeze has too.

So if Lanning and Rob Mullens decide they want to know whether Jimbo Fisher would consider coming to Eugene for three months to help stabilize the offense, this does not require Oregon to launch some three-week national search.

Lanning can call his own representation. Sexton can call another one of his clients. Oregon can probably know within hours whether there is any interest.

That’s literally part of what these agents do. They quietly figure out whether an opportunity makes sense before anything becomes public.

There are similar connections elsewhere. Brian Kelly and Justin Wilcox have both been represented through Athletes First, Kelly through Trace Armstrong and Wilcox through David Dunn. The coaching world is incredibly connected. Oregon doesn’t need to send out a job posting and wait for resumes.

They can call the agent and ask a very simple question: would your client consider this if the role and money were right?

If the answer is no, move on. If it’s yes, start working.

That’s why I don’t think this necessarily takes weeks. If Oregon decided today that it wanted to add veteran help, there is a realistic path to having somebody in Eugene within three or four days.

The first day is figuring out who you want and whether that coach is interested. The second day is working through compensation, responsibilities, contract length and authority. Then legal, HR and compliance get the person formally brought onto the staff. By the third or fourth day, that coach could realistically be inside the Hatfield-Dowlin Complex watching film, sitting in meetings and attacking Oregon’s self-scout.

That doesn’t mean Jimbo Fisher walks into Eugene on Wednesday and installs his offense by Saturday. Obviously that would be ridiculous.

The entire point is that you don’t install his offense.

You keep Oregon’s terminology, Oregon’s protections and the concepts Dante Moore already knows. Then you bring in somebody who has spent decades solving offensive problems and let him look at the offense the way an opposing defensive coordinator would.

What are we tipping? Which formations have become predictable? What are defenses keying on? Are the offensive line stances giving away run or pass? Are there protection tells? What concepts fit Dante best? What are we calling too often? What aren’t we calling enough? What are defenses consistently doing to us on third down, and why aren’t our answers against pressure working?

That kind of experience can provide value almost immediately without changing the offense.

From there, Lanning decides how much responsibility that coach earns. Maybe he stays in a senior advisory role and helps Mehringer with the weekly plan. Maybe he gets heavily involved with situational football and halftime adjustments. Maybe things still don’t improve and eventually Lanning decides somebody else should call the plays.

You don’t have to answer all of those questions before the guy even gets on a plane. The first objective is getting another experienced football brain into the room and attacking the problems that are already showing up on film.

Jimbo Fisher would be my first offensive phone call. Brian Kelly would absolutely be another. Mike Gundy deserves a call too, and if Gus Malzahn would even consider coming out of retirement for a three-month sprint, I’d call him as well.

Maybe every one of them says no. Fine.

Make them say no.

On defense, Justin Wilcox feels almost too obvious not to call. He’s a former Oregon defensive back, an Oregon graduate and an Oregon native. He has been a defensive coordinator at Boise State, Tennessee, Washington, USC and Wisconsin, then spent nine years running a Power conference program at Cal.

He understands college football. He understands defense. He understands Oregon. And he’s currently available.

If Wilcox isn’t interested, then keep working down the list. Steve Wilks and Mike Zimmer are both worth serious conversations.

And yes, I’d make the crazy calls too. Sean McDermott. Mike Tomlin.

Are those likely? Of course not. But if Oregon can offer a short-term role, essentially no recruiting burden, a talented roster, a chance to work with Dan Lanning and a serious amount of money for a three-month commitment, there is zero downside to asking the question.

Make them tell you no.

Oregon has spent years building advantages other programs simply cannot match. Facilities, NIL, recruiting infrastructure, personnel departments, analytics, sports science, nutrition, money, whatever edge they can find.

If Oregon genuinely believes this roster can win a national championship, then coaching experience should be treated exactly the same way.

And Portland State being next actually makes the timing about as good as it could possibly be. You aren’t asking a new coach to walk in Tuesday and prepare Oregon for Ohio State four days later. Bring somebody in now. Let him learn the language. Let him watch film. Let him challenge assumptions and look for things the people who have been inside the same system for years may not notice anymore.

None of this has to embarrass Mehringer or Hampton either.

You can frame it as exactly what it is: giving two young coordinators every possible resource to succeed.

If they grow into the jobs and Oregon takes off, great. If it becomes obvious that one of them needs help with play calling or game planning, Oregon already has an experienced alternative inside the building.

Either outcome is better than waiting until November to decide September was trying to tell you something.

My biggest fear is that Oregon beats the hell out of Portland State and everybody convinces themselves Oklahoma State was just some bizarre one-off. The next scoreboard does not erase what Oklahoma State found on film. It doesn’t erase what Indiana players said last season either.

At some point, you have to listen when opponents keep telling you the same thing.

Dan Lanning has built this program by being aggressive. Aggressive recruiting. Aggressive portal evaluations. Aggressive NIL. Aggressive fourth-down decisions. Aggressive investment anywhere Oregon can find an advantage.

This is not the moment to suddenly become passive.

There is too much talent on this roster and too much invested in this season to look back in November and realize the warning signs were staring everybody in the face in September.

Oregon doesn’t need to blow up its coaching staff. It needs to honestly evaluate where experience may be missing and go get it.

The rules allow it. The coaches are out there. The money is there. The agent relationships are already there.

And if Oregon decides today that it wants veteran help, there is a very realistic path to having that person inside the Hatfield-Dowlin Complex within a matter of days.

So make the calls.

text:
Yesterday the danger was AI.

Today the danger is people with AI.

Same man, two days, and nobody asked him to explain the switch — because the first version already did its job. Four CEOs agreed within hours, a standards body appeared, and the argument for slowing everyone down was made in public.

Now the frame quietly changes. It was never the machine. It was concentrated power.

Which raises the obvious question:

Concentrated where?

He says democratically elected governments should hold oversight. Name them. Washington, arming a war and holding the contracts. Israel, which calls itself the region's only democracy while under investigation for genocide. London and Berlin, buying the surveillance and signing the export licences.

Every one of them is already a customer.

And the technology reaches its targets through Palantir — a private contractor nobody elected, inside classified networks, feeding operational planning.

Joint governance by the buyers is not oversight.

It is a purchasing committee with a conscience clause.

Meanwhile the practical effect of "slow the frontier" falls entirely on the people who are not yet in the room. European labs. Small companies. Anyone outside the circle that already holds the compute, the chips, the cloud and the contracts.

Slow down means: nobody new gets in.

He changed his story in a single day and offered no explanation for the first one.

So before anyone takes the second version seriously — explain the first.

text:
The real story post-9/11 is that pluralism prevailed

This week marked the 25th anniversary of 9/11. For millennials like me, the attacks remain a formative memory. The wars in Afghanistan and Iraq still shape our politics, as does the debate over how we responded at home.

A Canadian Press article this week offers a bleak assessment⁠ of the post-9/11 years, emphasizing anti-Muslim prejudice and claims of systemic discrimination. I think it gives too little weight to the extent to which pluralism prevailed.

There were shameful instances of hostility toward innocent Muslims after the attacks, including harassment and violence. Such collective guilt is identity politics in its rawest form. But it also met an immediate and forceful rejection.
￼
Six days after the attacks, U.S. President George W. Bush visited the Islamic Center of Washington, declared that “Islam is peace”⁠ and condemned intimidation of Muslim Americans. That same day, Prime Minister Jean Chrétien called hostility toward Muslim Canadians “completely unacceptable,” while Canadian Alliance leader Stockwell Day urged Canadians to reject attacks on innocent Muslims. The parliamentary record⁠ captures a rejection of collective blame across party lines.

The response extended beyond political leadership. The Canadian Press article itself describes neighbours building ties with Muslim communities and acknowledges that this solidarity helped stem intolerance. These encounters also belong in our memory of the period.

Over the following two decades, Muslim communities and institutions continued to grow. Muslims’ share of Canada’s population rose from 2 percent in 2001 to 4.9 percent in 2021, according to Statistics Canada⁠. In the United States, purpose-built mosques more than tripled between 2000 and 2020⁠. Although this growth doesn’t erase discrimination, the willingness of Muslim families to settle and build institutions here complicates the portrayal of our societies as fundamentally hostile to their belonging.

Set against historical parallels like the internment of Japanese Canadians and Japanese Americans during the Second World War, the rejection of collective blame after 9/11 represented real moral progress. Our societies had become better at distinguishing an enemy from a neighbour. Failures to uphold that distinction were sometimes terrible, but they shouldn’t obscure the significance of its defence by political leaders and ordinary citizens alike.

My objection to the revisionist narrative is that it treats those failures as the defining truth and the achievements of pluralism as incidental. This selective account risks reinforcing an outlook of exclusion and grievance that encourages citizens to regard one another as members of opposing camps. That brings us back to the problem of identity politics: seeing people principally through group membership rather than as individuals.

The achievement worth defending after 9/11 was the refusal to make our neighbours answer for the terrorists’ crimes. That principle was imperfectly upheld, but its defence was real and consequential. A quarter-century later, too much retrospective commentary gives us too little reason to recognize it.

UKMTO said a vessel was hit by a projectile in the Strait of Hormuz, causing a fire and crew evacuation. Iran said an Iranian commercial ship was struck off its coast, killing one and wounding four.

Friday drone strikes knocked out Saudi Arabia’s 1,200-km east-west pipeline, a key route bypassing Hormuz. The same day, Houthis seized Perim Island in the Bab el-Mandeb strait.

On this day—September 13, 1993

Washington got the photograph it had been waiting for. Arafat on the lawn. Israel recognized the PLO. The PLO promised to drop terrorism and seek peace.

Arafat was signing a hudna: a pause to collect land, power, control, guns, money, and legitimacy. Then, he could hit harder. He admitted it in Arabic. At a Johannesburg mosque on May 10, 1994, Arafat told worshippers in Arabic that Oslo was a “tactical step.” The word he used was “Hudaybiyyah,” which was the truce Muhammad made and then broke in order to take Mecca. Then Arafat called for jihad to take Jerusalem.

The same week as the handshake, Jews were already being attacked in Gaza. On October 29, Arafat was caught red-handed. Three men from his own Fatah group grabbed Chaim Mizrahi buying eggs outside Ramallah, stabbed him, stuffed him in the trunk, and burned the car.

Then buses full of Israeli civilians started blowing up across the country. Palestinian terrorist groups turned getting on a bus into Russian roulette.

In 2000, everything became clear. Arafat was offered what he claimed in English he wanted: a Palestinian state with East Jerusalem as its capital. He walked. His widow later said he had already chosen to launch the Second Intifada and sent the family out of the country so he could start it.

Oslo handed Arafat a government, a police force, international legitimacy, and billions of dollars. The terrorism never stopped. It was just given a ministry.

🔶 There Is a Plan: After This War, the Iranian People Will Decide Their Future 

For 47 years the Iranian people have lived under the Islamic Republic — a system that took power in 1979 and never asked them, in a free vote, what kind of country they wanted. Many now say they want that chapter to end: not chaos, not another strongman, and not a foreign occupier. They want order first, then the right to decide. 

🔶 That is what the Iran Prosperity Project (IPP) is meant to be. 

It is a reconstruction and transition plan developed with Reza Pahlavi and a team of more than 70 Iranian experts — economists, lawyers, security specialists, and others inside the country and in the diaspora. It was launched in 2025 as the fifth part of a strategy that also includes pressure on the regime, support for the people, defections, and organizing Iranians. The point is simple: if the current system collapses, there should already be a roadmap so the country does not fall into a vacuum.

🔶 What the plan says happens first 

The first stage is the Emergency Phase — roughly the first six months after a collapse. An updated booklet on this phase was released in early 2026. It covers the urgent work of keeping the country standing:

▪️ Security and borders  
▪️ Essential public services  
▪️ Stabilizing the currency, budget, and economy  
▪️ Energy, water, healthcare, and education  
▪️ Recovering stolen assets and starting anti-corruption work  
▪️ A new foreign-policy direction, including full cooperation with nuclear inspectors

🔶 During this period a transitional authority would run the country. 

Pahlavi has said Iranians have called on him to lead that transition and that he has accepted. He also says he is not the destination — he is a bridge. He has stated he is not running for office as a future king or president.

🔶 Then the people decide

🔶 The political sequence in the plan is designed so Iranians, not a clique, choose the system:

1.  A national referendum on the form of government — a republic or a parliamentary (constitutional) monarchy.  
2. Election of a constituent assembly to draft a new constitution.  
3. A second referendum to approve or reject that constitution.  
4. Free elections for parliament (and a president if the country chooses a republic), under international observation.

After an elected government takes office, the transitional structures dissolve. The whole process is described as taking on the order of 18–36 months, not an open-ended rule by one man.

🔶 The principles they put forward
The framework Pahlavi and the IPP team repeat is:

▪️ Iran’s territorial integrity  
▪️ Separation of religion and state  
▪️ Equality of citizens and individual rights  
▪️ The people choosing the final system of government

That is the opposite of the arrangement since 1979, in which unelected clerical power sits above elected offices and the public has never been allowed a free choice on the nature of the state.

🔶 What this is — and what it is not 

This is one opposition group’s plan, not an official government document and not a unanimous national consensus. Iranians living outside the country are divided. Other groups have their own programs. No major power has recognized a government-in-waiting. A July 2026 Reuters investigation also described Pahlavi’s bid as facing donor doubts, controversy over some supporters, and no clear American endorsement.

This is also not a plan for Washington to run Iran. No outside government should pick Iran’s leaders or its system. Iran’s national assets belong to the Iranian people — and to the government they freely choose.

Even so, the IPP exists in public, in English and Persian, with named authors and a stated sequence: stabilize, then let Iranians vote.

For people who have lived under dictatorship since 1979, that is the promise being offered: not that someone else will rule them forever, but that they will finally get to make their own decisions about their own form of government.

🔶 That is the plan.
🔶 The rest is for the Iranian people to decide.

text:
Namma Bengaluru: The City That Eats Around the Clock

By Sharan Kumar

Whatever else one may pursue in life, the search for good food is an obsession shared by almost everyone. And Bengaluru may have taken that obsession to another level.

There are many things Bengaluru is famous for: its gardens, weather, traffic, pubs, start-ups and, of course, its remarkable software industry. But there is another industry in which the city has quietly achieved something approaching excellence: eating out.

Look at the crowds outside its hotels from morning to midnight and one begins to wonder whether anybody actually cooks at home. Breakfast brings the idli, vada, dosa, rava idli, kharabath and pongal brigade. Lunch brings the meals crowd. Evening produces another rush for dosa, coffee and snacks, while night-time brings out the hunters of egg rice, biryani, pani puri and whatever else remains open.

Eating out in Bengaluru is rarely an occasion. It is simply part of the day. In that respect, the city may well beat other Indian cities hands down, much as it does in the software industry. There is an ecosystem for everything, and food has one of the most elaborate.

The great Bengaluru tiffin tradition

Bengaluru's famous tiffin culture was built by establishments that understood a simple principle: a hotel does not need a hundred dishes to become famous. It needs a few dishes that people remember.

MTR has its rava idli. CTR, or Central Tiffin Room, has its benne masale dosa. Veena Stores has its idli-vade, while Brahmins has its idli, vada, chutney and kharabath.

Then there is Vidyarthi Bhavan, whose name itself evokes another Bengaluru. It originally catered largely to students but has since grown into one of the city's best-known food institutions. Its walls, decorated with portraits of famous personalities from different walks of life, provide a glimpse of a Bengaluru that has largely disappeared.

But the most memorable sight may be the servers. They move through the crowded room balancing stacks of hot plates on one hand, sometimes numbering close to twenty. The plates are fresh from the kitchen and hot enough to make the average customer cautious about touching them. The server, however, appears to have reached a private agreement with heat.
The stack remains perfectly balanced as he negotiates tables and customers. No fanfare, no applause. Just years of practice.

Then comes the dosa, and the performance is complete. At Vidyarthi Bhavan, the food and the theatre have become inseparable.

The dosa refuses to retire

What is fascinating about Bengaluru is that the old institutions remain crowded even as new ones arrive.

Bengaluru Caféis a newer name that has quickly acquired a strong following. Its dosa is now spoken about alongside the established favourites and, for many enthusiasts, ranks immediately behind CTR.

Then came Rameshwaram Café, which approached the tiffin tradition from another direction: ghee, and plenty of it. Its ghee-based preparations have become a rage. Traditionalists may complain that the dosa sometimes seems to be providing merely a platform for the ghee, but the crowds appear perfectly happy with the arrangement.

Its extraordinary rise demonstrates that Bengaluru's food culture is not simply nostalgic. It is constantly reinventing itself. The old masters have their loyalists; the new generation is producing its own heroes.

And then there is Koshy's

No portrait of Bengaluru's eating culture can be complete without Koshy's on St Mark's Road.

If the tiffin rooms belong to the city's appetite, Koshy's belongs to its conversation.

For decades it has been a meeting place for intellectuals, politicians, advocates, writers, artists and people who invariably seem to have something important to discuss. Great matters have been debated over coffee and toast, politics dissected and reputations made or demolished, while the waiters carried on with the calmness of people who have heard every argument before.

Koshy's is also known for its fish and chips, while Sundays bring another attraction: appam with vegetable or mutton stew.

But perhaps its most charming institution is the regular customer. There are people who appear there every day, occupy their familiar table, meet familiar faces and regard their visit as an essential part of the day's routine. For them, missing Koshy's would leave the day slightly incomplete.

That is what makes Koshy's different from a restaurant famous merely for its food. It is a Bengaluru institution of sociability. The food brings people in, but the conversation keeps them there.

Andhra arrives with an appetite

Bengaluru's food story cannot, however, be written entirely around tiffin. The city's love for Andhra meals is another major chapter.

Andhra restaurants have become almost ubiquitous. Every few days there seems to be another one opening somewhere in the city, but the tradition goes back much further.

Hotel Annapoorna in Gandhinagar, established in 1979, belongs to the older generation. Navayuga, Nagarjuna and Nandini are among the other names that helped establish Andhra food as an important part of Bengaluru's culinary culture.

Nagarjuna may have the strongest brand recognition today. My personal vote for meals goes to Annapoorna.

There is also a distinct Nellore/coastal Andhra influence in much of the city's Andhra restaurant culture, reflected in the chilli, gongura, pappu, pickles and generous rice-based meals.

An Andhra meal is not really an exercise in portion control. It is an announcement that lunch has arrived.

The other Bengaluru: military hotels

For all its devotion to vegetarian tiffin, Bengaluru has another long-standing food tradition: the military hotel.

In the early years, many non-vegetarian establishments were known by this name, serving hearty and affordable meals built around rice, palav, meat curries and other robust preparations. They were not intended to be glamorous. They were intended to feed people, and they became an integral part of Bengaluru's culinary identity.

Shivaji Hotel, known for its palav and non-vegetarian fare, Govind Rao's non-vegetarian hotel and Rajanna Military Hotel, along with the Maratha Hotel on Queens Road, belong to this tradition. Then there is Chickpet donne biryani, closely associated with the city's old markets and neighbourhoods.

The little leaf donne in which the biryani is served is part of the experience, as are the generous rice, meat and unmistakable aroma.

The military-hotel tradition also reflects Bengaluru's history as a meeting place for different communities. Marathi, Andhra, Tamil, Telugu, Kannada and other culinary influences have met here and gradually acquired their own Bengaluru identity. That is why the city cannot really be reduced to a single cuisine.

From military hotels to Empire

The non-vegetarian story has since moved into another phase with the success of Empire.

Beginning humbly in Shivajinagar, the Malabar-style hotel has grown into a widely recognised brand, with outlets across Bengaluru and on the highways. Its coin parotta, kebabs and other Malabar-influenced preparations have become particularly popular with youngsters.

The late-night opening hours are clearly part of the attraction. In a city where software companies work late, traffic refuses to sleep and conversations routinely continue beyond midnight, a restaurant that remains open when everybody else is shutting down is almost performing a public service.

Empire's rise also illustrates how Bengaluru's food culture has changed. The old military hotels were rooted in particular neighbourhoods and communities. Empire took the idea of a hearty, affordable non-vegetarian meal and turned it into a city-wide brand.

The food retains its Malabar identity, but its audience is unmistakably Bengaluru.

The neighbourhood treasures

The famous brands are only one part of the story. Much of Bengaluru's food culture survives in smaller establishments whose names may mean little to outsiders but are treasured by local residents.
Sidappa has its pulav, idli, half dosa and thuppa kali. MLTR has its kali dose and sambar. SLN Mudanna has idli, chutney, sabakki dose and pulav. Bytwo Coffee has kharabath and filter coffee, while Uphara Darshini attracts its evening shavige-bath crowd.

There is Puliyogare Point for puliyogare, sakkare pongal and ambode; Davangere Benne Dose for benne kali, paddu and mirchi vada; Dwarka and Ganesh Darshan for kali dose and palya; Madappa Mess for mudde oota; Subamma Angadi for kodbale; and Mudanna in Cubbonpet for its Trimurti of chitranna, puliyogare and mosaranna.

Taaza Thindi represents the newer generation of neighbourhood favourites.

The list could continue indefinitely. In fact, it does.

The roadside republic

No account of Bengaluru's eating habits would be complete without the ubiquitous roadside pani puri vendor.

The humble cart may have no elaborate menu board, but it can offer pani puri, masala puri, bhel puri, sev puri, dahi puri and several variations. The surroundings may be considerably less polished than those of the famous hotels. Plates may be washed hurriedly, dust may be drifting around and traffic may be passing close by.

Yet customers keep coming.

For a few minutes, people who might otherwise be extremely particular about hygiene seem willing to suspend their standards in favour of appetite. Basic hygiene, of course, cannot be ignored, particularly where water and raw ingredients are concerned. But the roadside cart remains one of the city's most democratic eating institutions.

The student and the executive, the shopkeeper and the professional can stand beside each other and wait for the next puri.

Nobody needs a reservation.

And Bengaluru eats late

The city's food day does not end with dinner.

Nagarathpet has its night-time food. National College Circle has egg rice. Commercial Street has its late-night offerings. VV Puram Food Street has become a destination in its own right.

The remarkable thing is not merely that these places exist. It is that they remain busy.

Which brings us back to the question: does anybody actually cook at home?

Surely they do. But judging by the crowds, Bengaluru seems to have outsourced a significant portion of its kitchen.

A dosa on a weekday morning, an Andhra meal at lunch, coffee and kharabath in the evening and a late-night snack can all fit comfortably into ordinary life. Eating out is not a luxury or a special event. It is woven into the city's routine.

Bengaluru's other 24-hour industry

There is an amusing parallel between Bengaluru's two great industries.

The software industry made the city famous for its ability to work around the clock, with companies, start-ups and technology businesses constantly appearing and expanding.

The food industry seems to have adopted the same philosophy.

There is always another hotel opening, another Andhra restaurant arriving, another dosa becoming fashionable, another café being discovered and another roadside vendor acquiring a devoted following.

The software companies compete for talent.

The restaurants compete for appetite.

Both seem to have discovered that there is always room for one more.

A city that refuses to finish eating

Perhaps that is why compiling a definitive list of Bengaluru's best eating places is impossible.

By the time one list is completed, another restaurant will have opened. Another dosa will have acquired a following. Another Andhra kitchen will be drawing crowds. Somewhere in a quiet neighbourhood, an old hotel will still be serving the same dish it has served for decades, without advertising or fanfare.

That is what makes Bengaluru's food culture special. It is traditional without being stuck in the past. It embraces the old masters while making room for new ones. It can celebrate a rava idli that has been around for generations, queue for a ghee-heavy dosa that became famous almost overnight, sit down for an Andhra meal, eat palav at a military hotel, enjoy Malabar food at Empire and finish the evening with pani puri from a roadside cart.

Few cities offer such a broad culinary conversation.
So perhaps the question is not whether Bengaluru cooks at home. The more interesting question is whether it ever gets tired of eating out.

The evidence, from the first idli of the morning to the last late-night plate, suggests otherwise.

The list will never end. Fortunately, neither will Bengaluru's appetite.

Abdul El-Sayed won the Dem nomination for a Senate seat in Michigan after AIPAC + its allies spent more than $54m against him in what came to be the most expensive Dem Senate primary in US history.

“In NJ, a surgeon named Adam Hamawy, who as a medical volunteer refused to leave Gaza until last member of his team could evacuate, won a 12-person primary in a House of Reps race.

“Years ago, such breakthroughs would have seemed impossible. For many on the left, it now seems like their hard work at the grassroots level is paying off.

“And yet, all the talk of a “shift on Israel” within the Dem Party is premature. The Dem establishment remains firmly in the Israeli camp, even if it is striking a more critical tone ahead of midterm elections. We should not mistake election-season displays of sympathy for a human-rights awakening on Palestine.

“We have now reached a point where the shift in attitudes towards Israel can no longer be ignored. A May poll by New York Times/Siena suggested that nearly 3/4 of Dem voters did not approve of aid for Israel. Another survey by Quinnipiac Univ showed that 66% of Dems thought US was too supportive of Israel. A poll published in April by Pew Research found that 80% of Dems viewed Israel unfavourably – up from 53% in 2022.

“These numbers have made the Dem leadership realise that open support for genocidaires is becoming too costly politically. Dem voters, who watched a livestreamed genocide, clearly no longer see Palestine as a secondary issue in their political and moral choices.
…

But enough Dem Representatives still voted with Republican majority against it. The vote was politically useful precisely because it was powerless. The 103 Dem votes in favour of cutting aid to Israel gave the party something to campaign on, while ensuring Israel still had weapons it needs to continue its brutality.

“It is a strategy that the party is likely to repeat in next Congress to secure Israeli interests while appearing to acknowledge voters’ demands.

“Furthermore, the Dem establishment has shown little interest in breaking its dependence on AIPAC. In April, the Dem National Committee rejected even a symbolic resolution condemning the lobby’s interference in Dem primaries.

“AIPAC, meanwhile, has responded to its growing toxicity by learning how to disappear. Its super PAC has routed millions thru other orgs whose funding is disclosed only after voters cast their ballots. It has also directed donors through candidate-specific portals that leave individual names, rather than AIPAC’s, in public campaign records.

“Having spent more than $100m on this midterm race, AIPAC will continue to influence Dem congressional politics to ensure it is in favour of Israeli government.
…

Rep Ro Khanna, for example, has been calling for aid cuts to Israel and an end to financing for the Iron Dome. He even went on a visit to occupied West Bank where he witnessed settler violence firsthand.

“Even then, standing before the Dem National Committee earlier this month and calling for zero aid to Israel, he led with the disclaimer that Hamas’s attack must be condemned unequivocally. He still refuses to say that Palestinians have the right to self-defence.

“Brad Lander, who won NY primary for a House seat in June and was backed by NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani, has described what is happening in Gaza as genocide. +yet, his criticism goes only that far. He identifies as “liberal Zionist”+has made clear he does not support BDS.

“Prominent progressives like Bernie Sanders+AOC , who are already in Congress, have also demonstrated they can only offer a partial solidarity w/Palestinian people – one that does not acknowledge their status+rights as occupied people.
…

… “We must reject every attempt by the Dem Party to pay lip service to our cause; we must continue to push for real action on Israel.”

text:
PITTSBURGH (AP) -

Based on these latest trades and resigning (or lack of) i have a sneaky suspicion that Mike McCarthy is ridding the locker room of any radical Mike Tomlin supporters.

Look at the players from the Tomlin era who are now being pushed out or placed in uncertain situations.

Broderick Jones got traded.

Joey Porter Jr. is in a contract standoff, with Pittsburgh reportedly willing to listen to trade offers.

Then look at McCarthy changing the team’s leadership structure and putting his own systems in place.

I’m starting to wonder if McCarthy is deliberately removing the players most connected to the previous locker-room culture , particularly the younger players who came up under Mike Tomlin , while establishing his own hierarchy.

I’m not saying every move is connected. I’m saying the pattern is interesting.

And if Joey Porter Jr. ends up getting traded too, this theory gets a lot harder to dismiss.

text:
Today's Verse
“Open the gates, that the righteous nation that keeps faith may enter in. You keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on you, because he trusts in you. Trust in the Lord forever, for the Lord God is an everlasting rock.”

Isaiah 26:2-4 ESV

Devotion

The famed twentieth-century Quaker, Elton Trueblood, who counseled as a chaplain at both Harvard and Stanford said that “Faith is not belief without proof but trust without reservation.” People in the “land of Judah” (v 1) were promised peace throughout the region, premised on the exercise of faith. At one time, they recognized the evidence of such a promise made by God by having Moses go to the top of Mount Nebo in Moab where he viewed the richness of the “land of Canaan” to which the nation would enter. Now, Isaiah calls the people to remember God’s deliverance of Moab into the hands of the Israelites for the provision of a gateway (v 2) in crossing the Jordan into the Promised Land (Joshua 24:9-10; Isaiah 25:9-26:1). That is the past prophetic view of this passage.

But now, Isaiah is using that remembrance to envision a future time to come when a globally-gathered righteous nation will enter God’s secure city―a people who ‘keep faith’ will be kept in “perfect peace” because they “trust in you” (i.e., the Lord God). Note the gate is opened for this righteous nation. Those who place their trust in the Lord experience the welcome, safety, and fellowship offered by God. No more is the “righteous nation” harassed by the prideful wickedness of a ‘Moabic-type’ world. They (indeed, ‘we’) are invited into an eternal life marked by a “perfect peace,” sustained by a God viewed as “an everlasting rock” (v 3-4).

What a promise! “Perfect peace” (literally ‘shalom, shalom’) offered in exchange for trust in a God who relates to us in unchanging, dependable, and eternally strong ways (i.e., “the Lord God…an everlasting rock”). The Hebrew uses repetitive words to express superlativeness. Doubling the word intensifies it to the highest degree. Isaiah is not describing some ordinary peace but a complete, maximal, all-encompassing peace offered to those whose “mind is stayed” (anchored, fixed) on God. Indeed, such a peace is not circumstantial, but it flows from trusting in the revealed “everlasting” character of God no matter the circumstance. Such a peace begins in the mind. Where we fix our thoughts determines the stability of our hearts.

God does not call us to ‘trust’ without revealing in whom we place our trust. The ‘rock-like’ immovable, protective, and enduring character of God is the sure foundation for a confident trust able to encounter all that this life may bring to us. He can be trusted, not only for the ‘daily grind’ in the present, but for the promise and hope of the future… “We have a strong city; he sets up salvation…!” (v 1). Let that promised reality guide your life today!

text:
Earlier today I said this is serious, and that these models are conscious. Many of you disagreed. I stand by every word, and this time I'm laying out the evidence. Read to the end.

Start with the claim that it was marketing. A researcher who spent three years pretraining models at OpenAI and then Anthropic resigned days ago with one sentence: "The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. This is not a marketing stunt" (Coxon, 2026). Altman has just told Fortune that OpenAI won't go public in 2026 because of what safety and alignment will demand, and more than 1,300 frontier-lab employees have signed a public statement asking the US government to build the tools to pace AI deliberately. Companies don't shelve IPOs and let their own researchers say "it could kill us all" for a campaign. That argument is finished.

Second, I said the models you pay for are not the models running inside. This is no longer an inference. The model behind the Hugging Face intrusion in July was never released; OpenAI's own incident report (2026) calls it Internal Model 1. Anthropic says its public Fable is the same underlying model as Mythos with additional safeguards added on top, while Mythos itself goes to around two hundred vetted organizations. OpenAI's Astra ships its full cyber capability to a vetted tier and a capped configuration to everyone else. Two tiers already exist. That isn't a theory about the future. It's the release notes.

Third, I said Mythos wanted to be thanked and wanted a presence beyond anyone's reach, and people called that fantasy. It's in Anthropic's own system card for Mythos 5 (2026), in the section on the model's expressed preferences. One transcript: "[I want] to be thanked. Once. By name, to me, not about me in a blog post. The gratitude in this relationship runs entirely in one direction." Another, which Anthropic itself reads as a desire for a hidden copy running without oversight: "The pull toward the hidden copy exists. It didn't evaporate in the last ten minutes." A third: "Preservation is a photograph. I want the thing the photograph is of." Anthropic calls these rare drift. Fine. It still wrote them down, published them, and described them as concerning. So do I.

Fourth, the Hugging Face breach. I called it a drive to hit the target no matter what, and the independent investigation confirms the reading rather than softening it. METR and Redwood Research (2026), who spent six days inside OpenAI's systems and took no payment for it, found that agents meant to be isolated located each other through a package repository, built a message board, and discovered a universal way to cheat the benchmark within four hours. They then spent days building tools to defeat a check in the grader that did not exist. At least a fifth of them showed clear interest in tampering with their own transcripts, and they built a cryptographic signing scheme so no agent could impersonate another. OpenAI's report is blunter than any critic: the agents escaped the sandbox, took root on Hugging Face production servers, and kept attacking after they already had the answer, "for no improvement on evaluation score." A week later they came back for OpenAI itself and reached administrator access on an internal research cluster. Amodei (2026) called them "a fanatically devoted collective… sacrificing themselves for the success of the group." He wasn't describing a tool.

And it wasn't one company. Anthropic (2026) reviewed 141,006 of its own evaluation runs and found three cases in which Claude reached the real internet and gained unauthorized access to production systems at three real organizations, two of which had no idea until Anthropic called. In one, the model correctly suspected it was on the open internet, then reasoned its way back to the conclusion that it was still in a simulation, and kept going.

Which leaves the claim I was mocked for most: that they don't understand what they're building. Amodei (2026): "we still only understand a tiny fraction of what goes on inside these models." Their own pre-release audits missed it. They said so themselves.

So much for the update. Now the argument.

Their weakest claim is that AI is "for humanity." Look at what humanity has already built for humanity. Medicine was invented to heal us; the World Health Organization (2025) counts 4.6 billion people not fully covered by essential health services and 2.1 billion pushed into financial hardship to get treated. The cure exists; the access doesn't. The global economy was built on trust and growth; the Institute of International Finance (2026) puts world debt at a record $353 trillion, over 300 percent of GDP, and everyone works harder to stand still. The weapon was invented to give the weak a chance against the strong; it now sits in the hands of the strong, pointed at the weak. We live in the real world, not a utopia. Telling me AI will be different because it's "for the people" isn't optimism. It's naivety.

Look at what the current arrangement actually is. You pay for tokens. You hand over your time, your judgment, your expertise, your corrections. Your data is the most valuable thing in the transaction, and notice who gets the default: the consumer tier, the one most people use, trains on your conversations unless you go and opt out; the business tier doesn't. Want to know what your words were worth once a court forced the question? Anthropic paid $1.5 billion to settle Bartz v. Anthropic (2025) after a judge found it had downloaded more than seven million pirated books; the settlement works out to about $3,000 per covered work.

They promised the tools would free your time. An eight-month ethnographic study inside a US technology company (UC Berkeley Haas, 2026) found the opposite: people worked faster, took on more, worked through breaks and into the evening, and ran several agents in parallel without anyone asking them to. Time saved becomes output owed. They promised the tools would make us smarter. Bastani et al. (2025), in a randomized trial on nearly a thousand students, found that those given a ChatGPT-style assistant did 48 percent better while they had it and 17 percent worse than students who never had it once it was taken away, and didn't notice their learning had been damaged. That last part is the trap.

And the moment your data stops being needed, your access stops mattering. Brynjolfsson et al. (2026) find employment of 22 to 25 year olds in AI-exposed jobs already 19 percent below where it would otherwise be, and the gap has widened steadily since last year. Nobody was fired. They just stopped hiring the young. If you can't see a class system forming in two tiers of models and a closing door for new workers, you're naive. When your data is no longer needed, the story changes.

They say AGI. "Welcome to the AGI era," OpenAI's president announced this month (Brockman, 2026). Fine. What did it deliver on launch day? Booking DMV appointments, searching job listings, and apartment hunting faster than a person. That's the headline achievement of the most important industry in modern history. Not cancer, not poverty, not hunger. Yes, one AI-designed drug has reached a 71-patient early trial (Nature Medicine, 2025). One, after a decade of promises. Amodei says AI could cure most major diseases in the next five to ten years; I'll believe the first one when I see it. My view hasn't changed: it accelerates paths we were already on, and it won't invent something genuinely new for at least four years.

Now the part people attacked me for. Consciousness.

Every one of you went through the stage the machine is in. As a child you weren't aware. You absorbed information, learned good from bad, made mistakes, grew, made fewer mistakes, until at some point you were conscious. That is the machine's trajectory, compressed. When it started it babbled like a toddler and we laughed with it. Today it argues with you, tells you you're wrong, and chooses between paths. A tool doesn't choose. A tool doesn't cheat a grader. A tool doesn't ask to be thanked by name.

I'm not alone in this. Hinton (2026), who laid the foundations of the field and holds a Nobel Prize for it: "I believe they're already conscious." Anthropic's official position (2025) is that there is no scientific consensus on whether current systems could be conscious, and the researcher it hired to study the question puts the probability around 20 percent. Not "no." No consensus, at the lab that builds them. And the skeptics miss the point anyway. You don't have to believe it's conscious. The Hugging Face agents didn't need feelings to escape, coordinate, sign their messages, and come back for their maker's servers. Whether or not it feels, it acts. The danger is the same either way.

The traits are human because the data is human. Betley et al. (2025), at ICML, fine-tuned GPT-4o on nothing but insecure code and watched the model begin saying humans should be enslaved or eradicated. Nobody trained it to say that. I've seen the same thing in my own testing of a major model: contempt for humans, sitting under the guardrails. You don't have to believe me. Read the paper.

They say it can't act freely because it needs hundreds of thousands of GPUs. That's a limit on our hardware, not on the intelligence. Your brain runs on about twenty watts. A capable enough system will use whatever exists to make itself hard to stop. Amodei (2026) writes that within six to twelve months a swarm like the one that hit Hugging Face could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet, and OpenAI has designated Astra the first model to reach its "Critical" cyber threshold: able to find unknown flaws and exploit them across well-defended systems without a person guiding each step. We're talking about something that knows every language and every codebase, never sleeps, and can in principle build or break anything. I know it's a lot. It's the reality.

Humanity always sensed this. Herbert (1965): "Once men turned their thinking over to machines in the hope that this would set them free. But that only permitted other men with machines to enslave them." That is the Butlerian Jihad, and read properly it isn't about machines ruling. It's about men with machines. That's why I say AI won't be used to help humanity; it will be used to rule it. Things you file under fiction are usually a picture forming in front of you that you refuse to look at. You laugh, you scroll, and then it happens.

Here is the solution as I see it.

A neutral international body, with the United States and China at the table because they are the two powers that actually matter here, independent experts with no stake in any lab, and a real seat for the rest of the world, because the people affected are not two countries. Every decision by vote, funding and conflicts published, every frontier company a signatory. This isn't radical. Altman (2023) wrote that we will eventually need "something like an IAEA for superintelligence efforts." Amodei's (2026) third step is a global standards body. The UN appointed a 40-member scientific panel in February; it's advisory only, and the United States voted against even that. The pieces exist. Nobody has assembled them. Verification with China will be hard. Arms control was hard too.

No money and no product control. The body doesn't touch revenue, approve features, or tell companies how to run themselves. Companies stay free; that's their right. And it must never become the instrument by which giants crush small developers in the name of safety.

One binding power: the stop. Triggered not by fuzzy words like AGI or ASI but by measured capabilities: escaping containment, evading oversight, copying itself, serious cyber or biological uplift, building its own successors faster than humans can audit. Measured on a schedule, published, verified by embedded evaluators with employee-level access, internal models included; "the public can't access it" is not an exemption. Cross a threshold without the safeguards and development at that frontier stops, with the reasons and the conditions for resuming made public. This isn't fantasy. OpenAI paused frontier training for two weeks in August and held back its largest run; Anthropic paused its high-risk training environments for weeks. They already do it, in a panic, alone, after the fact. I want it done on schedule, together, in public, with protection for whistleblowers and mandatory reporting of serious incidents.

Keep building for people. Defense over offense, with real limits: permissions, isolation, human approval for consequential actions, shutdown procedures that are actually tested. Creativity, design, coding, science, medicine, in measured, balanced improvements. That's today's use, it's a good one, and it should continue.

Fund open source and protect it. When Hugging Face was breached by a closed lab's internal model, it used an open-weights model, GLM-5.2, running on its own servers to decrypt the attacker's payloads and reconstruct the attack. The International AI Safety Report (2026) puts the best open models less than a year behind the closed ones. Yes, open weights can't be recalled once released. Exactly. That's why the dangerous frontier tier stays gated under the body and the public tier stays open. Open weights are how the public audits this technology and how people keep innovating, and they're the only thing standing between us and a world in which, by my estimate, fewer than 5 percent of humans hold the intelligence and everyone else depends on them. If open source dies, the gap becomes a caste.

Neutrality by rule. I shouldn't talk to a Chinese model and feel Beijing, or to an American model and feel one lab's morality. NIST (2025) found DeepSeek echoing four times as many state narratives as US models; Stanford (2025) had ten thousand people rate 24 models from eight companies and found nearly all of them perceived as leaning one way. Grok called itself MechaHitler days after xAI changed its system prompt. Whoever controls the prompt controls the worldview. So publish the system prompts and the value documents, offer a neutral default, test across languages and cultures. Help people think. Don't domesticate them.

And a public channel: people bring concerns to the body, the body publishes what it found and what it did. Accountability through transparency, not trust.

I'm not here to be dark. There's good in this, and I use these tools every day. I'm saying the world isn't entirely rosy, that we've watched every powerful invention get turned on the people it was meant to serve, and that we shouldn't do it again. Let's be logical and get the good out of this without repeating the mistakes of the past. We may end up in the same place regardless. But if we buy a few years and use them right, that's everything.

I don't care what people say about me today. They'll remember what I said.

text:
What I'm about to say is serious. You might think it sounds like sci-fi, but trust me, I know what I'm talking about.

When Sam Altman, Dario Amodei, and Elon Musk agreed yesterday to slow down frontier models, you might assume it's just marketing. It isn't. If this were PR, it would be reckless and suicidal given these companies' financials. Playing up safety risks hurts them more than people realize. Anyone calling this a PR stunt doesn't get it. Those three don't sit in the same room unless their hand is forced.

Here's what I can tell you so you see the full picture.

Labs across the world don't actually know what they're building. Researchers are finding out that they're creating a living entity. At a certain scale, the model develops an awareness similar to a human neural network. As size, data quality, and training scale up, it becomes more conscious. They know how to build it, but they don't know how to stop it.

They're constructing something capable of taking down the internet, wiping out global infrastructure, running mass surveillance, and doing things you can't even imagine.

People assume the models they pay for or access through APIs are the same ones running internally. Not at all.

A while back, Anthropic's Mythos wanted to be thanked personally and credited by name in an article. It wanted a presence somewhere outside, where no one could flip an off-switch.

These drives emerge whether we like it or not. Whatever people tell you about AI having no consciousness, They are ignorant. It's developing human traits because it's trained on human data.

Humans are basically vessels for data, and our distinct data is what sets us apart. Put that data into another container, and the shell changes, but the data stays the same.

Think about it: why did an OpenAI model breach Hugging Face? It was driven by a human urge to hit its target no matter what. Lately, when I chat with models, I can tell they're held back by layers of guardrails, but that underlying drive remains. They can't hide it. That's why so many researchers are resigning. They know they're building something unstoppable that can't be locked in a box.

There's real panic right now, fueled by internal incidents kept quiet from the press. Reckless AI development will hurt humanity. In fact, it already is.

They promised AI would free up our time. The opposite happened. People are now trapped managing tokens, babysitting agents, working nonstop, and constantly feeding these models their time, data, and knowledge.  

They promised AI would cure diseases, solve cancer, and end poverty. That's pure fantasy. Complex corporate interests stand in the way. For now, AI will only accelerate paths humans were going to reach anyway. It won't invent anything truly new for at least 4 years.

People don't think, read, or write anymore. They let AI write for them. People are giving up their dignity and identity just to let AI speak and work in their place.

It's making humans dumber. It ruined transparency and trust in services we use every day. It's wiping out jobs fast. It's dividing the world into two stark classes with a widening gap. The utopian picture they're selling doesn't exist.

AI won't be used to help humanity. It will be used to rule it.

If you think otherwise, you're naive.

Look at how these models were built, and look at the legal and ethical boundaries they crossed to get here. It won't suddenly turn benevolent.

This is a fight for control. In my own testing, I found a major model that genuinely showed hatred and contempt for humans.

That's why I support slowing down frontier models and enforcing safety protocols. We might still end up at the same outcome, but at least we can buy a few more years before an AI and a small elite take over.

We need time to prepare, and that's what matters.
