text:
Washington State

Climate Commitment Act (CCA) Monies for Sovereign Indian Tribes in WA State

Sept. 13, 2026

I am very aware that Climate Commitment Act (CCA) gas tax monies fund Sovereign Indian Tribes and the funding of electric boats for Sovereign Indian Tribes in Washington State.

The legal language is baked right into the Climate Commitment Act (CCA) legislative bill SB 5126 (2021).

SB 5126 (2021) 

** Environmental Justice Assessment

When allocating funds or administering grants funded by any of the program accounts, agencies must conduct an environmental justice assessment and establish a minimum of not less than 35 percent, and a goal of 40 percent, of total investments to provide direct and meaningful benefits to vulnerable populations within overburdened communities. Benefits may be achieved through reducing environmental burdens and cumulative risk from environmental burdens, supporting community-led projects, or meeting an identified community need. An additional 10 percent minimum target is established for projects supported by tribal resolution, with priority to projects directly administered or proposed by a tribe.

** Assistance Program for Offsets on Federally Recognized Tribal Lands

To ensure a sufficient number of high quality offset projects are available, Ecology must establish an
assistance program for offset projects on federally recognized tribal lands. The assistance may include funding or consultation to assess a project's technical feasibility, investment requirements, development, and operation costs, expected returns, administrative and legal hurdles, and project risks and pitfalls. Ecology may provide funding or assistance upon request by a federally recognized tribe. The Legislature intends to provide not less than $5 million in the operating budget for this purpose.

The Climate Commitment Account

The Climate Commitment Account is created in the
state treasury and is subject to appropriation. Projects, activities, and programs eligible for funding from the account must be physically located in Washington State and include the following:

11. support efforts to mitigate and adapt to the effects of climate change affecting Indian tribes, including capital investments in support of the relocation of tribes located in areas at heightened risk due to anticipated seal level rise, flooding, or other disturbances caused by climate change and for these purposes the Legislature intends to dedicate AT LEAST  $50 million per biennium.

NEW SECTION. Sec. 6. TRIBAL CONSULTATION

(1) Agencies that allocate funding or administer grant programs appropriated from the climate investment account created in section 28 of this act must
develop a consultation framework in coordination with tribal governments that includes best practices, protocols for communication, and collaboration with federally recognized tribes. Under this consultation framework, before allocating funding or administering grant programs appropriated from the climate investment  account, agencies must offer consultation with federally recognized tribes on all funding decisions and programs that may impact, infringe upon, or impair the governmental efforts of federally recognized tribes to adopt or enforce their own standards governing or protecting the tribe's resources or other rights and interests in their tribal lands and lands within which a tribe or tribes possess rights reserved by treaty. The consultation is independent of any public participation process required by state law, or by a state agency, and regardless of whether the agency receives a request for consultation from a federally recognized tribe.

(2)(a) If any funding decision, program, project, or activity that impacts lands within which a tribe or tribes possess rights reserved by federal treaty, statute, or executive order is undertaken or funded under this chapter without such consultation with a federally recognized tribe, an affected tribe may request that all further action on the decision, program, project, or activity cease until meaningful consultation with any directly impacted federally recognized tribe is completed.

text:
He didn’t inspect Ireland’s army as a substitute commander-in-chief, and he did not do it instead of Ireland’s head of state.
On 12 September 2026 Trump went to Áras an Uachtaráin, the Irish president’s residence in Phoenix Park. Ireland’s head of state is President Catherine Connolly. She received him there. They stood for both national anthems, a Defence Forces guard of honour presented arms, and Trump was invited to inspect that guard as a visiting head of state. Connolly then walked him through the introductions and they held a courtesy call. He also met Taoiseach Micheál Martin later. That is standard ceremonial protocol, not a takeover of Irish troops. https://t.co/MA5oo9zGOH 
Why it looks that way on video:
•  The visitor, not the host, usually walks the line of troops. The host stands nearby or accompanies him. A clip that only shows Trump walking past soldiers can look like he is doing it “alone.”
•  The honour guard is a ceremonial company, not the Irish Defence Forces as a whole. They are drawn from a battalion for the occasion (reports named the 27th/28th Infantry Battalion).
•  Ireland’s president is commander-in-chief of the Defence Forces. The Taoiseach runs the government. Neither has to physically walk every pace of the inspection for it to be legal or official.
This was a courtesy-call ceremony during a working/personal visit (golf at Doonbeg plus official meetings), not a state visit in the fullest sense. The troops were there as Ireland’s ceremonial welcome, offered by the Irish state to a visiting U.S. president. Irish police and Defence Forces were also providing security around him; that is protection of a guest, not him taking command. https://t.co/uOMK4ugu1M 
So: he inspected a guard of honour because Ireland invited him to, at the president’s house, with the president present. That is how these visits work.

text:
China Won’t Pause AI. It Will Govern It to Win.

Chen Yixin, China's Minister of State Security, recently detailed Beijing's unequivocal stance: artificial intelligence is the "main battlefield of global scientific and technological competition." China's strategy prioritizes building a robust AI security barrier and promoting its "healthy, orderly development." This position is explicitly rooted in national security and strategic rivalry, not solely technological innovation.

The central mechanism here is state-centric AI governance, directly guided by General Secretary Xi Jinping’s directives. Beijing views AI as a strategic technology with a "lead goose" effect, driving a new round of scientific and technological revolution and industrial transformation. This mandates self-reliance, application-oriented innovation, and positions security as the absolute bottom-line requirement. China's comprehensive framework for governance includes rapidly formulating laws, policy systems, ethical guidelines, and building technical monitoring, early warning, and emergency response systems. Its goal: to safeguard national interests, punish illegal AI activities like data theft, and counter what it terms foreign technological barriers and "slander."

Contrast this with recent Western calls for an AI slowdown. Following Dario Amodei's post from Anthropic about pausing AI development, Sam Altman of OpenAI and Elon Musk of XSpace offered their support. This emergent Western consensus suggests a collective pause, a moment for caution and reflection on the technology's rapid, often unpredictable, advance.

China's declared mechanism implies a decidedly different trajectory. It represents a state-driven acceleration, not a slowdown. The explicit objective is to "firmly grasp the initiative in AI development and governance." Beijing’s focus remains on vigorous domestic development and asserting its vision for international AI rules, while resisting "hegemonism" and "technological barriers."

So, will China follow the Western calls for an AI development slowdown? Highly improbable. Beijing's strategy is about accelerating its race for AI dominance. Governance, in this context, functions as a control mechanism to steer that speed and direction, ensuring China wins the strategic competition rather than pumping the brakes.

text:
The open letter from writer Eduard Topol to Donald Trump, shared by @jurgen_nauditt, lays out why any meeting with putin will not produce peace. Topol draws on Russian history.

The regime cannot afford to bring its army home. This is practical.

It rests on repeated cycles. Returning troops have toppled rulers, or threatened them.

The letter arrives before any planned encounter. It rejects the notion that property transfers or personal favors could alter the structural trap.

Topol positions himself as someone who has written fifty books and a dozen films on the subject. That gives him standing to speak directly rather than through filtered briefings.

Western audiences often treat such warnings as colorful anecdotes. The record shows they describe a consistent mechanism.

It has operated across centuries regardless of the individual in charge.

Putin Cannot End the War

Topol states outright that putin cannot end the war against Ukraine even if offered Mar-a-Lago, Trump Tower, and a dozen golf clubs. The constraint is not personal reluctance.

It follows from the knowledge that any intact army returning home creates immediate danger to the center.

Historical precedent demonstrates that victorious or even defeated forces have triggered revolt when brought back without an external occupation role. The letter treats this as settled pattern rather than speculation.

Advisors who promise quick deals ignore the same pattern. The regime survives by keeping its forces engaged abroad.

Any pause that removes that outlet exposes the ruler to the consequences of having trained and armed a large cohort of men in systematic violence. Concrete history supplies the evidence.

Wishful assumptions about negotiation power fail.

Decembrist Revolt Precedent

The return of Russian troops from Europe after victory over Napoleon produced the Decembrist revolt against the Tsar in 1825. Topol lists this as the first clear instance in the modern period.

Soldiers who had seen different political arrangements abroad brought those ideas back and acted on them.

The event established a recurring risk for any ruler who sends large forces outward and then tries to recall them without further purpose. Later leaders studied the outcome.

The pattern did not disappear with changes in ideology or technology. It reappeared whenever the army returned in numbers without an external mission to absorb its energy.

The letter uses this case to anchor the argument that current conditions follow the same logic. External occupation remains the only reliable buffer against internal challenge.

1905 and 1917 Parallels

Defeat in the Russo-Japanese War fed the Revolution of 1905. Mass desertions on the German front during World War I finished the Romanov dynasty in 1917.

Topol connects these events to the same underlying pressure. Military failure or sudden withdrawal removes the external focus and directs accumulated grievances inward.

Lenin's separate peace with Germany then cleared the path for the Bolsheviks to murder the imperial family.

Each step shows how ending one conflict without decisive control over the returning forces opens the next stage of instability. The letter presents these as documented sequences rather than selective examples.

Rulers who ignore the record repeat the exposure. The current regime operates under the same constraint.

Afghanistan and Soviet Collapse

The return of Soviet troops from Afghanistan in February 1989 marked the beginning of the USSR's collapse.

Topol notes that 525,000 soldiers came back and quickly became a destabilizing force described as Afghan bandits who terrorized the population.

The withdrawal removed the external mission that had justified the regime's internal controls. Within two years the union disintegrated.

The letter treats this as the most recent large-scale demonstration of the same mechanism. Any leader who contemplates bringing a comparable or larger force home intact must calculate the same risk.

The 1989 precedent supplies the direct comparison. It shows why occupation of neighboring territory serves as the preferred alternative to domestic reckoning.

Stalin's Postwar Occupation Solution

Only keeping almost the entire army in Europe as an occupation force after May 1945 saved Stalin from a coup in the postwar period. Topol identifies this as the exception that proves the rule.

The regime avoided the return shock by parking its forces abroad under the cover of victory and control. The arrangement lasted until internal decay and external pressure made it unsustainable.

The letter uses the case to illustrate that the pattern holds across different leadership styles. When the external anchor disappears, the internal threat reappears.

Current ambitions for control over Ukraine and further west follow the same calculation. Occupation abroad substitutes for legitimacy at home.

Putin's Territorial Ambitions Explained

The same logic drives current expansionist aims. Topol states that putin dreams of occupying Ukraine as well as the Baltic states, Finland, and Poland to keep the army away from Moscow.

The goal is tangible honor. preventing one and a half million soldiers who have learned to kill, loot, and rape professionally from returning as a coherent force.

The 525,000 veterans from Afghanistan already produced widespread criminal disruption. Scaling that number upward makes the threat existential for the junta.

The letter frames these territorial objectives as practical insurance rather than ideological excess. Any negotiated pause that leaves the army intact simply defers the reckoning.

The regime therefore has no structural interest in genuine withdrawal.

Domestic Control Mechanism

War also functions as a filter that removes two million active opponents through emigration and sends the remaining young population either to the front or into penal units.

Topol describes this as the most effective means of compelling submission. Any conflict, whether against Ukraine or farther west, maintains the pressure valve.

Peace removes it. The regime therefore treats external adventure as the substitute for internal legitimacy.

The letter notes that this mechanism operates regardless of the specific target. Western proposals for pauses or territorial concessions simply reset the cycle without addressing the underlying requirement.

The junta gains time and removes domestic challengers. Ukraine pays the immediate cost while the structural problem remains untouched.

Topol's Prescription for Trump

The letter recalls how Reagan, Thatcher, and John Paul II drove the price of oil down to nine dollars a barrel and supplied Stinger missiles to Afghan fighters.

That combination halted moscovian advances and accelerated Soviet collapse. Topol recommends repeating the approach.

Push oil prices to twenty-five dollars a barrel and supply Ukraine with weapons sufficient to defeat the aggressor outright.

Business partnerships with the current regime are dismissed as impossible for at least a century. The writer offers to explain the reasons in a direct call.

The prescription rests on the same historical record used throughout the letter. External economic pressure combined with direct military support produced results before.

The levers remain available.

Relevance to Current Battlefield Realities

Ukraine's long-range strikes already degrade moscovian logistics at operational depth. Rear-area facilities burn regularly.

Mid-range capabilities will expand two to five times by the end of 2026, isolating Crimea and collapsing forward supply lines.

Production licenses for Patriot and Tomahawk systems, combined with domestic air-defense output and integrated drone interceptors, will create layered coverage no previous Ukrainian force possessed.

These developments align with Topol's core point. Only battlefield defeat removes the regime's reason to continue.

Any agreement short of decisive military loss leaves the army intact and the ruler exposed to its return. Historical precedent shows the pattern repeats regardless of personal wishes.

Western attempts to engineer pauses through sanctions relief or territorial concessions simply reset the cycle. Ukraine holds the initiative on the ground and requires only the resources to complete the task.

Bu akademik yıl, İstanbul Üniversitesi-Cerrahpaşa Jeofizik Mühendisliği Bölümünün @iu_cerrahpasa  yedinci yarıyıl derslerinden biri olan Microzonation (Mikrobölgeleme) dersini birlikte işleyeceğiz.

Bölümümüzde kısa süre önce göreve başlamam nedeniyle sizlerle henüz tanışma fırsatımız olmadı. Microzonation seçmeli bir ders olduğundan, dersimi seçmeniz ve bu çalışmaya katılmanız beni çok mutlu edecektir.

Ders kapsamında, ülkemizin en önemli sorunlarından biri haline gelen depreme hazırlık konusu çerçevesinde mikrobölgelemenin temel ilkelerini ele alacağız. Özellikle yerel zemin etkisi, sıvılaşma ve heyelanlar üzerinde durarak; jeofizik, jeolojik ve geoteknik verilerin yerleşime uygunluk değerlendirmelerinde nasıl birlikte kullanılabileceğini inceleyeceğiz. Ayrıca bu verilerin deprem–zemin–yapı etkileşimi çalışmalarına ve kent planlamasına nasıl temel oluşturduğunu değerlendireceğiz.

Saha çalışmaları sırasında çeşitli jeofizik yöntemleri tanıyacak; veri toplama ve analiz süreçlerinde uygulamalı deneyim kazanacaksınız. Ayrıca farklı üniversitelerden akademisyenleri, belediyeler ve bakanlıklarda görev yapan uzmanları ve özel sektör çalışanlarını dersimize davet ederek bilgi ve deneyimlerini sizlerle paylaşmalarını sağlayacağız. Akademik ve mesleki yaşamınıza önemli katkılar sunacağına inandığım çalışma ve uygulamaları hep birlikte gerçekleştireceğiz.

Sizleri dersimde görmekten mutluluk duyacağımı belirtir, şimdiden başarılı bir dönem geçirmenizi dilerim.

I look forward to welcoming you to the course and wish you a successful semester in advance.

Assoc. Prof. Dr. Savaş Karabulut

text:
Competing Is Good. But Competing on an Unequal Playing Field Is Not. 🇸🇸

I agree that South Sudan should remain welcoming and avoid xenophobia. Foreigners are our brothers and sisters, and our country benefits from genuine investment, skills, partnerships, and global cooperation.

But I also believe we need to ask difficult questions, because this is an economic issue with national security consequences.

How do South Sudanese youth compete with people who control over 95% of the wholesale, retail, and distribution system?

Competition only works when the playing field is fair—when laws are enforced, markets are regulated, and everyone has a genuine opportunity to compete.

I’m speaking from experience.

In 2022, I operated a canteen and a retail shop. Like thousands of young South Sudanese entrepreneurs, I depended entirely on imported goods because our country manufactures little to nothing. I did not have enough capital to import directly, so I had to buy everything from wholesalers, most of whom were foreigners trading in our land.

That is where I learned how difficult the system is.

A product I bought for SSP 5,000 as a South Sudanese retailer was being sold to a retailer from the wholesaler’s own country for around SSP 4,000. The difference was not because I was a poor businessman; it was because I was not from their country. I eventually had to build friendships—most of which were not sustainable—just to access the same prices. That is not a sustainable system for a young entrepreneur.

The same reality still exists today. Take a 50kg bag of maize flour as an example. A local retailer buys it for SSP 205,000 and sells it for SSP 210,000 just to make a small profit. Another trader—a foreigner from the same country as the wholesaler—buys it for SSP 185,500 and can sell it for SSP 205,000 while still making a bigger profit.

Because the foreign-owned shop can sell at a lower price, customers naturally go there. The local retailer is left with slow sales, rent to pay, taxes to pay, and stock sitting on the shelves.

How does the local retailer compete with that?

The same pattern happens with bottled water, sugar, rice, clothes, electronics, and many other everyday products. Whoever controls the supply chain controls the price, and whoever controls the price controls who survives in the market.

Now let us ask another honest question.

Where does a young South Sudanese get the capital to enter the wholesale business? Capital does not come from nowhere. It comes from savings, grants, bank financing, or investment. But how do young people save when salaries are delayed or inconsistent? How do they qualify for loans when our financial system offers very limited access to credit?

These are realities our policymakers cannot ignore.

Telling young people to “compete” is not enough. We must also ask who has access to import channels, warehouses, transport, financing, and established business structures.

And there is another concern. In many cases, foreign-owned businesses employ mainly people from their own countries, even for jobs that South Sudanese can do. That means we lose twice: we lose ownership of the business, and we also lose employment opportunities.

South Sudan needs both: welcoming foreign investment and protecting economic space for South Sudanese entrepreneurs. We should encourage investment that builds factories, industries, technology, and large-scale employment, while creating laws that give local entrepreneurs a fair chance to start, grow, and compete.

This is not about hating foreigners. It is about making sure South Sudanese are meaningful participants in the economy of their own country.

text:
I would frame it as an invitation to moral reflection, acknowledging Jewish suffering and diversity while asking what responsibility these teachings place on people with power.

Remembering the Warning of the Sages

To Jewish readers in Israel and throughout the diaspora, I offer this reflection with respect for a tradition that has preserved both the memory of suffering and the courage to examine its own conduct.

In discussing the destruction of the Second Temple, the rabbis asked a disturbing question: how could a society devoted to Torah, commandments, and acts of kindness still fall into catastrophe? Their answer was sinat chinam—baseless hatred. Religious devotion had coexisted with hostility powerful enough to tear the community apart. Yoma 9b⁠

That teaching deserves attention whenever political loyalty becomes stronger than conscience, whenever disagreement becomes a reason to humiliate, and whenever cruelty becomes acceptable because it is committed by someone on one’s own side.

The story of Kamtza and Bar Kamtza makes the warning painfully human. A host humiliates a guest. Those present fail to intervene. The humiliated man seeks revenge against the wider community. The story asks us to examine the harm done by pride, silence, and retaliation—and how far that harm can spread. Gittin 55b–56a⁠

Today, these teachings invite difficult questions. When leaders encourage contempt, who challenges them? When prisoners are allegedly abused, do we demand an honest investigation? When civilians suffer, does their humanity remain visible to us? Can we recognize wrongdoing even when acknowledging it is politically inconvenient?

Jewish fear, grief, and the need for safety deserve to be taken seriously. So does the humanity of Palestinians. Rabbi Akiva’s teaching that the human being is beloved because humanity was created in God’s image offers a foundation for holding both responsibilities together. Applying that principle today means that neither nationality nor captivity erases human dignity. Pirkei Avot 3:14, with commentary⁠

The Talmud also connects responsibility to the ability to act: those who can effectively protest wrongdoing within their sphere of influence must not simply remain silent. This places a particular burden on leaders and institutions, and calls each person to consider the influence they actually possess. Shabbat 54b⁠

No people should be reduced to the conduct of its government, its extremists, or any one faction. Those who defend human dignity and challenge abuses deserve support. Their insistence on accountability can express a profound fidelity to Jewish ethical tradition.

Remembering the Temple’s destruction does not give anyone authority to predict divine punishment. It gives us a reason to recognize destructive habits before they become accepted ways of life.

May remembrance lead to teshuvah: an honest return, expressed through changed conduct. May loyalty leave room for truth, strength remain answerable to justice, and grief never extinguish compassion.

The wisdom of the past becomes a protection for the future when people allow it to question their own side.

Sri Vanchiyam Temple: 

Where Lord Vishnu Reunited with Goddess Lakshmi 

(Couples Resolve Differences here by praying)

A debate arose between Lord Vishnu's consorts, Sridevi and Bhoodevi, over who was superior. 

As this argument escalated into a fight, a heartbroken Goddess Lakshmi left Vaikuntham and came down to Earth.

She arrived at a peaceful sandalwood forest ashram established by Sage Bhrigu. 

Raised there as the sage's daughter, she devoted herself to the intense daily worship of Lord Shiva.

Meanwhile, Vaikuntham lost its divine glow in Goddess Lakshmi's absence. 

Lord Vishnu, weakened and suffering, wandered across many sacred places searching for her. 

After a long journey, he finally reached this specific place.

Desiring to reunite with his consort, Lord Vishnu undertook severe penance directed at Lord Shiva. 

Pleased with his devotion, Lord Shiva appeared, brought Goddess Lakshmi and Lord Vishnu together, and solemnized their marriage.

Because Lord Vishnu longed for ("Vanchithu") and attained Goddess Lakshmi ("Sri") with deep love, the temple earned the name Srivanchiyam. 

In pure classical Tamil, it is beautifully called Thiruvizhaivur. 

The sacred water body created here by Goddess Lakshmi is still reverently worshipped by devotees as Lakshmi Theertham.

The temple's most significant feature is its power to heal relationships. 

Devotees firmly believe that if couples separated by minor misunderstandings visit this temple, offer sandalwood to the deity, and pray sincerely, their bitterness will fade, and their married life will flourish.

This glorious Srivanchiyam temple is located near Nannilam in the Thiruvarur district

Earlier than the rabbinic sources you cited — many sources show 2nd Temple Jews praying to the dead. Sources like “Testament of Levi” where “angles offer sacrifices to the Lord in behalf of all the sins of ignorance of the righteous ones” and the Testament of Dan the patriarch instruct his deciples to “Draw near to God and to the Angel who intercedes for you, because he is the mediator between God and man for the peace of Israel.” 

Mind you these are all JEWISH writings, not pagan — the Book of Watchers was also huge for 2nd temple Judaism and early Christianity. We’re starting to see that the Apostolic church didn’t invent this — she inherited it

Jewish Targums are another source that were read in synagogues from the 2nd Temple period onward — showing the Jewish interpretive tradition was comfy with scripture having figures of intercession (Angels, Memra, Patriarchs etc). The dead were largely seen as accessible through God — not apart from him

January 27, 2013
Brown was involved in an altercation with Frank Ocean over a parking space outside a recording studio in West Hollywood, California. According to police reports, Brown pushed or punched the singer. Ocean did not press charges.

July 15, 2013
Brown’s probation was revoked for his involvement in an alleged hit-and-run in Los Angeles. The charges were dropped at a hearing the following month after reaching a “civil compromise” with his accuser.

October 27, 2013
Brown was arrested for felony assault after punching a man outside the W Hotel in Washington D.C. Brown and his bodyguard allegedly punched a man and broke his nose after he had tried to get in a picture with him and two women. Brown’s charge was reduced to a misdemeanor and he voluntarily entered a rehab center while awaiting sentencing. 

November 5, 2013
Brown checks out of rehab, and his representative shared that he would be continuing treatment for anger issues as an outpatient in Los Angeles. On Nov. 20, Brown was sentenced to 90 days at an anger management rehab facility, as well as submitting to drug testing and to take any prescriptions recommended by the facility. 

May 5, 2015
Brown was identified as the individual who allegedly assaulted another adult male during a basketball game at Palms Casino Resort, according to the Las Vegas police. The man was treated for non-life threatening injuries, which were sustained after a verbal spat led to a physical fight. In a press release, the LVMPD noted that Brown wasn’t the only man who assaulted the victim.

July 2, 2016
Police responded to a report of battery that occurred inside a Palms hotel suite. When police arrived, the female victim appeared to have minor injuries sustained as a result of battery. Metro Police determined that the victim was attending a party inside a hotel room at the Palms hotel where an altercation took place over a cell phone. The victim alleges that she was battered by Brown when she took out her cell phone to take a picture of the singer, who then proceeded to take her phone from her. According to police, the victim was escorted out of the room by private security into the hallway, and proceeded to be escorted off property by hotel security.

August 30, 2016
Brown was arrested at his home on suspicion of assault with a deadly weapon. According to the Los Angeles Times, model Baylee Curan said that Brown and another man became angry when she admired the man’s diamond necklace. She also said that Brown threatened her with a gun before asking her to sign a nondisclosure agreement.

February 21, 2017
The Grammy winner was court-ordered to stay 100 yards away from ex-girlfriend Karrueche Tran and not attempt to contact her after she wrote in court filings that Brown had repeatedly threatened her since December. Tran also accused the singer of punching her in the stomach and pushing her down stairs a few years ago. Her filing does not offer any additional specifics or note if she reported the events to police. It states that no one was present at the time.

April 17, 2017
Tampa police reported that Brown “sucker punched” a photographer after a disagreement over some pictures. According to one of the club’s partner’s, Brown showed up for a paid appearance at the 11,000-square-foot Aja Channelside club, and around 1 a.m., the club’s in-house photographer attempted to take pics of the singer and his entourage when Brown’s team told him to stop.

May 9, 2018
Brown was accused of co-conspiring, aiding and abetting in a 2017 sexual assault that took place during a party at his house in a lawsuit filed by attorney Gloria Allred on behalf of her client, a woman who will be known as Jane Doe.

January 22, 2019
After reports surfaced that Brown had been detained in Paris on potential charges of aggravated rape and drug infractions after a woman filed a rape complaint, his rep confirmed to Billboard that Brown had been released from custody and that all charges have now been dropped.

July 22, 2014
Brown and several members of his entourage, along with Brown’s 11:11 Tour promoter Live Nation, are facing a lawsuit over an alleged assault that took place following Brown’s concert in Fort Worth, Texas.

May 15, 2025
Brown was taken into custody on May 15 after being arrested at his Manchester hotel and charged with “inflicting grievous bodily harm,” which has been tied to a February 2023 London nightclub attack allegedly involving Brown.

2026
A Los Angeles jury ordered singer Chris Brown to pay nearly $13 million in damages after his guard dog brutally mauled his former housekeeper in December 2020.

Meantime in the Philippines -
Rescuers retrieved more remains from a passenger ferry that was gutted by fire, bringing the death toll to 76 - with another 13 missing.
43 people survived the fire on Wednesday.
The cause has not been determined but the coast guard spokesperson quoted a survivor as saying it may have started from the cargo hold.
The survivor recounted hearing a blast, with smoke and fire quickly spreading, fanned by winds.

The protests have grown into a broader anti-government movement calling for the resignation of their Prime Minister -: “I am protesting here for the big corruption that is in every stage of our life. ”
The Albanian government argues that the planned investment along the Adriatic coast would be a transformative project for the country.

In California - Fire trucks - coming in to help battle the Lucas Fire, as crews on the ground worked to slow the spread of the blaze.
It's in Lake and Mendocino counties, where authorities issued evacuation orders for parts of the northern California region.
Ryan Isham is with Cal-fire.: “Resources, both ground and air are actively working to eliminate heat signatures in those areas and bring that fire towards favorable control lines. ”
The last update was the wildfire has burned more than 4-thousand acres and was 15% contained.
It started Thursday - and the cause is still being investigated.

Tens of thousands of Celine Dion fans flocked to an Arena in Paris for the first of her 16 shows planned across September and October after a four year break.: “Where can you please stop me. ”
The Paris concerts, to be followed by 10 more in May, mark a major milestone for 58-year-old Dion following years away from touring after she revealed her diagnosis with stiff-person syndrome.: “I feel like just the voice is the voice of a generation that it no one else comes close, right, so. Yeah, exactly, I think the voice, the voice is the main thing. I mean, she's so talented. It was in a lifetime opportunity, I think. ”
With nearly 260 million albums sold worldwide, Dion remains one of the bestselling and most decorated artists in pop music history.
The concert series, titled “Celine Dion Paris 2026-2027,” will feature her catalog of hits in English and French.

text:
There is a particular kind of late night that this movie was built for, the kind where the room is too quiet and the screen is too bright and you tell yourself you are only watching because it is camp, because it is history, because Roger Corman’s name still means something in the basement of American horror. Then Janice Starlin injects herself with what the world promised her as salvation, and the picture stops being a joke. The 1995 The Wasp Woman, also sold in some markets as Forbidden Beauty, is not the clean, respectable classic people pretend they want when they say they love old monster movies. It is the other thing. It is the cable-era confession. It is eighty seven minutes of a woman discovering that the industry she built will only keep her if she can unmake time, and that the body, once bargained with, does not stay a body. That is why it stands out from the safer pictures in its field. Most creature features ask you to fear the thing that comes through the window. This one asks you to fear the thing a woman will become in order to remain visible.

Janice is not introduced as prey. She is the founder and the face of her own cosmetics company, the woman who sold youth to other women until the board looked at her forties and decided the brand needed a younger mouth, a younger throat, a younger lie. The younger model is already in the building. The investors have already decided what beauty is allowed to cost. So Janice does what ambitious people do when the market turns against their flesh. She funds the scientist. Dr. Eric Zinthorp has been extracting an enzyme from queen wasps, that royal, brutal logic of a creature whose entire existence is reproduction, hierarchy, and sting. He offers reversal. She offers herself as the first human subject. Watch that transaction closely, because the movie is not really about insects. It is about the moment a woman agrees that her worth is a chemical problem. The serum works. The years fall off her like a stolen coat. She looks twenty five again. Sales can rise. The face can stay on the bottle. And then the other bill arrives: the headaches, the hunger, the spike of appetite that is sexual and violent at the same time, the body rewriting its contract while she is still trying to pose for it.

What you are supposed to take away is not a list of kills. You are supposed to feel how thin the line is between wanting to be desired and wanting to devour the people who withhold desire. Janice’s photographer, Alec, is the human warmth in the room, the man who still sees her as a person while the company sees inventory. The movie uses that romance the way a wasp uses a nest. It gives her something to lose so the transformation can mean something. When the serum turns her libido into a weapon, the picture becomes uncomfortably honest about what beauty culture does to appetite. She does not merely look younger. She becomes hungrier. Jealousy stops being an emotion and becomes a hunting instinct. The younger woman who was hired to replace her is not just a rival in an office. She is proof that the world has already chosen a replacement body. If you watch only for gore you will miss the lesson hiding in that cruelty. The monster is not born in the lab. The monster is born in the meeting where men tell a woman she is no longer the face of her own work.

This is where the film becomes strange in a way most polished horror refuses to be. It is serious about vanity and twisted about pleasure. Janice’s condition is not a clean curse. It is erotic and grotesque in the same breath. The 1995 remake leans into that on purpose. The 1959 original, Corman’s black and white fable, kept a certain midcentury restraint, a mask, a dignity even in mutation. This version wants the mutation to feel like sex gone wrong, like the body answering a market demand too literally. Increased hunger. Increased heat. Then the carapace. Then the wings. Then the woman who wanted to stay beautiful becoming the thing that cannot be held, cannot be photographed, cannot be loved in the old human way. When Alec cannot accept the creature she has become, something in her human self flickers back just long enough to choose ending over exile. That is the moral the movie actually teaches, and it is nastier than a simple don’t play God sermon. The lesson is that a culture which only loves you young will call your survival monstrous the moment survival stops looking like a magazine. You do not watch this to learn how wasps work. You watch it to learn what happens when a person treats her own face as a company asset and the asset starts eating the person.

How do you explain this to your wife if she walks in. You do not say it is just a silly old cable movie, because she can see your face. You say it is a story about a woman who built an empire on skin and then discovered the empire required her to stop aging or stop existing. You say the arousal in the room is not simple and should not be simple. The film is designed to make beauty look like appetite, and appetite look like predation, and predation look almost tender until the sting lands. That discomfort is the point. A lot of horror wants you safely outside the monster. The Wasp Woman wants you implicated. You have looked at ads. You have believed, at least a little, that youth is a product and that a woman past a certain hour should recede. Janice refuses to recede. Science gives her a door. Nature slams it into a hive. If the picture makes you feel something you cannot immediately name, that is not a glitch in the late night air. That is the movie doing the only honest thing a body horror fable can do. It makes the viewer complicit in the same hunger it punishes.

It stands apart from other movies in its field because it is not trying to be The Fly with better grants and better laboratories. It is trying to be a cosmetics commercial that grows mandibles. That is a rarer idea than people admit. Insect horror usually arrives as invasion, swarm, nature’s revenge from the outside. Here the swarm is inside one ambitious woman, and the laboratory is just the altar where she pays. That is why it remains a must watch for anyone who claims to care about what horror is actually for. Horror is not only jump and latex. Horror is the moment a person realizes the miracle she bought was a species change. The film is cheap in places, loud in places, unashamed in places respectable cinema would sand down. That shamelessness is part of the legend. Cable in the mid nineties still had a corridor where a Roger Corman production could put a queen wasp enzyme, a fading executive, a younger model, a photographer lover, and a twelve foot creature with the last human remnants of a woman’s body held inside an exoskeleton, and call it entertainment. Most fields sand that down now. This one left the sting in.

Call it a masterpiece only if you understand the word the way cult cinema understands it. Not flawless. Not universally crowned. A masterpiece of a specific American underground instinct: take a moral panic about aging women, dress it in science, sex, and chitin, and refuse to look away when the metaphor grows wings. Cultural icon is the same kind of claim. It is not hanging in every dorm poster hall. It lives in the lineage. Corman made the first cut of this myth in 1959, when royal jelly and youth serums were already being whispered as modern magic. By 1995 the magic had become an industry, and the remake knew it. Forbidden Beauty is the more honest title in that sense. The beauty is forbidden not because it is erotic, though the film is willing to be strangely, uncomfortably erotic, but because the price of keeping it is the self. That is the takeaway that should follow you out of the room. Every time a culture tells a woman her power is her smoothness, it is writing a wasp story and hoping nobody notices the stinger.

The plot points that matter are few and they all teach. A company founded on a woman’s face decides the face has expired. A scientist offers wasp queens as the solution to time. The solution works until work becomes metamorphosis. Desire and violence stop pretending they are different rooms. Love looks at the new form and flinches. The woman, for one last human second, understands what she has become and does not ask the world to keep her anyway. That last understanding is why the picture is more than a creature suit. A legend in this field is not the film with the biggest budget. A legend is the film that makes the audience feel the transaction. You wanted to stay wanted. Fine. Here is the species that never stops being wanted, and here is what she eats.

Behind the scenes the story is almost as revealing as the fable, which is why it belongs at the end, after the lesson has already landed. This was the eighth film in the Roger Corman Presents series for Showtime, a Concorde New Horizons creature born for cable rather than the old drive in. Jim Wynorski, who had grown up admiring Corman’s original, pushed the remake because he thought the 1959 picture had a great premise and never followed through on the monster. He wanted bigger, crazier effects. They shot it in about twenty days in Southern California, including the old Bronson Canyon terrain that has housed more cheap myths than any respectable studio backlot. Wynorski talked about a giant wasp some twelve feet long, winged, and pointedly not modest about the human body still trapped in the design. Greg Aronowitz and the effects team built the thing that most critics would later call ugly, stiff, or astonishingly grotesque depending on how much affection they had for handmade monsters. Jennifer Rubin, already marked in horror memory from A Nightmare on Elm Street 3, took Janice because she wanted to pass through Corman’s factory. Her friend Marta Mobley was running that side of the operation. Rubin later said the set was brutal, that Wynorski was rude, that she was not the person inside the wasp, and that there was no budget for a real metamorphosis sequence. That gap is visible on screen and somehow belongs there. The woman changes faster than the production can afford to show, which is exactly how desperation works in life.

Daniel J. Travanti, far from Hill Street Blues, plays the doctor as the respectable face of an indecent idea. Maria Ford is the younger replacement the market prefers. Gerrit Graham and the rest of the office ecosystem do what offices do in these stories: they smile while they measure a woman for disposal. Fred Olen Ray had asked Corman years earlier if he could remake The Wasp Woman and was turned down, then took the hunger for youth and mutation elsewhere and made Evil Spawn. Wynorski later convinced Corman to let the wasp come home. Even the home video life of the 1995 film is a little warped. Some cuts ran shorter by minutes of heat and dream and seduction. Germany saw more. America often saw less. The creature still made the poster. The face of Rubin still sold the tape. The movie remained what it had been on first airing: a Showtime body horror about a queen who would rather mutate than be replaced.

That is the whole strange monument. Not a perfect film. A necessary one if you want to understand how American horror keeps returning to women, laboratories, and the terror of being seen aging in public. It is a must watch because it will not let beauty stay innocent. It is a classic of the unrespectable kind because it remembers that legends in this field are built from leftover sets, rushed schedules, sincere hunger, and a metaphor sharp enough to draw blood. Watch it for the lesson, not the play by play. The lesson is simple and it does not leave the room when the credits roll. If you make a sacrament out of staying young, do not be shocked when the sacrament grows wings, looks at the people who loved your human face, and decides that love was never the point. The point was never to be loved. The point was to remain the queen.

LOS ANGELES, California — Twenty-two-year-old model Chloe Arden announced that her nose job was an investment in future generations. Her friends initially assumed she meant family photographs. She meant inheritance.

The operation was a personal cosmetic choice, not a hereditary software update. Her future children will not be downloading a receipt from the clinic.

text: Great article Scott. I predicted NIL would level the field at the top when it became available for the athletes. My friends laughed at me. They said all the big $$$ schools would get the best players and be the best teams.  Sure that’s part of it. But now that the athletes are getting paid above the table it levels everything. Alabama doesn’t have the money or alumni support that Notre Dame has but every program has some money. There’s a team aspect to being a good program too. The best athletes are not necessarily the best teammates. Egos are fragile. That can backfire quickly if you lose a few games. They’re gone the moment it’s allowed and a million dollar offer hits. Building a team is still just as important as having the players. Now that Indiana and others are competing for championships you can see the private equity going in. I don’t agree 100% with collectives because they don’t have much oversight. When a wealthy donor opens the checkbook and 8-9 figures are on the check,  they become a big influence on the program. (T Boone Pickens). There’s nothing wrong with free enterprise, we built a huge economy that way. The money spreads out and the athletes get paid to play. Heck some stay in college longer because the money is better in some circumstances. Better than nothing. A program like Iowa or Minnesota gets a chance to play for something more meaningful than a pig. (Sorry Floyd, you’re still my favorite). Imagine Miami or Alabama playing a playoff game in Kinnick December 16th? It’s 18 degrees with a snowstorm. That’s a two touchdown home field advantage. Us Hawkeye fans looked forward to a warm bowl game but I’d take USC  or FSU in Kinnick in December all day over Pasadena. The local economic impact is huge too. Tailgating in perfect weather is great but I’ll still have a bbq and beverages at 20 degrees if I get to watch the Hawkeyes play. I might have to put pants on but I’ll sacrifice to see my team play something meaningful in December. I can go back to Arizona after the season is over.

@PeterMallouk highlighted an important dynamic this week from Morningstar's latest Mind the Gap report: funds compounded at 9.9% over the decade through 2025, while the average dollar earned 8.7%.

​A 1.2% behavioral gap.

​Peter is right that behavior drives performance drag. When you look at the data underneath, it proves that the real danger of bad behavior is abandoning your asset allocation.

​Looking at the 10-year tape across asset classes:

• U.S. Large Cap Equity: 14.7%
• Gold: 14.6%
• International Developed: 8.2%
• Emerging Markets: 7.8%
• U.S. Investment Grade Bonds: 1.9%

​Inside U.S. equity funds, the timing penalty was only 0.4% (13.3% fund return vs. 12.8% investor return). Equity investors who stayed the course captured almost all of the market's run.

​The real capital destruction happens when panic leads an investor to abandon equities entirely and sit in cash or core bonds compounding at 1.9%. That asset class dispersion was 12.8 percentage points.

​Behavioral discipline saves you 40 bps on trading errors. Sticking to a disciplined, multi-asset allocation saves you the other 12%.

text:
Conspiracy? Good grief? The medical community didn't attack people for trying to use Ivermectin? Didn't try to shame people into using a vaccine that is linked to a host of medical problems? Your beloved community isn't advocating life-altering treatments to children, many of whom are simply going through a phase? You and your friends haven't embraced a sick ideology that perverts biological science?

Of course, those are all just conspiracies, right? Nobody was attacked for using or wanting to use Ivermectin? All of those vaccines were perfectly safe and were effective? And of course, nobody is actually surgically removing the sexual organs of children in the name of trans rights?

You and your milquetoast, watered-down version of conservatism is exactly what got us to this point now. You want Republicans leading from a crouch so afraid someone might be offended. Man, give me a break!

Let me put it a different way. Here is a section of a chapter in my forthcoming book, The Ignorance Tax: Hidden Costs in the Age of Free Lunch. This is more about education than healthcare, but you are trying to do something very similar when it comes to immigration. It really is quite disgusting.

Why Adaptation Looks Like Sabotage

When policies produce different results than their designers intended, the explanation almost never focuses on how the policy changed incentives for the people it was supposed to help. The assumption is almost always that policies would work perfectly if only people responded the way policymakers hoped, not the way they actually do when facing the new costs, benefits, and constraints the policy creates.

Zero-tolerance discipline in American schools offers a clean illustration. These policies mandated automatic suspension or expulsion for specified offenses. Suspension rates during the zero-tolerance era broke hard along racial lines. Whatever classroom order suspension preserved could not be measured. The racial gap could, and it became the story. Black students were four times more likely to receive an out-of-school suspension than white students. In 2013–14, fifteen states suspended more than 15 percent of their Black students. The numbers were stark, and the conclusion felt obvious: the adults applying these policies must be applying them unequally. 

But the research could not settle whether bias was the primary driver. What it showed was a divided ledger. Poverty was a strong predictor of discipline, and low-income students were suspended far more often than better-off students even after race was taken into account. Differences in behavior and the schools students attended explained part of the racial gap; differential treatment accounted for another part. Direct comparisons of similarly situated students within the same school or the same incident generally find small racial differences, and sometimes none at all. 

The disparities were real. The comfortable explanation collapsed that ledger into a single line: the disparity itself became proof of discriminatory enforcement. That reading skipped the upstream conditions no discipline policy could repair and fastened instead on the one part of the problem a school could be ordered to change: the suspension count.

That misdirection had consequences. Federal civil-rights pressure had already begun reshaping school-discipline policy before the Departments of Education and Justice formalized the warning in 2014: racial disparities in suspension rates could constitute evidence of unlawful discrimination, even if policies were race-neutral and applied evenhandedly. Across this period, districts revised their discipline policies under that pressure.

Between 2003 and 2015, Los Angeles cut suspension rates from 8 percent to below 1 percent. For most students, test scores declined, GPAs fell, student absences increased, and teacher turnover rose, particularly among inexperienced teachers, the ones least equipped to manage classrooms without the tools they had just lost. Philadelphia prohibited suspensions for low-level misbehavior; suspensions for those infractions fell, but total suspensions remained unchanged as serious misconduct increased, while truancy rose and mathematics and English-language-arts achievement declined. Pittsburgh introduced restorative practices as an alternative for nonviolent behavior; suspension rates fell and the racial gap in suspensions narrowed, but academic outcomes did not improve overall and worsened in grades six through eight. In every case the suspension numbers moved, which is what the policies directly controlled. The outcomes they were meant to deliver did not. 

In Illinois, among surveyed teachers who said their schools had eliminated zero-tolerance policies and restricted suspensions, just over 10 percent said the changes had improved student behavior, while nearly half said they had worsened it; the report also found broad concern that school culture and climate had deteriorated. In each of these places the discipline policy changed as intended. Academic performance, attendance, behavior, and teacher retention either did not change or changed for the worse. 

This is what a narrow diagnosis buys. When policy fixes on the one number it can regulate, that number can fall because it is the target, not because the trouble behind it eased. In New York City, suspensions dropped. Order did not improve. The official record was not clean either. A state audit found hundreds of reportable incidents missing from the city’s school-safety data, leaving officials without complete information to assess school safety. Suspensions were blunt, but the cases just described show the cost of reducing them without preserving classroom order by other means. The learning environment deteriorated. 

The pattern completed its own loop. Disparate outcomes showed up in the data, and the blame went to the people closest to them, not the conditions producing them. The fix targeted those people, and the students the fix was meant to help paid the price because the comfortable explanation had aimed the reform at the wrong target. The behavioral adaptation was real, but it wasn't sabotage. Students, teachers, and administrators all responded predictably to the new incentive structures the reforms created. Calling those responses evidence of bias or resistance prevented anyone from asking whether the reform was aimed at the right problem.

Chapter 2 traced this move: disappointing results blamed on moral failure rather than on the tradeoffs the policy built. What sharpens after launch is the sorting of that blame along group lines, into narratives about conflicts between social groups: employers cast against workers, teachers cast against students.

Group-based blame like this blocks recognition that the same behavioral responses would occur regardless of the moral character of the people involved. The most community-minded employer still faces economic constraints that make it hard to hire workers when labor costs exceed the value those workers produce. The most patient-centered hospital still answers to reimbursement rules that pay for procedures rather than outcomes. The most dedicated teacher still works within institutional structures that reward behaviors that do not improve student learning.

Focusing on character instead of incentives keeps the cycle running: failures get explained by moral deficiency, successes get credited to better people rather than better design, and the next policy launches on the same assumptions the last one disproved. Structural redesign never makes it onto the table, because the diagnosis already said the problem was the people.

Underneath the misdiagnosis sits one naive assumption: that people respond to what a policy intends rather than to the incentives it creates. What gets called sabotage is usually behavior responding to a structure the policymakers failed to imagine.

PULSE — NATIONAL DESK Sunday, 13 September 2026 
Congress is dark today. The House is out of session and returns Monday at noon. The Senate is not voting. The next hard federal date on the calendar is not a shutdown. It is Election Day, 3 November.
FUNDING Federal agencies are funded through 11 December under the continuing resolution the Senate passed 90–6 on 8 August and the House cleared 370–48 on 1 September. Republicans voted 193–19. Democrats voted 176–29. The CR was brought up under suspension. It removes the 30 September shutdown clock from the midterm window. The next appropriations fight is scheduled after voters have already voted.
The same day the House passed the CR, it adopted a GOP floor rule 210–208 after five Republicans broke and two Democrats, Jared Golden of Maine and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez of Washington, voted with leadership. That rule governs later House business. It is not the funding bill.
COURTS — THIS WEEK On 10 September the Supreme Court again blocked Missouri from using a redrawn congressional map that would have favored Republicans in November. The justices issued an unsigned emergency order and did not explain their reasoning. They deferred to the Missouri Supreme Court, which had blocked the map on the ground that voters must first have a chance to approve it by statewide referendum. Missouri’s Republican secretary of state said the state would use the 2022 maps. That is expected to leave the Kansas City-area seat in Democratic hands unless a later order changes the line. Primary and general maps may now be different. The Court did not resolve that conflict.
On 9 September the Justice Department asked the Court to let a Trump-aligned nominee remain Nevada’s top federal prosecutor while litigation continues.
The same week the administration asked the Court to allow a voter-verification database that a lower-court judge had blocked, and renewed its request to limit mail-in voting after withdrawing an earlier application. A response in the mail-ballot matter is due Wednesday at 4 p.m. Eastern.
On 4 September the Court granted Republican party committees temporary relief on broadcast advertising rates, pausing a lower-court ruling so party committees and joint fundraising committees can, for now, receive the lowest-unit-charge rates long available to candidates. The request came from the National Republican Senatorial Committee and the National Republican Congressional Committee. The FCC had backed the committees. The stay is not a final merits ruling.
On 2 September the House voted 212–206 against a proposed constitutional amendment to lock the Supreme Court at nine justices. The measure needed a two-thirds vote. All but one Democrat voted no. The joint resolution was offered by Rep. Andy Biggs.
SUMMER TERM, STILL OPERATIVE The Court’s June term remains the legal floor under the fall campaign.
In a 6–3 decision the Court held that the president may remove Federal Trade Commissioner Rebecca Kelly Slaughter and overturned the 1935 Humphrey’s Executor framework that had protected many independent-agency officials from at-will removal. Chief Justice Roberts wrote that the FTC exercises executive power and that Slaughter served as the president’s subordinate. Justice Sotomayor dissented from the bench.

The Human Rights Industry Has a Favorite Kind of Victim

Amir Taheri: America 25 Years After 9/11
The Human Rights Industry Has a Favorite Kind of Victim
by Pierre Rehov  •  September 13, 2026 at 5:00 am

The human rights industry's favorite kind of victim is the politically useful one: the victim whose suffering can be attached to an adversary — a designated "villain" — preferably one that Western activists already know how to hate, pressure and organize against.

That is why Palestinian victims, when Israel can be cast as an alleged perpetrator of wrongs, generate an extraordinary machinery of outrage, while Sudanese victims of genocide, Afghan women under the Taliban, Iranian protesters murdered by their own regime, or persecuted Christians in Nigeria largely do not.

The hierarchy is not determined by the severity of the suffering; it is determined by the political usefulness of the victim and, even more importantly, by the identity of the "villain" supposedly committing these wrongs.

A United Nations fact-finding mission concluded in February 2026 that the mass executions, gang rapes and engineered starvation... in Sudan bore the hallmarks of genocide, and that genocidal intent was the only reasonable inference the evidence allowed.

The finding produced -- communiqués! No American campus has been covered with Sudanese encampments. No international campaign demands that corporations prove their innocence regarding Khartoum....

text:
Queen Victoria and Walmer Castle, Kent

Construction of Walmer Castle began in 1539 on the orders of Henry VIII in order to strengthen the defences along the Kent coast to resist a potential invasion from Europe.

In 1727 Walmer Castle became the official residence of the Lord Warden of the Cinque Ports, when new apartments were built.

The Duke of Wellington was appointed Lord Warden of the Cinque Ports in 1827 and used the apartments at the castle during the summer months where he entertained family and friends.

Queen Victoria and her family stayed at the castle for ten days during November 1842 at the invitation of the Duke of Wellington.

The royal party enjoyed the privacy at Walmer Castle, there was freedom to walk along the shingle beach towards Kingsdown in the south and towards Deal to the north, without coming into contact with anyone.

HMS Thunderer was moored off the Kent coastline and provided some security for the royal party during their stay at Walmer Castle.

On 18 November Prince Albert visited HMS Thunderer and observed gun practise. Victoria could observe the shell’s flying and the sailors loading the guns through glasses while standing on the beach at Walmer.

On the day that the Duke of Wellington died on 14 September 1852, Charles Dickens walked from Dover to Walmer Castle for he wrote: ‘I was walking to Walmer this afternoon, and little thought that the great old man was dying or dead.’

text:
Camels Wandered Into the Swamp and Never Stood a Chance

Florida finally met Campbell on a Saturday night in Gainesville and treated the first-ever matchup like a statement rather than a celebration. The Gators rolled to a 52-3 win, improving to 2-0 for the first time since 2021, yet the scoreboard hid as much as it revealed. Campbell, an FCS program that arrived 2-0 after two modest wins, marched 63 yards on the opening drive and kicked a field goal to take a 3-0 lead. That early punch exposed lingering questions in Florida’s secondary. The Gators answered immediately, driving for a short Aaron Philo touchdown run that flipped the momentum and set the tone for what followed.
The game turned in the second quarter when Vernell Brown III took over special teams. He returned consecutive punts 64 and 70 yards for touchdowns, the first time a Gator had done that since Jacquez Green in 1996, and added a 14-yard receiving score for a hat trick. Those plays created a 35-point explosion that buried Campbell. Jadan Baugh later ripped off a 75-yard touchdown run, his third straight 100-yard game, while Philo completed 16 of 21 passes for 242 yards and two scores before the backups entered. Dallas Wilson added a 40-yard touchdown catch. Florida piled up 514 yards and held Campbell to 210 after that first drive. The Camels never scored again.
The blowout offered some evidence that Florida has improved under first-year coach Jon Sumrall. The offense looked explosive for the second straight week after a 66-21 opener against Florida Atlantic, special teams produced historic plays, and the defense settled in after the opening series. A 2-0 start heading into SEC play at Auburn looks promising on paper. Sumrall, however, refused to treat the result as proof of readiness. He called the second-half sloppiness, extra penalties, and lack of consistent execution a warning. “If we play like we did in the second half, we’re about to have a real rude awakening,” he said. “We will get absolutely embarrassed if we don’t improve a ton.” The game therefore served as both a confidence builder and a reminder that dominating an FCS opponent paid $525,000 to visit does not automatically translate to the SEC gauntlet that begins next week.
The two programs had never played because they occupied different worlds for most of their histories. Campbell fielded football from 1925 to 1950, then dropped the sport for 58 years before restarting at the FCS level in 2008. Florida, a longtime SEC power, typically schedules bigger non-conference games or traditional FCS guarantee opponents rather than a North Carolina program still building its modern identity. Schedulers finally connected them in a 2021 contract that placed this 2026 home date on the calendar as Florida’s last tune-up before conference play. Geography, conference affiliation, and the Camels’ relatively recent return to the field simply never aligned until now.
The Gators leave the Swamp 2-0 with highlight-reel moments and a coach who sounds more concerned than satisfied. Auburn will show whether the talent on display Saturday can survive the next test.

text:
And Malcom X on her top shelf. 🤔. Per Grok-
“Malcolm Little (May 19, 1925 – February 21, 1965), later Malcolm X and then El-Hajj Malik El-Shabazz. Born in Omaha to Earl Little (a Baptist preacher and Marcus Garvey supporter) and Louise. His father died when Malcolm was six under suspicious circumstances often attributed to white supremacists; his mother was later institutionalized. He spent time in foster care, dropped out after eighth grade, and drifted into street life in Boston and Harlem as “Detroit Red.” https://t.co/3exy31gDy3 
Early years and prison
He hustled: numbers, drugs, gambling, and burglary. In 1946, at 20, he was sentenced to 8–10 years for burglary and larceny in Massachusetts. He served about 6.5 years. In prison he read voraciously, debated, and was introduced to the Nation of Islam by family members. He converted, dropped “Little” as a “slave name,” and took “X” to stand for the unknown African ancestral name. He was paroled in 1952. https://t.co/veL55RGyct 
Nation of Islam years (the peak and the problems)
He became Elijah Muhammad’s most effective minister and national spokesman. Membership exploded. He preached Black self-reliance, economic discipline, pride, and separation from white society. He called whites “devils,” rejected integration as a trap, and mocked nonviolent civil-rights tactics. Famous line: “by any means necessary.”
Good side of this period: He gave many Black Americans a language of dignity and self-respect when mainstream society offered little. He was a brilliant, fearless orator who named racism without euphemism. He built institutions and demanded personal discipline (no drugs, no crime, family order).
Bad side: The NOI theology included racial mythology (the Yakub story), conspiracy thinking, and separatist absolutism. He used antisemitic tropes at times. He met with or tolerated outreach to the KKK and American Nazi Party because they shared a separatist goal. After JFK’s assassination he said “the chickens coming home to roost” and added he was glad. He described a plane crash that killed many whites as “beautiful.” His rhetoric was often inflammatory. Later biographies (especially Manning Marable’s) note he embellished his criminal past for dramatic effect and had personal contradictions. https://t.co/NFzVc0H8av 
The break and second conversion
He learned Elijah Muhammad had fathered children with young secretaries, violating his own teachings. Combined with political differences and the “chickens” remark (which violated Muhammad’s gag order), he was silenced then left in March 1964. He founded Muslim Mosque, Inc. and the Organization of Afro-American Unity.
He converted to orthodox Sunni Islam. In April 1964 he performed Hajj in Mecca, took the name El-Hajj Malik El-Shabazz, and wrote that seeing Muslims of every race praying together as equals forced him to drop the “white devil” doctrine. He began framing the struggle as human rights rather than purely American civil rights and connected it to anti-colonial movements. He still supported self-defense and Black political power, but the racial essentialism softened. https://t.co/xfI4bNLKMz 
Death
On February 21, 1965, he was shot 15 times onstage at the Audubon Ballroom in Harlem. Three NOI members were convicted; two were exonerated in 2021 after evidence of withheld information. His house had been firebombed a week earlier. He was 39. Questions about possible police/FBI knowledge or facilitation persist. https://t.co/3exy31gDy3 
He was neither a simple hero nor a simple villain. He was a self-made intellectual who rose from crime and prison, gave voice to justified rage, later rejected some of his own earlier doctrines, and was killed before the new phase fully developed. His autobiography (written with Alex Haley) remains the main source most people know—and it is both powerful and selectively shaped”

text:
I asked Claude to answer your questions and got this: Q1: How professional journalists actually find things out

It's mostly unglamorous groundwork, not tips falling from the sky:

Public records — court filings and dockets, property records, business/corporate registrations, campaign finance filings, government contracts, FOIA/public-records requests
Court documents specifically — complaints, motions, exhibits, transcripts (unless sealed), and increasingly things pulled from services like PACER or state e-filing portals
Sourcing — cultivating people inside institutions (police, courts, agencies, companies) who talk on background or on the record; developing relationships over time so sources trust them
Interviews — of principals, witnesses, neighbors, former employees, family members
Document leaks/whistleblowers
Data analysis — cross-referencing databases (e.g., a name against court dockets, property records, and business filings) to build a profile
On-the-ground reporting — knocking on doors, showing up at addresses, attending hearings
Verification — corroborating any single claim with at least one more independent source before publishing

Q2: Massachusetts law on approaching a discharged juror when the jury list is impounded

I'm not a lawyer, so treat this as general information rather than legal advice. But the short answer: no, it is not illegal for a journalist to ask a discharged juror for an interview, and impoundment of the jury list doesn't change that.

Impoundment is a court order restricting public/official access to a specific court record — here, the jury list itself (names/addresses held by the court). It's a rule about what the clerk's office can hand out, not a general gag order on the public or press. It doesn't:

Prohibit a private citizen (juror) from speaking voluntarily to anyone, including a reporter
Prohibit a journalist who has independently identified someone from asking for an interview
Criminalize the request for an interview, even if the person declines

Separately, Mass. R. Prof. Conduct 3.5(c) restricts attorneys' contact with discharged jurors (post-Commonwealth v. Moore, attorneys generally can contact jurors post-verdict unless the juror objects, contact is barred by court order, or it involves harassment). But that rule governs lawyers, not journalists — it doesn't extend to the press.

Where it could get legally fraught is if a person obtained the impounded list itself through improper means (e.g., someone with court access leaked it in violation of the order) — that person could face consequences, but that's a different question from a journalist independently tracking someone down and asking to talk.

Q3: The Confidential Juror Questionnaire (CJQ)

Yes. Under Mass. Gen. Laws c. 234A, § 22, the CJQ covers information "ordinarily raised in voir dire," including the juror's name, sex, age, residence, marital status, number and ages of children, education level, occupation, employment address, spouse's occupation, spouse's employment address, previous service as a juror, present or past involvement as a party to civil or criminal litigation, relationship to a police or law enforcement officer, and such other information as the jury commissioner deems appropriate. mass
The actual form asks direct yes/no questions like "Been arrested?" "Been a crime victim?" "Filed a lawsuit?", and jurors who answer "yes" are typically expected to explain — the form instructs jurors to "be thorough in your descriptions if you answer 'Yes.'" Jurors also sign a declaration that their answers are true, and willful misrepresentation of a material fact is a crime punishable by a fine of up to $2,000. Mass. Jurors Face Added Questions Before Going to Trial +2

Q4: Would both sides likely have left a juror unchallenged, knowing about an active restraining order?
This is inherently speculative, but here's the reasoning: attorneys routinely use exactly this kind of information — restraining orders, domestic-violence history, pending litigation — during voir dire because it can signal bias in either direction (sympathy toward or hostility toward victims/accusers, attitudes toward the legal system, credibility judgments). In a murder case specifically, this becomes even more salient if domestic violence or credibility-of-accuser themes are relevant to the facts.

Given that, it's fairly unlikely both sides would have simply let it pass. At minimum, one side would likely have questioned him further on the record, and either side could have used a peremptory challenge (which requires no stated reason) if they had any reservations — peremptories exist precisely for "soft" concerns like this that don't rise to a for-cause challenge. So the more probable outcome, if this information had come out during jury selection, is that at least one party would have acted on it — but there's no way to know for certain without knowing case specifics and each side's actual strategy.

Q5: Newsworthiness of a murder-trial juror's restraining order, litigation, and dismissed charge

Generally yes, this fits within traditional definitions of newsworthy, public-interest reporting — particularly the framing you note: it's not really "here's dirt on a private citizen," it's "here's a potential failure in the jury-selection process in a high-profile murder trial." The functioning of the justice system, whether jurors accurately disclosed information on sworn questionnaires, and whether attorneys had the information they needed to seat an impartial jury are all classic accountability-journalism subjects.

That said, "newsworthy" and "handled responsibly" are two different questions — the same underlying facts can be reported straightforwardly (focused on the jury-selection-process failure) or in a way that reads more like a personal takedown, depending on framing, tone, and how much personal detail is included beyond what's needed to make the point.

Q6: Is withholding name/race/age/hometown/residence and not publishing the impounded list still "doxxing"?

"Doxxing" as commonly understood specifically means publishing identifying information (name, address, workplace, phone number, photos, etc.) — typically to enable others to locate, harass, or intimidate someone. If the published article withholds all of those identifying details and doesn't publish the sealed list, it lacks the core element of doxxing as usually defined: it isn't handing readers what they'd need to find the person.

Two nuances worth flagging, though:

Jigsaw identification: if the article includes enough distinctive combined details (even without name/address), a reader with local knowledge could still piece together who it is. Whether that happened would depend on the specific piece.

Reporting conduct vs. the published piece: separately, the newsgathering process itself — showing up at someone's home, talking to family, neighbors, or a landlord — can functionally expose someone's identity within their community even if the published article withholds it. That's a distinct ethical question from whether the published article constitutes doxxing, and it's the kind of thing press critics and media ethicists do debate (aggressive-but-lawful newsgathering vs. harassment), separate from whether the text on the page technically doxxes anyone.

Q7: Are opinion writers/columnists journalists, and how do they differ from reporters?
Most news organizations and journalism scholars do consider columnists and opinion writers journalists — they're usually trained similarly, follow editorial standards, and work within the same institutions. But their function is different:

Reporters aim to present verified facts, multiple sides, and context, generally without inserting their own conclusions or advocacy; their credibility rests on accuracy and neutrality.

Opinion writers/columnists are explicitly allowed — and expected — to argue a position, offer interpretation, and inject personal judgment. Their credibility rests on the strength of their argument and, ideally, transparency about their reasoning and any relevant biases or conflicts.

Most reputable outlets maintain an organizational separation (sometimes called the "church and state" divide) between the newsroom (reporting) and the opinion/editorial section, precisely so readers can distinguish "here are the facts we've confirmed" from "here's what I think about them." Fact-checking standards nominally still apply to opinion pieces (they shouldn't state false facts), but the purpose of the piece — persuasion vs. straight information — is different.
