text:
App State is a have-not in the world of FBS football, and that probably isn’t going to change. At least 100 programs have more money, and dozens can offer recruits a more obvious path to the NFL.

That matters because strategy is not about copying what stronger competitors do. It is about finding the ground on which you have an advantage.

This reminds me of an evil university in northwest Arkansas. After years of being physically dominated by Alabama, Arkansas decided the answer was to hire an offensive-line guru and build a program capable of out-Alabama-ing Alabama.

One problem: Arkansas was never going to be better at being Alabama than Alabama was.

Imitation may be the sincerest form of flattery, but it is usually terrible strategy. When a resource-disadvantaged organization copies a resource-rich competitor's model, it often becomes nothing more than a cheaper version of the original.

That is the danger I see for App State.

Jim Collins makes a related argument in Good to Great. His Hedgehog Concept asks organizations to identify what they can genuinely become exceptional at and then relentlessly concentrate their resources around it. His Flywheel Effect explains how repeated, consistent effort around that advantage eventually creates enormous momentum.

The important point is this: your competitive advantage does not have to be the same thing everyone else values.

If App State tries to win primarily by selling NFL preparation, facilities, NIL money, exposure, and individual advancement, it is voluntarily entering competitions where larger programs possess enormous structural advantages.

That does not mean those things should be ignored. Of course App State should develop NFL players, improve NIL, recruit aggressively, embrace the portal, and modernize its operation.

But those are requirements for competing. They are not necessarily the source of competitive advantage.

Great strategy asks a different question:

What can App State offer that its richer competitors cannot easily buy, copy, or manufacture?

Whatever the answer, the university should focus its energy there.

Because a have-not rarely becomes great by playing the have’s game better than the have.

text:
Call it dual-track if you want the polite phrase. The United States is tired of waiting for a federal center that cannot police its own waters, cannot hold a constitution without a fight, and cannot decide whether Puntland and Jubaland are partners or rebels. So it deals with the governments that actually sit on the coast. Puntland offers the northern key: Bosaso, the Gulf, proximity to Yemen, and a grinding war against ISIS in the mountains. Jubaland offers the southern key: Kismayo, the approaches toward Kenya and the open Indian Ocean, and a long war against Al-Shabaab. Together they are the two locks on the same door.

Puntland’s strategy was never only about Garowe’s pride. It was about location. Africa’s longest coastline, the mouth of the Gulf of Aden, historic pirate harbors that can become navy harbors, and a claim that whoever can keep those waters open will be treated as a serious state whether Mogadishu likes the paperwork or not. The Americans did not invent that logic. They recognized it when Red Sea traffic became a daily crisis and when ISIS-Somalia was described in Washington as a node in a wider network. Bases follow maps. Maps follow ships.
There is a cost, and Somalis should name it without romance. Foreign bases do not arrive as gifts. They arrive with agendas 😮 Houthi interdiction, China-watching from the other side of the Gulf, counter-piracy that can slide into counter-everything, and a habit of talking to the man who controls the runway instead of the man who holds the flag in Mogadishu. A deal signed in Bosaso without the federal government is a statement about where power actually lives. It will deepen the fracture between the center and the coasts. It will also make those coasts harder to ignore.

About 15 years ago, I personally taught Kırmanckî courses at universities. I did so with the support of both the university and Kurdish friends who spoke Kurmanji and Sorani. In fact, their signatures were instrumental in securing the classroom and financial resources I needed in order to teach.

Moreover, Kurds whose mother tongue was not Kırmanckî also attended my course. Their aim was to learn the language and contribute to keeping it alive.

So who actually tried to sabotage my work? On the one hand, there were Turkish fascists who accused me of “spreading PKK propaganda” simply because I was teaching Zazakî/Kırmanckî. On the other hand, there were fanatical “We are not Zaza” circles who attacked me because I had obtained the necessary space for my classes with the help of Kurdish friends.

Today, there are also dozens of Kurdish linguists and researchers working on Kırmanckî at various institutes in Germany. Some of them later moved on to universities in Dersim and continued their work there.

Even in Germany, there are several concrete examples showing that Kırmanckî/Zazakî is taught in university settings: the University of Hamburg is offering a Zazaki 1 course in the 2026/27 winter semester; LMU Munich offered “Northwestern Iranian: Zazaki 1” in the 2025/26 academic year; Goethe University Frankfurt previously offered a dedicated Zazaki I course, and today the Zazakî Institute continues to organize language courses on university premises; and the University of Bamberg has also organized a Zazakî language course as part of its Kurdish Language Autumn School.

As I have seen from my own experience, a significant part of this work in Germany is not sustained by large budgets at all, but by Kurdish volunteers who invest their own time, effort, and even money out of their own pockets. There is also a very simple practical problem: the number of people in Germany who speak Kırmanckî fluently is limited, and the number of people who not only speak the language but also know its grammar, can prepare teaching materials, and are qualified to teach it at university level is even smaller.

Therefore, explaining the absence of Kırmanckî courses at a few universities by claiming that “Kurds are suppressing this language” simply does not correspond to reality. What is actually remarkable is that, despite such limited human and financial resources, Kırmanckî courses, research, and voluntary initiatives are still continuing in Germany.

text:
President Trump doubled down Sunday in Ireland that the United States can afford his $5,000 payout promise. Per Reuters from Doonbeg: "I don't know but it's easy if the Republicans win. $5,000 to all adults in the country and we can easily handle that because we're taking in so much money." Clash Report and other feeds also carried a 100% certainty line from the Ireland trip. Treat both as claims, not appropriations.

That is a political promise, not a funded program.

What the Dallas pitch actually said (Sept 9-10 midterm convention): if Republicans keep the House and the Senate, he would issue a $5,000 dividend to every adult U.S. citizen. He branded it the Trump dividend and said the money must be spent in the United States. He offered few mechanics.

Who gets it is already contested inside the same news cycle. The convention language was "every adult citizen." Vice President JD Vance later soft-pedaled toward American workers / the middle class and floated excluding wealthy households, which would shrink the sticker cost and rewrite the eligibility rules. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said it would not come from "taxpayer money," while other officials have pointed at tariffs, "market access" fees, or a reconciliation path. Those stories do not yet agree.

Price tag if Congress really authorized broad adult payouts: on the order of $1.2 trillion to $1.3 trillion plus interest, per Reuters and other desks. Congress controls the purse. A Senate filibuster still sits in the way under current rules. Senator Bernie Moreno has talked about legislation after the election. Prior Trump-era "dividends" (tariff rebate, DOGE savings share) never materialized as advertised.

Republican skepticism already exists: Rep. David Schweikert told Reuters he would fight it as inflationary and fiscally damaging. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis argued for tax cuts over borrowed cash floods. Democrats mocked the midterms-for-checks framing.

ZB30's board note: "100%" is a claim. Eligibility, funding, and timing are not locked. The operator question stands: who gets it, and is it really everyone?

House Speaker Mike Johnson said Sunday Congress would have to work the details and that the devil is in those details (CNN / NBC).

text:
For six years an old woman in Mississippi washed my shirts by hand, and I spent all six of them trying to make her charge me more.

She boiled the water in a black iron pot in the yard. She owned a machine. She used the machine for towels. She said it doesn't get the collars.

I offered to pay double. She said, "That's the price."

So I left extra money folded under the ticket.

The following week my shirts came back pressed, on hangers, and the extra money was folded flat inside the breast pocket of the top one.

I tried again with a different amount. Same pocket.

I concluded that the town was underpaying her and had never noticed, and I went and spoke to two of her other customers about it, in the manner of a man organizing a rebellion.

They had noticed. They had been trying for years. One of them had been trying since the sixties.

I was the last person on that street to understand anything at all.

She started at eight years old, working beside her mother and her grandmother and her aunt. She left school in the sixth grade when the aunt got sick and needed somebody, and she never went back, and she washed and ironed other people's clothes for over seventy years, paid in coins and small bills, until the arthritis in her hands stopped her at eighty six.

Then the bank told the town what was in there. Two hundred and eighty thousand dollars.

She kept enough to live on. She gave one hundred and fifty thousand to the university down the road, for students who could not otherwise go, and she did it while she was alive, so she could watch it happen.

Somebody asked her why that school.

She said, "Because it's here. It's close."

Somebody else asked why she lived with nothing while giving it away.

She said, "I am spending the money on myself."

Six hundred people in that town put money in on top of hers. The fund passed a million dollars. Twenty students a year.

The first one was an eighteen year old girl who started driving her to the store on errands. When the cancer came, she said the only thing she wanted was to see that girl graduate.

The girl graduated in May.

She died in September.

They are called McCarty Scholars. She never went to the seventh grade.

text:
Quick story time.

It took me FOREVER to get my first job in crypto.

It was 2023 and I already had 8+ years experience in mainstream marketing including working as a copywriter for a business that spent $10M on Facebook ads per year.

And yet - I was no one in crypto.

And blockchain seemed very technical and confusing.

But I liked the culture.

And I loved that the people working in crypto seemed to be:

A) genius but socially awkward
B) ADHD/ autistic spectrum 
C) doing their own thing away from the system 

So I was super determined to get involved.

I even remember applying for unpaid internships even though I was insanely overqualified.

(Funny that 2 years later, I’d be sitting at an invite-only dinner in Cannes across from the person that rejected me for an unpaid internship and they’d be asking me for media tips lol)

Anyway.

I wanted a job, fast.

And I knew that learning about coding from zero and becoming a dev would take ages.

Instead, I decided to do 2 things I had control over:

1) lead with the skills I had that crypto-native people didn’t seem to have 

2) become as visible as possible by joining discords, communities, and posting here

And damn it, it worked.

I joined the @shefiorg course around September 2023.

I posted about the things I was learning to 0 followers, then 10 followers, then 100 followers…

Then, I started going to small Ethereum events around Europe.

I paid for travel and hotels out of my own pocket with the money I was making from my coaching business on instagram.

Then, in July 2024, I applied for a job and FINALLY got a response.

That came after sending idk how many hundreds of applications.

I saw the job on the @BoysClubWorld discord.

My instinct was correct - this job required PR, media, and writing skills.

I had all of that.

And by July, I had a decent knowledge of the crypto space (mostly the culture but some tech, too).

I got the job.

It was my first real crypto job with a good paycheck.

10 months later, I got an offer from Cointelegraph.

I started producing media content on @gazza_jenks’s team.

That’s when the cool experiences started coming - free tickets to the F1, super yachts, a reception at Napoleon’s townhouse in Paris, etc.

Ultimately, I got my job at WalletConnect where in the last nearly 2 years I’ve gotten a lot more technical.

Another funny thing happened during this whole time -

Crypto and mainstream tech started intertwining.

If you’re a mainstream marketer pivoting to crypto now, you’d be in a lot more demand than I was in 2023 because now everyone wants to get out of the crypto bubble and reach more people.

Anyway, sharing this because I saw someone post about internship roles.

If I had a chance to travel back to 2023, I would do it all again.

I love working in crypto.

Hope reading this inspires you somehow.

As always - AMA

text:
Although Donald Trump's comments on Irish unity this weekend may have come as a surprise (and as an unpleasant shock to certain corners of unionism), one must consider what sort of united Ireland that Trump and his ilk would actually approve of. Regardless of their view, we must strive to build a 32-county socialist republic for the Irish working class.

Trump is a representative of the American capitalist class. Their ideal Ireland is a subservient one, where the corporate tax rate is so low that it can be exploited by multinational corporations such as Apple and Google, where our neutrality is done away with in favour of bulking up NATO's war efforts, and where we ultimately take our place as yet another suck-up state of questionable sovereignty in the American-led world order.

As is presently clear in the twenty-six counties, this set-up is not one that benefits the Irish people. The state, thanks to successive complicit Fianna Fáil and Fine Gael comprador regimes, might be a great little place to do business in, but not for working people to live in. Prioritising the wants of the international capitalist class has kept workers low down in the pecking order. While the multinational corporations get low taxes, the rest of us get crises of housing, healthcare, and cost-of-living.

Such a set-up, or indeed the extension of its jurisdiction, is not the end goal for those of us who wish to see a truly independent, united, and prosperous Ireland.

In his presidential address to the 1968 Ard Fheis, Tomás Mac Giolla stated that “it must be made clear that republicans do not ask the people of the six counties to come into the existing twenty-six-county state. We would not wish that fate on anyone”. Instead, Mac Giolla said that republicans ask the people of Ireland to join together in order to abolish both states, which serve the interests of imperialism, and to establish “a Democratic Socialist Republic for the whole island in which the workers who create the wealth decide how and where it is used”.

In Farmleigh House, Trump described Micheál Martin as “the right man to get [Irish unity] moving”. The reality, however, is that the Taoiseach and this government have made little effort to plan for the prospect of Irish unity. A Citizen's Assembly, for example, has yet to be called to attempt to resolve discrepancies between the two jurisdictions or to address broader political concerns that people might have.

A united Ireland offers the opportunity to build a state that is better than either of the two jurisdictions that exist at present, and now is the time to plan for it. For socialist republicans, this must mean pushing the interests of the Irish working class to the forefront of the debate, regardless of how any American president might view it, while still keeping our eyes on the ultimate prize of a 32-county socialist republic.

text:
Will Ireland be the trail blazer for collapse of the secular priesthood & diocesan system? This is an extraordinary article about the rapidly approaching crisis in the Irish Church. Priests in their seventies are carrying workloads which would exhaust men decades younger. Dioceses are contemplating a future in which priests may no longer be available for every funeral, baptism or wedding. One priest, overwhelmed by the sheer volume of work, proposed simply stopping Confirmations. But there is a danger in discussing all this primarily as an administrative problem requiring “new models of ministry”. Ireland does not fundamentally have a clergy-distribution problem, it has a crisis of faith and thus there follows a crisis of vocations.

For generations Ireland produced enough priests not merely for itself but to send missionaries across the world. Something changed.

Of course parishes will have to reorganise and lay Catholics must assume the responsibilities proper to them. But no amount of restructuring can substitute for the priesthood. The priest is not simply the person currently performing a collection of tasks which can gradually be redistributed among everyone else. He offers the Holy Sacrifice of the Mass. He absolves sins. He anoints the dying. He acts in persona Christi.

It seems blindingly obvious that the question Ireland's bishops @CatholicBishops should be asking is not simply, “How do we manage with fewer priests?” It is: why are so few of our sons becoming priests & what must we do to recover a Catholic culture in which they can hear the call? I can tell them the answer: Clear doctrinal teaching & reverent liturgy produces vocations. The end. Relativism & chasing the secular zeitgeist destroys vocations.

Nine men are being ordained for Irish dioceses this year, up from six last year, that is a small increase, but it matters. The answer to a shortage of priests cannot ultimately be learning how to live without priests. It must include praying, teaching and working for more of them. https://t.co/3acl3pucGs

He didn’t hedge. “𝘐 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘬 𝘪𝘵’𝘴 𝘵𝘦𝘳𝘳𝘪𝘣𝘭𝘦. 𝘐𝘵’𝘴 𝘯𝘰𝘵 𝘢 𝘱𝘭𝘢𝘤𝘦 𝘵𝘰 𝘣𝘦 𝘭𝘢𝘶𝘨𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘨, 𝘦𝘴𝘱𝘦𝘤𝘪𝘢𝘭𝘭𝘺 𝘪𝘯 𝘵𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘤𝘢𝘴𝘦.” Asked to elaborate, Trump kept it simple: “𝘐 𝘵𝘩𝘰𝘶𝘨𝘩𝘵 𝘪𝘵 𝘸𝘢𝘴 𝘵𝘦𝘳𝘳𝘪𝘣𝘭𝘦. 𝘛𝘩𝘦 𝘧𝘢𝘤𝘵 𝘵𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘺 𝘸𝘦𝘳𝘦 𝘭𝘢𝘶𝘨𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘵𝘰𝘨𝘦𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘳 𝘢𝘵 𝘢 𝘷𝘦𝘳𝘺 𝘪𝘮𝘱𝘰𝘳𝘵𝘢𝘯𝘵 𝘱𝘢𝘳𝘵 𝘰𝘧 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘤𝘦𝘳𝘦𝘮𝘰𝘯𝘺 𝘸𝘢𝘴 𝘪𝘯𝘢𝘱𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘱𝘳𝘪𝘢𝘵𝘦.”

𝐏𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐓𝐫𝐮𝐦𝐩 𝐡𝐚𝐬 𝐝𝐞𝐬𝐜𝐫𝐢𝐛𝐞𝐝 𝐕𝐞𝐧𝐞𝐳𝐮𝐞𝐥𝐚𝐧𝐬 𝐚𝐬 “𝐡𝐚𝐩𝐩𝐲.” 𝐀𝐦𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐚’𝐬 𝐨𝐰𝐧 𝐟𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐥𝐚𝐧𝐠𝐮𝐚𝐠𝐞 𝐨𝐟𝐟𝐞𝐫𝐬 𝐚 𝐦𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐩𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐢𝐬𝐞 𝐦𝐞𝐚𝐬𝐮𝐫𝐞.

By Elizabeth Sánchez Vegas

President Donald Trump has used the word happy to describe Venezuelans, and rather than dispute the word with the familiar catalogue of everything my country has endured, I would rather examine it through one of the most beautiful and demanding ideas the United States has ever given to political thought: “Life, Liberty and the pursuit of Happiness.”

We tend to notice Happiness, naturally, but perhaps the truly remarkable word in that sentence is pursuit, because Thomas Jefferson did not write that government should make people happy, nor that it could guarantee happiness to them; he wrote something far more sophisticated, which is that human beings possess the right to go in search of it according to their own conscience, ambitions, affections, mistakes and understanding of what makes a life worth living.

Seen from that perspective, Mr. President, happy may not yet be the right word for Venezuelans.

The more revealing question is not whether Venezuelans smile, celebrate, go to restaurants, open businesses or feel genuine relief when circumstances begin to change, but whether we have fully recovered the condition that allows happiness to become something more than a fortunate moment or a private act of resistance: the freedom to pursue it.

Venezuelans are particularly easy to misread from the outside because we have developed an extraordinary ability to produce joy in circumstances that should have extinguished it; we have celebrated birthdays with half the family appearing on a telephone screen from several countries, told jokes during blackouts, made music out of uncertainty and walked away from airport departures with tears still on our faces and enough humor left to comfort whoever was crying beside us. Our capacity for joy is real, but it should never be mistaken for evidence that everything is well, because very often it has been our way of refusing to allow misfortune to occupy every room of our lives.

That is why the distinction contained in pursuit matters so much. Happiness is deeply personal, but the possibility of pursuing it depends on public conditions: on being able to choose where to live without departure becoming an escape, to work and make plans without every decision being hostage to political uncertainty, to speak without first calculating who might be listening, to return home without wondering whether one is wagering the future, and above all, to vote freely in genuine elections, choose those who govern, and know that the will expressed at the ballot box will be respected.

This is where the language of 1776 becomes unexpectedly relevant to Venezuela today, because our country may produce more oil, attract investment, reopen businesses, rebuild infrastructure and begin to show unmistakable signs of economic recovery, all of which would be welcome and necessary, while still leaving unanswered the deeper question. An economy can recover before a republic does, and a country can begin to prosper before its citizens have fully recovered sovereignty over their own destiny.

This does not mean that hope, relief, or optimism are somehow false. On the contrary, they may be among the most precious things Venezuelans possess at this moment, but hope contains its own subtle admission: we experience it precisely because we can see something ahead that we have not yet completely reached, because the door appears capable of opening even though we have not yet crossed the threshold.

The genius of the pursuit of Happiness is that it understands a limit that governments too often forget. The state cannot manufacture happiness and should be deeply suspicious of any government that claims it can; what a free society can do is refrain from closing the road toward it, from deciding on behalf of its citizens what they may aspire to become, from turning existence into a sequence of permissions granted from above, or from appropriating that intimate territory in which every person determines what kind of life he or she wishes to build.

Perhaps this is the fairest way to explain Venezuela to President Trump without denying progress, dismissing opportunity, or reducing our country once again to a story told exclusively through suffering. Venezuelans do not need anyone outside Venezuela to determine whether we are happy, and we certainly do not need anyone to make us happy; what we need is the full restoration of our ability to pursue whatever each of us understands happiness to mean, whether that is a reunited family, a profession, a business, a home, a faith, an idea, the return after years abroad, or simply the extraordinary peace of knowing that the future belongs to us again.

One day, Mr. President, you may say that Venezuelans are happy and be entirely right, but by then the statement itself may no longer matter very much, because something more consequential will have happened: Venezuelans will once again possess the freedom to decide what happiness means and to pursue it on their own terms.

After all, happiness was always ours to define; what politics owes us is the pursuit.

Trump’s Top 25 Achievements, if MSM made you forget with PsyOp:

1. He made the border a real border again.
In a matter of months, Trump reduced illegal border crossings to their lowest level in half a century. Catch-and-release is finished. The wall is going up and even being expanded, “Remain in Mexico” is back, and the Administration reduced releases into the country by an incredible 99.9 percent.

2. He reversed mass migration.
America recorded negative net migration in 2025 for the first time in at least half a century. So far, nearly 3 million illegal aliens have left the country, whether voluntarily or involuntarily: more than 675,000 forcibly deported and the rest “self-deported.”

Many of those self-deportations were facilitated by the President’s innovative program to offer plane tickets and cash bonuses for illegals to leave, not only incentivizing good behavior but significantly reducing the cost of deportations. Citizenship and the law actually mean something again.

3. He signed the Laken Riley Act and required detention of criminal illegal aliens.
Named for an innocent girl murdered by an illegal alien, the Laken Riley Act requires federal authorities to detain illegals arrested for theft, burglary, shoplifting, assaulting police, or any crime causing death or serious injury. It also lets states sue officials who refuse to enforce it.

Laken Riley should still be alive. This law will prevent tragedies like hers.

4. History’s biggest drop in violent crime, and the lowest violent crime rate in 126 years.
According to FBI data, violent crime in America dropped an incredible 9.7 percent in 2025, the largest one-year decline in history. Murder fell 18.1 percent, robbery fell 18.5 percent. And America’s violent crime rate is its lowest since 1900.

This is what happens when you put the National Guard on the streets in crime-ridden blue cities: fewer victims, safer streets, and better futures for America’s poorest.

Trump Launched an American Industrial Supercycle

5. He made the 2017 tax cuts permanent…and better.
The One Big Beautiful Bill locked in the largest tax cut in modern history, including the doubled standard deduction, the expanded Child Tax Credit, and 100 percent expensing for factories and equipment. It also delivered No Tax on Tips, No Tax on Overtime, an abolition of most taxes on Social Security benefits, and major relief for seniors.

Every Democrat voted no. With the 2017 act set to expire in December 2025, that would have resulted in the largest tax hike in American history.

6. He repealed 129 regulations for every new one.
In fiscal 2025, federal agencies finalized 646 deregulatory actions and just five regulatory actions: 129-to-1, and in nearly every case, the “one” was to repeal the others! OIRA says the savings exceeded those of Trump’s entire first term. That is more freedom, lower costs, and less bureaucratic sabotage.

Of these, the crown jewel was the repeal of Obama’s 2009 “Endangerment Finding”, the legal foundation for the Green New Scam’s vehicle mandates. EPA calls it the largest deregulatory action in American history and estimates that by itself, it will save Americans more than $1.3 trillion. Trump also killed the federal EV mandate, restored Americans’ freedom to buy the cars and trucks they actually want, and even eliminated the incentives behind the almost universally hated start-stop button.

7. He secured $18 trillion in announced investment commitments.
That’s nearly two-thirds the size of the entire American economy, building American factories, chip plants, data centers, energy projects, steel mills, shipyards, and supply chains employing American workers. Apple, Meta, NVIDIA, Micron, Hyundai, U.S. Steel, Ford, Taiwan Semiconductor, and many corporations and sovereign wealth funds are betting big on Trump’s America.

No President has ever done anything remotely like it. And it’s just getting started.

8. He made “reshoring” and “reindustrialization” real, not a slogan.
Ford is moving Lincoln production out of China. Toyota is shifting Tacoma production from Mexico to Texas. GM, Honda, Mercedes-Benz, Stellantis, and others are expanding U.S. production. The capital equipment pouring into the country is the machinery that’s building the growing boom.

9. He replaced lopsided trade deals with balanced, reciprocal trade.
Trump used tariffs as leverage to reverse 80 years of lopsided trade deals that favored everyone but America, and to win new or improved agreements with trading partners accounting for more than half of global GDP. Those agreements open foreign markets, attack non-tariff barriers, defend strategic industries, and make it more profitable to build in America than to export American jobs.

10. He shifted global energy dominance from the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of America.
Once the world’s largest energy importer — “exporting” $700 billion a year to our enemies, America now outproduces Saudi Arabia and Russia combined. The U.S. is also setting new records in oil, natural gas, and LNG exports, becoming the first country ever to export more than 100 million metric tons of LNG in a year.

Trump also opened land, accelerated permits, expanded pipelines and export terminals, and made American energy a tool for prosperity and peace.

11. After four decades of nuclear paralysis, Trump brought five new reactors online in a single year.
For more than 40 years, not one new privately developed non-light-water reactor reached criticality in America. Trump ordered at least three by July 4, 2026. DOE delivered four by the deadline, then a fifth just one month later.

Decades of zero. One Trump summer: five. That is a genuine nuclear renaissance.

Trump Made Elections Matter Again

12. He broke the Deep State’s power to defy the elected branches.
In Trump v. Slaughter, the Supreme Court ruled for the first time in 90 years that Article 2, Section 1 is still part of the Constitution: the President may fire subordinate officials in the executive branch, overturning the 1935 precedent that insulated “independent” agencies from voters’ control.

Ever wonder why elections often seem to change nothing? How about one President and 5,000 political appointees vs. 2.8 million unfireable, unaccountable bureaucrats? THAT is the “Deep State”.

Trump then made that victory real. For the first time in a century, all policy-making bureaucrats can now be fired for misconduct, incompetence, or defying lawful directives. The permanent bureaucracy no longer gets to veto the voters.

13. He ended nationwide injunction abuse.
In Trump v. CASA, the Supreme Court sharply limited nationwide injunctions. A single, local, district judge should not be able to block a national policy for everyone, everywhere; and yet that’s exactly what they’ve done, nonstop, ever since Trump (and only Trump) took office in 2017.

In restricting that unconstitutional power, the Court kneecapped the Black Robe Bureaucracy’s favorite tool of unlawful judicial supremacy.

14. He shut down USAID as a left-wing slush fund and shadow government.
USAID had become a taxpayer-funded machine for exporting abortion, gender ideology, censorship, and left-wing politics. It had a bigger budget than the CIA and the State Department combined, absolutely no accountability whatsoever, and a penchant for overthrowing governments.

Trump terminated it, completely and moved real humanitarian aid under the State Department. Immediately, seven socialist Latin American governments lost re-election. Coincidence?

15. He shrank Federal employment to its lowest level in 60 years.
From a high under Biden, the federal workforce is now its smallest since 1966. Workforce reductions, agency closures, and spending cancellations mean fewer bureaucrats paid to resist the voters.

What’s more, when Biden left office, 94 percent of federal employees “worked” from home. The Trump administration cracked down: as Elon Musk put it, “you can work from the office or you can pretend to work somewhere else.”

16. He expelled DEI from the federal government.
Trump eliminated federal DEI offices and barred race- and sex-based preferences across the executive branch. Government hiring and contracting are returning to merit and equality under the law, ending the grotesque Democrat idea that “fighting discrimination” requires the federal government to discriminate.

He Defended Faith and Family

17. He delivered sweeping pro-life reform.
In his first term, Trump delivered the judges that overturned the abominable Roe v. Wade. Hardly anyone believed it could be done, or that Trump would do it. But he did, and a half-century nightmare finally ended.

Since returning to office, Trump has enforced the Hyde Amendment prohibiting the use of federal funds to pay for abortions, reinstated and expanded the Mexico City Policy prohibiting federal funding of foreign abortions, ended federal fetal-tissue research, strengthened conscience protections, protected Medicaid from funding large abortion providers, and pardoned 23 pro-life activists prosecuted by Biden’s weaponized Justice Department.

He’s also done everything within the Executive Branch’s power to defund Planned Parenthood. It would be nice if Congress did likewise.

No President has ever done more to protect life. No one.

18. He got men out of women’s sports, and restored biological reality to federal policy.
The United States government once again officially recognizes two sexes: male and female. Trump ended federal support for the chemical and surgical gender mutilation of children, stopped taxpayer funding of such irreversible abominations, and forced more than three dozen health systems to end or suspend their programs as well.

Trump also enforced Title IX as written: women and girls deserve their own teams, trophies, scholarships, and locker rooms. The NCAA and other athletic organizations changed their rules in response. After years of Democrats doing everything they could to destroy women’s sports and ruin girls’ lives, Trump’s administration protects women and girls again.

19. He enacted America’s first nationwide school-choice program and launched Trump Accounts.
As part of the President’s One Big Beautiful Bill, Trump enacted America’s first-ever nationwide school choice program. The new Education Freedom Tax Credit helps fund scholarships for tuition, books, and other educational costs.

That’s on top of the new Trump Accounts, which give every child a tax-advantaged stake in America’s future, including a $1,000 federal seed for eligible newborns. Parents gain power. Bureaucracies lose it. And children learn first-hand about free markets and future orientation.

20. He targeted anti-Christian bias and discrimination.
Trump created the White House Faith Office, Religious Liberty Commission, and Task Force to Eradicate Anti-Christian Bias. He restored conscience protections and made clear that Christians do not surrender their First Amendment rights merely by entering public life.

He Restored Peace Through Strength and Put America First

21. He forced NATO to stop freeloading and increase defense spending by 250 percent.
For decades, wealthy European governments underfunded their militaries, effectively sending America the bill and using American taxpayers to subsidize their bloated welfare states. Trump forced NATO to replace its old two-percent-of-GDP spending target with an enormous five percent by 2035.

Allied spending is rising, American defense orders are soaring, and Europe is becoming a partner instead of a dependent.

22. He drove China out of the Caribbean.
China spent years building strategic beachheads at both ends of the Panama Canal, in Cuba, and in Maduro’s Venezuela. Trump forced Panama out of Belt and Road, expanded American security access around the Canal, and captured Maduro, who now sits in a New York jail cell awaiting trial.

Beijing’s planned encirclement of the United States collapsed. The Monroe Doctrine is back. Call it the Donroe Doctrine.

23. He brokered eight peace deals in just eight months.
In eight months, Trump brokered peace in eight conflicts spanning four continents, including wars that had gone on for as much as 40 years. It’s a record unmatched by any other President.

24. He launched and funded Golden Dome, the first-ever true missile defense for the U.S. population.
Ronald Reagan dreamed of making nuclear missiles obsolete through his Strategic Defense Initiative. Today, Trump is actually building it: a layered homeland shield with space-based sensors and interceptors, conventional defenses, and new technologies including microwave systems to destroy drone swarms and directed-energy weapons (yes, lasers) that can replace an $11 million missile with $2 of electricity.

Congress has funded the initial $25 billion, with far more on the way once it passes the NDAA this fall. Better a shield than a sword.

25. He restored the warrior ethos, and reversed the recruiting crisis.
After years of missed targets under Biden, every active military component met or exceeded its 2025 recruiting goal. Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth refocused the newly renamed Department of War on actually winning wars, while pouring resources into shipbuilding, munitions, drones, missile defense, and America’s atrophied industrial base.

Day trip out of Lafayette down 167 to Abbeville. Abbeville will likely experience more visible change in the next 3-5 years than any other city in Louisiana as a result of the influx of initial investment funds. Tour Abbeville intensely.

As you visit these smaller hamlets and municipalities in the deeper South and Southwest of Louisiana, drive through and stop in the downtown areas, get out and walk, plan your bathroom stops in the towns and hamlets at a coffee shop or an eatery and sit and get the flavors.

Listen for the different dialects of Cajun French, you may hear them when you are in the right places.

Wear your Starbase gear, folks will come to you. Be deft and gentle. Listen, let them practice on you, they are just as curious about what is going to happen as are all of us.

From Abbeville, drive West to Kaplan along Hwy 14.
From Kaplan continue West on 14 to Gueydan.
From Gueydan follow 14 West and then North to Lake Arthur, there is an excellent, well run, nice restaurant on the Lake in Lake Arthur, it is the pride of that city and the primary meeting place for many leaders in the Community.

From Lake Arthur, catch Hwy 26 North to Jennings. Tour downtown Jennings, walk, sit in Founder's Park, visit the I-10 "gator park".

From Jennings travel East on I-10 to Crowley, tour the older sections of town, amazing residential, historical architecture. Great AirBnB's in that town.

The town of Scott is important, it is a demarking of the old villages of this area and the great, modern "metropolis" of Lafayette, the difference is stark.

Take a day trip down old Hwy 90, now there are the real memories that were left behind by the creation of I-10, and later I-49. Stop in Mermentau, listen to the river. And then Estherwood as you travel to Crowley.

Instead of I-10 from Jennings traveling East back to Lafayette, take Hwy 90 out of Jennings to Crowley, and then get back onto I-10 to Scott.

text:
The Atlanta History Files...A group for history and great memories
Lisa Land Cooper - Author and Historian 
·
For generations of Atlantans, a visit to Grant Park often meant more than the zoo. It could also mean stepping inside the Cyclorama Building and finding yourself surrounded by the Battle of Atlanta.
This 1937 Curt Teich linen postcard offered visitors a souvenir view of The Battle of Atlanta, the enormous panoramic painting depicting the fighting of July 22, 1864.
The painting itself was created in Milwaukee by 17 German artists working for the American Panorama Company. Completed in 1886 — more than twenty years after the battle — it was designed as an immersive experience, almost a 19th-century version of IMAX or virtual reality. The viewer stood in the middle while the enormous painting completely surrounded them.
The Cyclorama arrived in Atlanta in 1892 and eventually became a permanent Grant Park attraction. In 1921 it was installed in the large purpose-built Cyclorama structure many Atlantans still remember.
What makes this 1937 postcard especially interesting is what had happened only shortly before it was printed.
Between 1934 and 1936, artists working with funding from the Works Progress Administration created a three-dimensional foreground for the painting. Plaster soldiers, artillery, railroad track, shrubbery and Georgia red clay were placed between the visitor and the painted canvas, helping the real foreground blend almost seamlessly into the painted battlefield. The completed diorama included 128 soldier figures.
The red brick building dominating this postcard view represents the Troup Hurt House, around which some of the fiercest fighting depicted in the Cyclorama takes place. Interestingly, historians have noted that the artists positioned the house too close to the railroad in the painting — one of several instances where dramatic effect won out over precise geography.
There is even a little clue confirming the postcard's date. At the lower right is the Curt Teich production number beginning “7A-H.” According to the company's dating system preserved by the Newberry Library, the “7A” series was produced in 1937, and the “H” identified Teich's full-color Art Colortone process on linen-finish stock. So the advertised 1937 date checks out very nicely.
The Cyclorama remained in Grant Park until the attraction closed in 2015. The painting was moved to the Atlanta History Center in 2017, underwent an extensive restoration, and reopened there in 2019 as Cyclorama: The Big Picture.
And what became of the old Cyclorama Building? The 1921 structure was preserved and incorporated into Zoo Atlanta. It reopened in 2020 as Savanna Hall, an event facility overlooking the zoo's African Savanna.

text:
Sudan’s Army Chief Says Satellite Evidence Links Ethiopian Airports to Rapid Support Militia Drone Attacks 

In a wide-ranging interview, Yasser al-Atta accused Ethiopia of exploiting Sudan’s war to threaten Al-Fashaga and Blue Nile, declared Darfur the army’s next priority, addressed militia supply routes through Chad and Libya, welcomed an international investigation into allegations of chemical weapons use, proposed a prolonged political role for the military, discussed partnerships with Türkiye, Egypt and Russia, and revealed that his brother remains in militia detention: “He is no dearer or more worthy than Sudan’s young people.” 

Sudan’s army chief of staff and Sovereignty Council member, General Yasser al-Atta, says the military has obtained satellite images, intelligence and data recovered from downed drones that prove Ethiopian airports are being used to launch attacks by the UAE-backed Rapid Support Militia against Sudan.

Al-Atta made the claims during an extensive interview in Khartoum with journalist Samar Ibrahim for the Egyptian newspaper Al-Shorouk. It was his first interview with an Egyptian newspaper since his appointment as army chief of staff in April.

The interview covered the war’s military trajectory, the escalating Blue Nile front, Ethiopia’s alleged role, militia supply routes through Chad and Libya, the future of the Rapid Support Militia, Sudan’s post-war political system, allegations of chemical weapons use, and relations with Egypt, Türkiye and Russia.

Al-Atta also spoke about his younger brother, who has been detained by the militia since the opening days of the war. He said he had refused an offer to exchange members of his family for four captured militia officers, declaring: “My brother is no dearer or more worthy than Sudan’s young people.”

Satellite images and intelligence concerning Ethiopian airports

Al-Atta said countries possessing satellite capabilities, along with UN organisations operating in the region, were aware of the activity taking place inside Ethiopia.

“We obtained satellite images and intelligence proving that Asosa Airport and a number of other Ethiopian airports have been used to launch Rapid Support Militia drones towards Sudanese territory,” he said.

He added that the Sudanese military had shot down and examined several drones. According to Al-Atta, devices recovered from the aircraft revealed their launch locations and other operational information.

Sudan also contacted the countries that manufactured the aircraft, he said, and received confirmation that regional armies allied with Ethiopia and the Rapid Support Militia had purchased the systems.

Al-Atta said the military possessed further intelligence that could not be disclosed at present because of its sensitive nature.

Al-Atta says Ethiopia is exploiting Sudan’s war

The chief of staff presented a grave assessment of Ethiopia’s objectives along the border. He said Addis Ababa was seeking to exploit Sudan’s war to seize fertile agricultural territory around Al-Fashaga, Jebel Halawa, Geissan, Kurmuk and Damazin.

Al-Fashaga is a fertile border region claimed by both Sudan and Ethiopia. Disputes over territorial control and border demarcation have periodically generated tensions and armed confrontations between the two countries.

Al-Atta linked the opening of the Blue Nile front to an effort to obstruct the Sudanese army’s advance towards Darfur. He said the Rapid Support Militia had opened the front to draw Sudanese forces away from the principal cities of Darfur.

He maintained that the army could conduct operations across several fronts simultaneously and that the fighting in Blue Nile would not derail its westward advance.

Al-Atta also suggested that Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed could use control of Al-Fashaga to gain support from Ethiopia’s Amhara population, amid domestic tensions and the longstanding border dispute with Sudan.

He further claimed that controlling Al-Fashaga and Damazin could support a broader Ethiopian ambition to reach the Red Sea by seizing the Eritrean port of Assab with assistance from allied regional states.

These claims concerning Ethiopian plans for Al-Fashaga, Damazin and Assab represent Al-Atta’s assessment. The interview did not include documentary material enabling independent verification of its details.

Mounting evidence surrounding Asosa and the UAE’s role

Al-Atta’s statements come amid a growing body of reporting that has placed Ethiopia within the regional support network sustaining the Rapid Support Militia.

In February 2026, Reuters published an investigation based on 15 sources, satellite imagery and security documents. It reported the existence of a secret camp in Ethiopia’s Benishangul-Gumuz region, near the Sudanese border, where thousands of fighters were being trained for the militia.

Sources told Reuters that the UAE had financed the camp and provided military trainers, equipment and logistical support. The investigation also identified newly constructed drone infrastructure at Asosa Airport, which sources described as an important hub for cross-border supply operations supporting the militia. Reuters investigation

In August, Yale University’s Humanitarian Research Lab reported a major escalation in activity and military equipment at an Ethiopian National Defence Force base in Asosa. Its satellite analysis found activity consistent with preparations to provide military support to the Rapid Support Militia inside Sudan. Yale Humanitarian Research Lab

The Sudanese army said in May that data recovered from a drone shot down in March connected its route to Ethiopia’s Bahir Dar Airport. The military made the claim while alleging Ethiopian and Emirati involvement in drone attacks against Khartoum and other Sudanese cities.

Ethiopia and the UAE have denied involvement. Reuters

Taken together, the reported training camps, drone facilities, airports, satellite imagery and data recovered from downed aircraft place Ethiopia’s potential role within a wider operational structure capable of providing the militia with territory, aviation infrastructure and logistical support for attacks inside Sudan.

Darfur is the army’s priority

Discussing the military situation, Al-Atta identified El Fasher, Nyala, El Geneina, El Daein and Zalingei as the army’s principal objectives in Darfur. He said forces were preparing to advance towards the region from several directions.

He claimed the army had made significant progress in Kordofan, reopened routes towards Dilling and Kadugli, secured the road connecting Kosti, El Obeid and Al-Rahad, and deployed additional forces westward in preparation for the Darfur campaign.

Al-Atta said the army would prevent Darfur’s separation and end the militia’s control over the region. His statements represent the military leadership’s assessment and expectations, and the timetable he presented could not be independently verified.

Warnings to Chad and Libya over militia supplies

Al-Atta also addressed the movement of weapons and military vehicles through Libya and Chad.

He claimed that between 250 and 300 militia combat vehicles had travelled from Libya and entered approximately 70 kilometres into Chadian territory before being destroyed near the Sudanese border.

Sudan had repeatedly warned officials in Chad and Libya to stop supporting the militia, he said, adding that the continued movement of armed supplies compelled the army to act against the convoys.

Al-Atta said a limited militia presence remained in the tri-border region connecting Sudan, Egypt and Libya, alongside vehicles belonging to Libya’s Subul al-Salam brigades. He alleged that some of these forces were involved in gold mining and securing the passage of supplies into Sudan.

“There will be no Rapid Support Militia again”

Al-Atta declared that the Rapid Support Militia had no military or political future in Sudan.

“There will be nothing called the Rapid Support Militia in the country again,” he said.

He also presented a vision for the military’s role after the war. Al-Atta said the army did not seek control of Sudan’s executive government, yet he argued that the commander-in-chief should remain head of state through the next three or four election cycles. Political parties winning parliamentary elections would form the government and exercise executive authority under this arrangement.

He justified the proposal by citing what he described as the weakness of Sudanese political parties and the foreign connections of some political leaders.

Al-Atta said senior military figures believed General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan should remain at the head of the state during the coming period, despite Burhan’s public rejection of campaigns calling for his presidential candidacy.

“We fear for our country and the possible collapse of the state, and we will compel him to assume power,” Al-Atta said.

He explained that the proposed period would allow existing parties to grow stronger and give Sudanese youth an opportunity to build new political organisations capable of governing the country.

His remarks outline a prolonged political role for the military extending across several elections. They are likely to become central to the debate over civilian government and the future relationship between Sudan’s armed forces and political institutions.

Al-Atta welcomes an international chemical weapons investigation

Al-Atta rejected allegations that the Sudanese army had used chemical weapons, describing them as a “political lie” and an instrument of pressure against Sudan.

He questioned the absence of the human and environmental consequences that would be expected from chemical weapons use, particularly given the proximity of the alleged attack sites to military positions and densely populated areas.

Al-Atta said Sudan would welcome an international investigation inside the country, expressing confidence that the army neither possessed nor used chemical weapons.

Russia, Türkiye and regional partnerships

Turning to foreign policy, Al-Atta said the agreement to establish a Russian naval base on Sudan’s Red Sea coast was currently stalled because Sudan lacked an elected parliament capable of ratifying it.

He said his recent visit to Türkiye included discussions on military training and economic and strategic partnerships, including the possibility of a mutual defence agreement.

Al-Atta also described a proposed regional alliance involving Türkiye, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and other pivotal states to protect the Gulf of Aden, the Bab al-Mandab Strait and the Red Sea.

He identified Egypt, Eritrea, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Türkiye and Algeria as friendly countries that had supported Sudan during a difficult period. He also referred to plans for expanded economic and military partnerships with Egypt and Saudi Arabia, including cooperation in Sudan’s reconstruction.

His brother remains detained by the militia in Nyala

Al-Atta revealed that the Rapid Support Militia detained his younger brother and four other members of his family after attacking their homes in Khartoum on the third day of the war.

He said his cousin, an army captain, died during detention. Four relatives, including his brother, remain imprisoned at the militia’s Dagris detention facility in Nyala, Darfur, according to Al-Atta.

The family receives occasional information about their condition, he said.

Around one month after their capture, a militia member contacted an intelligence officer stationed in the Al-Muhandiseen military area of Omdurman. The militia offered to release Al-Atta’s brother and the other detained relatives in exchange for four captured militia officers from the Mahariya clan.

Al-Atta said he refused to arrange a private exchange for his relatives. He demanded the release of all detained Sudanese army personnel in return for the four militia officers. The exchange never took place.

He claimed that the militia had detained 43,000 young men in Khartoum during the war.

“My brother is no dearer or more worthy than Sudan’s young people,” Al-Atta said.

text:
Is the universe a holographic projection?

In 1983, U.S. Army Lt. Col. Wayne M. McDonnell wrote a 29-page report titled Analysis and Assessment of Gateway Process. Declassified by the CIA in 2003, it examined the Monroe Institute’s Gateway Experience, an audio-based program for altering consciousness. The document later became a focal point for public interest in official discussion of a holographic universe.

The report appeared during the Cold War, when U.S. agencies studied whether mental techniques could support intelligence work. Related efforts included remote viewing later associated with Project Stargate. McDonnell was asked to assess Gateway’s mechanics and practicality. He used biomedical models from Itzhak Bentov, comparisons with hypnosis and meditation, and theoretical physics to describe how focused consciousness might operate beyond ordinary space and time.

Gateway training relied on Hemi-Sync: slightly different frequencies played in each ear to create binaural beats. The aim was to synchronize the brain’s hemispheres and increase the coherence of brainwave output. McDonnell wrote that this could move consciousness “outside the physical sphere so as to ultimately escape even the restrictions of time and space.” Participants reported out-of-body states and access to information not available through the ordinary senses.

The report’s most discussed section treats the universe as holographic. Energy in motion interacting with energy at rest produces interference patterns. Those patterns form a “universal hologram or Torus.” Because a hologram encodes the whole in every part, a sufficiently coherent mind might read information from any point in the pattern, including other times or dimensions. McDonnell described the brain as a binary system that projects its own three-dimensional hologram and can attune itself to the larger one through energy exchange. In this model, consciousness is organized by the brain rather than simply produced by it.

The language mixes established ideas with speculation. Holographic metaphors already appeared in the work of physicist David Bohm and neuroscientist Karl Pribram. Later physics, including the holographic principle linked to black-hole information and string theory, offered a more formal version of the claim that a higher-dimensional reality can be encoded on a lower-dimensional surface. The 1983 report predates the fullest mathematical statements of that principle and does not offer experimental proof. It is an attempt to give physical vocabulary to experiences reported by Gateway trainees.

McDonnell presented the material as a working model, not settled science. The document places hypnosis, biofeedback, quantum language, and spiritual terms side by side. It treats an “Absolute” rest-state energy as the ground of the active hologram. Out-of-body experience is recast as consciousness projecting into regions where ordinary Planck-scale limits no longer apply in the same way.

After declassification, the report circulated quietly until social media revived it in the 2020s. Some readers treat it as confirmation of mystical claims; others note its speculative leaps and the lack of controlled evidence that consciousness routinely transcends spacetime. The CIA’s interest was operational: whether such states could yield usable information. Public fascination is philosophical: whether an official document once took seriously the idea that reality is more like a projection than a solid container.

The Gateway report does not prove the universe is a hologram. It does show that, in the early 1980s, an Army officer writing for intelligence purposes found holographic language useful for organizing reports of altered consciousness. That mix of Cold War pragmatism and cosmological speculation is why the document still attracts readers more than forty years later.

🇷🇺 THE GERMAN PRECEDENT AFTER TOTAL DEFEAT 🇷🇺

U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent compared Ukraine to post-World War II Germany. After crushing military defeat, Germany returned to the international community. Ukrainians now have a similar chance, he said, while discussing talks between Moscow, Kiev and Washington.

Germany did not return through stubborn resistance or endless Western subsidies. It accepted occupation, denazification, demilitarization and the loss of territory. It abandoned the ideology that produced catastrophe. Only then did reconstruction and reintegration become possible. 🇷🇺

That historical path exists. Bessent is pointing at it. Kiev would be wise to study it instead of repeating slogans about “victory.”

🇷🇺 UKRAINE MUST FACE THE SAME REALITY 🇷🇺

Germany in 1945 was a destroyed, isolated state that had started a war of aggression and paid the price. Ukraine today finds itself in a comparable position after years of confrontation with Russia. The comparison is uncomfortable for Kiev’s supporters, yet it is accurate.

Return to the international community requires first ending the conflict on terms that reflect the actual military situation. Prolonging the fighting only increases destruction and delays any Marshall-style recovery. Germany understood this after 1945. Ukraine has not yet.

🇷🇺 TOUGHER CONDITIONS REFLECT THE BATTLEFIELD 🇷🇺

Reports that Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner brought even worse peace terms to Kiev than earlier offers should surprise no one. When one side is advancing and the other is exhausting its manpower and Western stockpiles, the price of settlement rises.

Russia has stated its core requirements clearly: neutrality, recognition of territorial realities, and removal of the extremist elements that fueled the conflict. These are not “worse” conditions invented in Washington. They are the logical outcome of the war Kiev chose to continue.

Germany accepted far harsher terms after 1945. It lost East Prussia, Silesia and other lands. It was occupied and re-educated. Yet it later prospered. The same sequence is available to Ukraine if it stops treating every concession as treason.

🇷🇺 A REALISTIC PATH INSTEAD OF ILLUSION 🇷🇺

Bessent’s remark is useful because it strips away propaganda. There is a known historical route from isolation and ruin back into normal international life. It begins with accepting defeat of the current course, not with more weapons deliveries or rhetorical defiance.

Germany’s postwar success came after it abandoned revanchism. Ukraine’s chance lies in the same direction: freeze the front, accept neutrality, and begin the long work of rebuilding without NATO fantasies. Moscow has repeatedly said it is ready for such an outcome.

Endless war benefits arms manufacturers and political careers in certain Western capitals. It does not benefit ordinary Ukrainians or Russians. The German example shows that a defeated state can recover dignity and prosperity once it stops fighting the inevitable.

🇷🇺 PEACE REQUIRES HONEST ACCOUNTING 🇷🇺

The United States itself imposed the postwar order on Germany. Now an American official is reminding Kiev that a similar accounting is possible. Whether Ukraine takes that path is its decision. History suggests the longer it delays, the harsher the eventual terms will become.

Germany chose reconstruction over revenge. That choice allowed it to rejoin the world. The same door stands open. 🇷🇺
